bank.q: What is a chemical reaction in which electrons are transferred from one reactant to another?
bank.why: Redox = transfer of electrons. In a non-redox reaction there is no NET electron transfer.

bank.q: A non-oxidation-reduction (non-redox) reaction is one in which...
bank.a: There is no net transfer of electrons between reactants
d: There is a net transfer of electrons between reactants
bank.why: Non-redox: no NET electron transfer, so no oxidation number changes.

bank.q: The memory aid OIL RIG stands for...
bank.a: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons)
d: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of protons)
Oxidation Is Lowering, Reduction Is Gaining (of oxidation number)
Oxidizer Is Lost, Reducer Is Gained (in the products)
bank.why: Oxidation is losing electrons (oxidation number goes up); reduction is gaining electrons (it goes down).

bank.q: In a redox reaction, the substance that is oxidized...
bank.a: Loses electrons and acts as the reducing agent
d: Gains electrons and acts as the oxidizing agent
Loses electrons and acts as the oxidizing agent
Gains electrons and acts as the reducing agent
bank.why: The substance oxidized gives its electrons away, so it is what reduces the other one: the reducing agent.

bank.q: In a redox reaction, the oxidizing agent is the substance that...
bank.why: The oxidizing agent takes electrons from the other reactant, so it is itself reduced.
bank.hint: Agents are named for what they do to the OTHER substance.

bank.q: An increase in an atom's oxidation number means the atom has...
bank.why: Losing negative electrons makes the oxidation number more positive. Gaining electrons lowers it.

bank.q: When chlorine (Cl₂) forms Cl⁻ ions, its oxidation number...
bank.a: Decreases from 0 to −1, so chlorine is reduced
d: Increases from 0 to +1, so chlorine is oxidized
Increases from −1 to 0, so chlorine is oxidized
Stays at 0, so it is not a redox change
bank.why: Each Cl gains an electron: 0 → −1. Gaining electrons is reduction.

bank.q: Which change is a reduction?
bank.why: Fe³⁺ gains an electron to become Fe²⁺: the oxidation number decreases. The others lose electrons.
bank.hint: Look for the oxidation number going down.

bank.q: Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). What happens to magnesium?
bank.a: It loses electrons and is oxidized (0 → +2)
d: It gains electrons and is reduced (0 → −2)
It acts as the oxidizing agent
bank.why: Mg goes from 0 to +2 in MgO, so it loses electrons; it is the reducing agent and O₂ is the oxidizing agent.

bank.q: In Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), which species is the oxidizing agent?
bank.why: Cu²⁺ gains 2 electrons (it is reduced), so it oxidizes zinc. Zinc is the reducing agent.

bank.q: In Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g), which is the reducing agent?
bank.why: Zinc goes from 0 to +2 (loses electrons), so it reduces the H⁺ of HCl to H₂. HCl is the oxidizing agent.

bank.q: In 2Fe³⁺(aq) + Sn²⁺(aq) → 2Fe²⁺(aq) + Sn⁴⁺(aq), which species is oxidized?
bank.why: Sn²⁺ → Sn⁴⁺ loses 2 electrons (oxidized). Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺ gains electrons (reduced).

bank.q: The charge an atom appears to have when the electrons in each of its bonds are assigned to the more electronegative atom is its...
bank.why: That is the slides' definition of oxidation number (oxidation state). Formal charge splits bonding electrons equally instead.

bank.q: Which statement about redox reactions is TRUE?
bank.a: A redox reaction always involves a change in oxidation numbers.
d: The oxidizing agent is the substance that gets oxidized.
An increase in oxidation number means electrons were gained.
In an electrochemical cell, oxidation occurs at the cathode.
bank.why: Redox always changes oxidation numbers. The oxidizing agent is reduced, an increase means electrons were LOST, and oxidation happens at the anode.
bank.hint: Three of these were false items on the past quiz.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: In an electrochemical cell, oxidation occurs at the cathode.
d: The substance that is oxidized loses electrons and acts as the reducing agent.
Oxidation and reduction always occur together.
Elements in their free, uncombined state have an oxidation number of zero.
bank.why: Oxidation occurs at the ANODE (reduction at the cathode). The other three are true.

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: Electrons lost in oxidation must equal electrons gained in reduction.
d: A non-redox reaction has a net transfer of electrons.
An element can be oxidized without anything else being reduced.
bank.why: Electrons are not created or destroyed, so the totals lost and gained must match; that is how redox equations are balanced.

bank.q: The oxidation number of an element in its free, uncombined state (Na, Mg, O₂, Cl₂) is...
d: Equal to the charge of its common ion
bank.why: Rule 1: an element in its elemental state has oxidation number 0.
bank.hint: No bonds to a different element.

bank.q: The oxidation number of a monatomic ion such as Mg²⁺ or Cl⁻ is...
bank.a: Equal to the charge of the ion
d: Equal to its number of valence electrons
bank.why: Rule 2: Mg²⁺ is +2 and Cl⁻ is −1.

bank.q: Oxygen is usually −2, but in hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) and the peroxide ion (O₂²⁻) it is...
bank.why: Rule 5: oxygen is −1 in peroxides. Check: 2(+1) + 2(−1) = 0 in H₂O₂.

bank.q: In most hydrogen-containing compounds, hydrogen has an oxidation number of...
bank.why: Rule 4: hydrogen is +1 in most compounds.

bank.q: In their compounds, Group 1A and Group 2A metals have oxidation numbers of...
bank.why: Rule 3: Group 1A = +1, Group 2A = +2.

bank.q: For a polyatomic ion, the sum of the oxidation numbers of all its atoms equals...
d: The number of atoms in the ion
The charge of the most electronegative atom
bank.why: Rule 7: compounds sum to 0; polyatomic ions sum to the ion's charge (e.g. −2 for CO₃²⁻).

bank.q: Which statement about oxidation numbers is FALSE?
bank.a: Oxygen has an oxidation number of −2 in every compound.
d: Elements in their free, uncombined state have an oxidation number of zero.
In a neutral compound, the oxidation numbers add up to zero.
In binary molecular compounds, the more electronegative element gets the negative oxidation number.
bank.why: Oxygen is −1 in peroxides such as H₂O₂, so 'every compound' is false. The other statements are rules from the slides.

bank.q: Which statement about oxidation numbers is TRUE?
bank.a: For polyatomic ions, the oxidation numbers add up to the net charge of the ion.
d: Hydrogen is −1 in most hydrogen-containing compounds.
The oxidation numbers in a polyatomic ion always add up to zero.
Group 2A metals are +1 in their compounds.
bank.why: Polyatomic ions sum to their charge. Hydrogen is usually +1, compounds (not ions) sum to zero, and Group 2A is +2.

bank.term: Ox. no. of Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇?
bank.why: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0, so x = +6. +12 forgets that there are two Cr atoms.
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.term: Ox. no. of C in CO₃²⁻
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of C in CO₃²⁻?
bank.why: x + 3(−2) = −2, so x = +4. +6 ignores the 2− charge of the ion.
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.term: Ox. no. of Mn in MnO₂
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of Mn in MnO₂?
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.term: Ox. no. of P in PCl₅
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of P in PCl₅?
bank.why: Cl is the more electronegative, so Cl = −1: x + 5(−1) = 0, x = +5.
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.term: Ox. no. of S in SF₄
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of S in SF₄?
bank.why: F is always −1 in compounds: x + 4(−1) = 0, so x = +4.
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.term: Ox. no. of Mn in KMnO₄
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of Mn in KMnO₄?
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.term: Ox. no. of S in H₂SO₄
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of S in H₂SO₄?
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.term: Ox. no. of N in NO₃⁻
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of N in NO₃⁻?
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.term: Ox. no. of Cl in ClO₄⁻
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of Cl in ClO₄⁻?
bank.why: x + 4(−2) = −1, so x = +7. +8 forgets the ion's charge.
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.term: Ox. no. of N in NH₄⁺
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of N in NH₄⁺?
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.term: Ox. no. of Fe in Fe₂O₃
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of Fe in Fe₂O₃?
bank.why: 2x + 3(−2) = 0, so x = +3. +6 forgets to divide by the two Fe atoms.
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.term: Ox. no. of Cl in KClO₃
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of Cl in KClO₃?
bank.why: +1 + x + 3(−2) = 0, so x = +5 (it becomes −1 in KCl when KClO₃ is heated).
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.term: Ox. no. of Cu in Cu₂O
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of Cu in Cu₂O?
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.term: Ox. no. of I in IO₃⁻
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of I in IO₃⁻?
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.term: Ox. no. of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻
bank.q: What is the oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻?
bank.hint: Set the sum of oxidation numbers equal to the charge.

bank.q: What is the oxidation number of oxygen in sodium peroxide, Na₂O₂?
bank.why: 2(+1) + 2x = 0, so x = −1: it is a peroxide.

bank.q: What type of redox reaction is Mg(s) + CuCl₂(aq) → Cu(s) + MgCl₂(aq)?
bank.why: An active metal (Mg) replaces a metal ion (Cu²⁺) from solution: a (metal) displacement reaction.

bank.q: What type of redox reaction is Ni(s) + Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) → Pb(s) + Ni(NO₃)₂(aq)?
bank.why: Ni displaces Pb²⁺ from solution (the slides' exercise c).

bank.q: What type of redox reaction is 2KClO₃(s) → 2KCl(s) + 3O₂(g)?
bank.why: One compound breaks into simpler substances: decomposition (Cl +5 → −1, O −2 → 0).

bank.q: What type of redox reaction is 2N₂O(g) → 2N₂(g) + O₂(g)?
bank.why: N₂O breaks into N₂ and O₂: decomposition (the slides' exercise a).

bank.q: What type of redox reaction is 6Li(s) + N₂(g) → 2Li₃N(s)?
bank.why: Two substances combine into one product: combination (the slides' exercise b).

bank.q: What type of redox reaction is 2Al(s) + 3Br₂(l) → 2AlBr₃(s)?
bank.why: Two elements combine into one compound. Al 0 → +3, Br 0 → −1.

bank.q: What type of redox reaction is 2NO₂(g) + H₂O(l) → HNO₂(aq) + HNO₃(aq)?
bank.why: Nitrogen goes from +4 to both +3 (HNO₂) and +5 (HNO₃): one element is oxidized and reduced (exercise d).

bank.q: What type of redox reaction is CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)?
bank.why: A fuel reacting with oxygen to give CO₂ and H₂O with heat and light: combustion.

bank.q: A redox reaction in which one element is simultaneously oxidized and reduced is called...
bank.why: Disproportionation: the same element ends up in a higher AND a lower oxidation state.

bank.q: In 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g), oxygen goes from −1 to −2 (in H₂O) and to 0 (in O₂). This makes it a...
bank.why: The same element (O) is both reduced (−1 → −2) and oxidized (−1 → 0). It is the slides' example of disproportionation.

bank.q: In a disproportionation reaction, the element that disproportionates must...
bank.a: Be in an intermediate oxidation state, with higher and lower states possible
d: Be in its highest possible oxidation state
Have an oxidation number of zero only
bank.why: It can only go both up and down if it starts in the middle; such elements have at least three oxidation states.
bank.hint: It has room to go both ways.

bank.q: Cu₂O(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + Cu(s) + H₂O(l). What kind of reaction is this?
bank.a: Disproportionation: Cu goes from +1 to both +2 and 0
d: Displacement: sulfate replaces the oxide ion
Combination: Cu₂O and H₂SO₄ combine into CuSO₄
Not a redox reaction: no oxidation number changes
bank.why: Cu is +1 in Cu₂O, +2 in CuSO₄ and 0 in Cu metal. Copper is both oxidized and reduced. (Test II on the past quiz.)

bank.q: In I₂(s) + OH⁻(aq) → IO₃⁻(aq) + I⁻(aq) + H₂O(l), iodine's oxidation number changes from 0 to...
bank.why: In IO₃⁻: x + 3(−2) = −1, so x = +5; I⁻ is −1. Iodine disproportionates. (Test II on the past quiz.)

bank.q: In CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), carbon's oxidation number changes from...
bank.why: C in CH₄: x + 4(+1) = 0, x = −4. C in CO₂: x + 2(−2) = 0, x = +4. Carbon is oxidized.

bank.q: According to the activity series of metals, which is the most reactive?
bank.why: Li is at the top of the activity series and Au (gold) at the bottom.

bank.q: The activity series of metals is useful for...
bank.a: Predicting whether a displacement reaction will occur
d: Balancing the charges in a half-reaction
Finding the oxidation number of oxygen
Predicting the pH of a salt solution
bank.why: A metal can displace the ions of any metal BELOW it in the series (and H₂ from acids if it is above hydrogen).

bank.q: A gold ring is accidentally dropped into hydrochloric acid. What happens?
bank.a: No reaction; gold is below hydrogen in the activity series
d: Gold dissolves and hydrogen gas bubbles off
Gold displaces chlorine from the acid
Gold is reduced to Au⁻ ions
bank.why: Only metals above hydrogen displace H₂ from acids. Gold is the least reactive metal (the slides' exercise).
bank.hint: Where is Au in the series?

bank.q: Copper metal is placed in a silver nitrate solution. What happens?
bank.a: Copper dissolves as Cu²⁺ and silver metal deposits
d: No reaction, because copper is below silver
Silver dissolves and copper metal deposits
bank.why: Cu is above Ag in the activity series, so Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s).
bank.hint: Cu is more active than Ag.

bank.q: Which reaction will NOT occur?
bank.why: Copper is below hydrogen, so it cannot displace H₂ from an acid. Zn and Mg are above hydrogen; Cu is above Ag.

bank.q: Cl₂(g) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(l) takes place because...
bank.a: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromide
d: Bromine is more reactive than chlorine
bank.why: Halogen displacement works like metal displacement: a more active halogen replaces a less active one.
bank.hint: Like the activity series, for halogens.

bank.q: Which statement about the types of redox reactions is TRUE?
bank.a: All combustion reactions are redox reactions.
d: All combination reactions are redox reactions.
All decomposition reactions are redox reactions.
Double-replacement reactions are generally redox reactions.
bank.why: Combustion always involves oxygen gaining electrons. Many (not all) combination and decomposition reactions are redox; double replacement generally is not.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: Every decomposition reaction is a redox reaction.
d: All single-replacement (displacement) reactions are redox reactions.
Combustion releases heat and light as a substance reacts with oxygen.
In a disproportionation, one element is both oxidized and reduced.
bank.why: Many decomposition reactions are redox, but not all (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ changes no oxidation number).

bank.q: Al(s) + Ni²⁺(aq) → Al³⁺(aq) + Ni(s) has the same atoms on both sides. Why is it still not balanced?
bank.a: The charges (electrons lost and gained) are not equal
d: There are more Al atoms on the right
Water and H⁺ must be added
bank.why: Left side charge is +2 and right side +3: Al loses 3 e⁻ but Ni²⁺ gains only 2 e⁻. Electrons must balance too.

bank.q: What is the oxidation half-reaction for Al(s) + Ni²⁺(aq) → Al³⁺(aq) + Ni(s)?
bank.why: Oxidation loses electrons, so the electrons appear on the product side: Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻.
bank.hint: Electrons are a product in oxidation.

bank.q: Which half-reaction is the reduction in Al(s) + Ni²⁺(aq) → Al³⁺(aq) + Ni(s)?
bank.why: Reduction gains electrons, so they are on the reactant side.
bank.hint: Electrons are a reactant in reduction.

bank.q: To make electrons lost equal electrons gained for Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ and Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni, multiply the half-reactions by...
bank.why: The lowest common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6: 2 × 3e⁻ = 3 × 2e⁻ = 6e⁻.

bank.q: What is the balanced net ionic equation for aluminum and nickel(II) ions?
bank.why: After multiplying (×2, ×3) the 6e⁻ cancel. Check charge: left +6, right +6.

bank.q: How many electrons are transferred in 2Al(s) + 3Ni²⁺(aq) → 2Al³⁺(aq) + 3Ni(s)?
bank.why: Two Al atoms each lose 3 e⁻ (6 total) and three Ni²⁺ each gain 2 e⁻ (6 total).

bank.q: Which is the balanced net ionic equation for copper metal in silver nitrate?
bank.why: Cu loses 2 e⁻ and each Ag⁺ gains 1 e⁻, so two Ag⁺ are needed. Charge: +2 = +2.

bank.q: Which half-reaction is an oxidation?
bank.why: Only zinc loses electrons (they are written as a product). The others gain electrons: reductions.

bank.q: Is Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → 2CrO₄²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) a redox reaction?
bank.a: No; chromium stays +6 and no element changes oxidation number
d: Yes; chromium is oxidized from +6 to +7
Yes; OH⁻ is the reducing agent
Yes; oxygen is reduced from −2 to −1
bank.why: Cr is +6 in both Cr₂O₇²⁻ and CrO₄²⁻; O stays −2 and H stays +1. It is an acid-base reaction (the slides' exercise b).

bank.q: When potassium chlorate is strongly heated, 2KClO₃(s) → 2KCl(s) + 3O₂(g). Which element is reduced?
bank.why: Cl goes from +5 in KClO₃ to −1 in KCl (gains electrons). Oxygen is oxidized from −2 to 0.

bank.q: In 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), which element is oxidized?
d: Neither; it is not a redox reaction
bank.why: H goes from 0 in H₂ to +1 in H₂O. Oxygen is reduced from 0 to −2.

bank.q: In acidic solution, MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺. How many electrons does each MnO₄⁻ gain?
bank.why: Mn goes from +7 (in MnO₄⁻) to +2: a decrease of 5, so 5 electrons are gained.

bank.q: 3I₂(s) + 6OH⁻(aq) → IO₃⁻(aq) + 5I⁻(aq) + 3H₂O(l). Why are there 5 I⁻ for every IO₃⁻?
bank.a: Forming one IO₃⁻ loses 5 e⁻, and each I⁻ gains only 1 e⁻
d: Five OH⁻ are needed per iodate
bank.why: 0 → +5 loses 5 electrons; 0 → −1 gains 1. Electrons lost = gained, so 5 I⁻ form per IO₃⁻ (balanced Test II item).

bank.q: In 2Fe³⁺ + Sn²⁺ → 2Fe²⁺ + Sn⁴⁺, why are two Fe³⁺ needed for each Sn²⁺?
bank.a: Sn²⁺ loses 2 electrons, but each Fe³⁺ gains only 1
d: Iron is more electronegative than tin
bank.why: Sn²⁺ → Sn⁴⁺ + 2e⁻, and Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺, so the iron half-reaction is multiplied by 2.

bank.q: Salt hydrolysis is the reaction of...
bank.a: The cation or anion of a salt (or both) with water
d: A salt with an acid to form a new salt
Water splitting into H₂ and O₂
A salt with oxygen at high temperature
bank.why: Hydrolysis: an ion of the salt reacts with water, which usually changes the pH.

bank.q: The word 'hydrolysis' comes from Greek words meaning...
bank.why: hydro = water, lysis = to split apart.

bank.q: A salt is...
bank.a: An ionic compound formed by the reaction between an acid and a base
d: A covalent compound of two nonmetals
Any compound that dissolves in water
An acid that has lost all its oxygen
bank.why: Salts are ionic and are strong electrolytes: they dissociate completely in water.

bank.q: In water, salts are...
bank.a: Strong electrolytes that dissociate completely into ions
d: Molecules that do not form ions
bank.why: Salts dissociate completely; what changes the pH is whether those ions then react with water.

bank.q: An aqueous solution of NH₄Cl is expected to be...
d: It depends only on the amount dissolved
bank.why: NH₄⁺ (from the weak base NH₃) donates H⁺ to water; Cl⁻ (from the strong acid HCl) does nothing.
bank.hint: Which ion comes from a weak acid or a weak base?

bank.q: An aqueous solution of FeCl₃ is expected to be...
bank.why: Fe³⁺ is one of the slides' acidic cations (NH₄⁺, Al³⁺, Fe³⁺); Cl⁻ is neutral.
bank.hint: Which ion comes from a weak acid or a weak base?

bank.q: An aqueous solution of NaNO₂ is expected to be...
bank.why: Na⁺ is neutral; NO₂⁻ is the conjugate base of the weak acid HNO₂ and makes OH⁻.
bank.hint: Which ion comes from a weak acid or a weak base?

bank.q: An aqueous solution of NaNO₃ is expected to be...
bank.why: Strong base (NaOH) + strong acid (HNO₃): neither ion reacts with water.
bank.hint: Which ion comes from a weak acid or a weak base?

bank.q: An aqueous solution of CH₃COONa is expected to be...
bank.why: Acetate, CH₃COO⁻, accepts H⁺ from water and produces OH⁻.
bank.hint: Which ion comes from a weak acid or a weak base?

bank.q: An aqueous solution of NH₄I is expected to be...
bank.why: NH₄⁺ is acidic and I⁻ (from the strong acid HI) is neutral: the slides' exercise 1.
bank.hint: Which ion comes from a weak acid or a weak base?

bank.q: An aqueous solution of KBr is expected to be...
bank.why: K⁺ (Group 1) and Br⁻ (from the strong acid HBr): neutral.
bank.hint: Which ion comes from a weak acid or a weak base?

bank.q: An aqueous solution of NaCN is expected to be...
bank.why: CN⁻ is on the slides' list of basic anions (F⁻, NO₂⁻, CN⁻, CH₃COO⁻).
bank.hint: Which ion comes from a weak acid or a weak base?

bank.q: Which salt produces an ACIDIC solution in water?
bank.why: Al³⁺ is an acidic cation (like NH₄⁺ and Fe³⁺). KCl is neutral; F⁻ and CH₃COO⁻ make basic solutions.
bank.hint: Look for NH₄⁺, Al³⁺ or Fe³⁺.

bank.q: Which salt produces a BASIC solution in water?
bank.why: F⁻ is the conjugate base of the weak acid HF. NaClO₄ and CaCl₂ are neutral; NH₄NO₃ is acidic.

bank.q: A salt derived from a strong base and a weak acid gives a solution with a pH that is...
bank.why: The anion (conjugate base of the weak acid) makes OH⁻ by hydrolysis.

bank.q: A salt derived from a strong acid and a weak base gives a solution that is...
bank.why: The cation (conjugate acid of the weak base) donates H⁺ to water, lowering the pH.

bank.q: Why is an ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl) solution acidic?
bank.a: NH₄⁺ gives H⁺ to water, forming H₃O⁺
bank.why: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺. This is the hydrolysis of NH₄⁺; Cl⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid and does not react.
bank.hint: Which ion has a removable H?

bank.q: Why is a sodium nitrate (NaNO₃) solution neutral?
bank.a: Neither Na⁺ nor NO₃⁻ reacts with water
bank.why: Hydrated Na⁺ neither donates nor accepts H⁺, and NO₃⁻ (conjugate base of the strong acid HNO₃) has no affinity for H⁺: pH about 7.

bank.q: Group 1 and Group 2 cations give neutral solutions with Cl⁻, Br⁻ or NO₃⁻, EXCEPT...
bank.why: The slides list Group 1 and Group 2 'but not Be²⁺' as neutral cations.

bank.q: Which anion makes a salt solution basic?
bank.why: CN⁻ comes from the weak acid HCN. Cl⁻, NO₃⁻ and ClO₄⁻ come from strong acids and stay neutral.

bank.q: Which statement about salts in water is FALSE?
bank.a: A salt from a strong acid and a weak base gives a basic solution.
d: A salt from a strong base and a weak acid gives a basic solution.
Salts are strong electrolytes that dissociate completely.
Hydrolysis of a salt usually affects the pH of the solution.
bank.why: Strong acid + weak base gives an ACIDIC solution (e.g. NH₄Cl). The other three are true.

bank.q: Concentration is...
bank.a: The amount of solute present in a specified amount of solution
d: The amount of solvent needed per mole of solute
The total mass of a solution
bank.why: Concentration compares the amount of solute with the amount of solution.

bank.q: The terms 'concentrated' and 'dilute' are...
d: Names for saturated and unsaturated solutions
bank.why: Concentrated = higher solute-to-solvent ratio; dilute = smaller ratio. They describe, they do not measure.

bank.q: Percent by mass (% w/w) is expressed as...
bank.a: Grams of solute per 100 g of solution
d: Grams of solute per 100 g of solvent
Grams of solute per 100 mL of solution
mL of solute per 100 mL of solution
bank.why: % w/w = mass of solute / mass of solution × 100, where mass of solution = solute + solvent.
bank.hint: Per 100 g of the whole solution.

bank.q: Percent by volume (% v/v) is used when...
bank.a: Both the solute and the solvent are liquids
d: The solute is a solid and the solvent is a liquid
bank.why: Volume percent describes a pure liquid diluted with another liquid, e.g. 5% (v/v) methanol.

bank.q: Mass-volume percent (% w/v) is used when...
bank.a: The solute is a solid and the solvent is a liquid
d: Both the solute and solvent are liquids
The solute is a liquid and the solvent a solid
bank.why: % w/v = grams of solute per 100 mL of solution (e.g. 5% w/v AgNO₃).

bank.q: Why must the units always be stated for a mass-volume percent?
bank.a: Mass and volume are different dimensions
d: It is the only percent unit used in IUPAC
Volume changes with the solute's color
bank.why: The slides stress that the units must be defined because grams and milliliters are different dimensions.

bank.q: Nitric acid is sold as a 70% (w/w) solution. This means it contains...
bank.a: 70 g of HNO₃ per 100 g of solution
d: 70 g of HNO₃ per 100 g of water
70 g of HNO₃ per 100 mL of solution
70 mL of HNO₃ per 100 mL of solution
bank.why: w/w uses the mass of the whole solution: 70 g HNO₃ in every 100 g of solution.

bank.q: A solution with a mass percent concentration of 10% contains...
bank.a: 10 g of solute and 90 g of solvent
d: 10 g of solute per 100 g of solvent
10 g of solvent and 90 g of solute
10 g of solute in 100 mL of solution
bank.why: 10 g solute in 100 g of solution, so the solvent is 100 − 10 = 90 g (the slides' exercise).

bank.q: Which statement about percent concentration is FALSE?
bank.a: In % w/w, the mass of the solution is the mass of the solvent minus the mass of the solute.
d: In % w/w, the mass of the solution is the mass of the solute plus the mass of the solvent.
% v/v is commonly used when a pure liquid is diluted with another liquid.
% w/v gives grams of solute per 100 mL of solution.
bank.why: Mass of solution = solute + solvent. (False item from the class mock quiz.)

bank.q: What is the percent by mass of glucose in a solution made by dissolving 5.5 g of glucose in 78.2 g of water?
bank.why: Mass of solution = 5.5 + 78.2 = 83.7 g; 5.5 / 83.7 × 100 = 6.6%. Dividing by the water only gives 7.0%.

bank.q: A commercial sodium chloride solution is 12.0% (w/w). How many grams of NaCl are in 250.0 g of the solution?
bank.why: mass of solute = 12.0/100 × 250.0 g = 30.0 g.

bank.q: What is the volume percent of solute in 30.0 mL of methyl alcohol with enough water to give 435 mL of solution?
bank.why: 30.0 / 435 × 100 = 6.90%. The 435 mL is already the total, so do not subtract the 30.0 mL.

bank.q: How many milliliters of pure ethanol are needed to prepare 500 mL of 5.25% (v/v) aqueous ethanol?
bank.why: Volume of solute = 5.25/100 × 500 mL = 26.3 mL; then add water up to 500 mL.

bank.q: A technician uses 12.5 mL of pure acetone to make a 2.50% (v/v) acetone solution. What is the total volume of the solution?
bank.why: Volume of solution = 12.5 mL / 0.0250 = 500 mL. 488 mL is only the water you would add.

bank.q: A nurse prepares a 5.00% (w/v) glucose solution. How many grams of glucose are needed for 250.0 mL?
How many grams of sodium chloride are needed to prepare 150 mL of 0.90% (w/v) NaCl?
bank.why: 0.90 g per 100 mL × 150 mL = 1.35 g, which is 1.4 g with 2 significant figures (the slides' exercise).

bank.q: 10.0 g of KCl is dissolved in enough water to make 250 mL of solution. What is the % (w/v)?
Molarity (M) is the number of...
bank.a: Moles of solute per liter of solution
d: Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
Moles of solute per liter of solvent
Gram equivalents of solute per liter of solution
bank.why: M = mol solute / L of SOLUTION (not of solvent). Per kg of solvent is molality; equivalents per liter is normality.

bank.q: A concentration of 1 M is also equal to...
bank.a: 1 mmol of solute per mL of solution
d: 1 mol of solute per mL of solution
1 g of solute per mL of solution
1 mmol of solute per L of solution
bank.why: mol/L = mmol/mL, since both are divided by 1000.

bank.q: 4.35 moles of KMnO₄ are dissolved in enough water to give 750 mL of solution. What is the molarity?
What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 23.4 g of Na₂SO₄ (142.00 g/mol) in enough water to form 125 mL of solution?
16 g of NaOH (40.00 g/mol) and 16 g of KCl (74.55 g/mol) are each dissolved to make 250 mL of solution. Which is correct?
bank.a: NaOH is 1.6 M and KCl is 0.86 M
d: Both are 1.6 M because the masses are equal
NaOH is 0.86 M and KCl is 1.6 M
bank.why: Equal masses do not mean equal moles: 16/40.00 = 0.40 mol NaOH (1.6 M); 16/74.55 = 0.215 mol KCl (0.86 M).

bank.q: What is the molarity of HNO₃ (63.00 g/mol) in a solution with a specific gravity of 1.42 that is 70.5% HNO₃ (w/w)?
bank.hint: Use the density, then the percent.

bank.q: How many grams of NaOH (40.00 g/mol) are needed to prepare 500.0 mL of 0.150 M NaOH?
What volume of 12.0 M HCl is needed to prepare 500.0 mL of 0.500 M HCl?
bank.why: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂: V₁ = (0.500 × 500.0) / 12.0 = 20.8 mL of the concentrated acid, then dilute to 500.0 mL.

bank.q: Normal blood calcium is less than 10.5 mg/dL. A patient's blood calcium is measured at 0.95 g/L. Is it within the normal range?
bank.a: No; 0.95 g/L = 95 mg/dL, far above 10.5 mg/dL
bank.why: 0.95 g/L × 1000 mg/g = 950 mg/L; 1 dL = 0.1 L, so 950 × 0.1 = 95 mg/dL. That is far above 10.5 (Test III on the past quiz).

bank.q: Which statement about molarity is TRUE?
bank.a: Molarity uses the volume of the final solution, not the volume of the solvent.
d: Molarity uses the mass of the solvent in kilograms.
1.0 M means 1.0 g of solute per liter of solution.
Molarity and molality are always numerically equal.
bank.why: M = moles per liter of SOLUTION. Mass of solvent is molality, and 1.0 M is 1.0 mol (not g) per liter.

bank.q: Molality (m) is the number of moles of solute per...
bank.why: Molality uses 1000 g (1 kg) of SOLVENT, not the final solution.

bank.q: A solution containing 1.0 mol of NaCl dissolved in 1.0 kg of water is described as...
bank.why: 1.0 mol per 1.0 kg of solvent = 1.0 molal.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: Molality is the number of moles of solute in exactly 1 liter of the final solution.
d: Molality is based on the mass of the solvent.
Molarity is based on the volume of the solution.
The unit of molality is mol/kg.
bank.why: That definition is molarity's (moles per liter of solution). Molality uses kilograms of solvent (false item on the mock quiz).

bank.q: What is the molality of a solution of 127 g of NaCl (58.44 g/mol) dissolved in 1000.0 g of distilled water?
4.25 g of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆, 180.18 g/mol) is dissolved in 250.00 g of water. What is the molality?
bank.hint: Convert grams of water to kg.

bank.q: How many grams of urea (CON₂H₄, 60.06 g/mol) must be dissolved in 500.0 g of water to make a 0.500 m solution?
bank.hint: m × kg of solvent × molar mass.

bank.q: Convert a 0.850 m NaCl solution (58.44 g/mol) to percent by mass.
bank.why: Take 1 kg of water: 0.850 mol × 58.44 = 49.7 g NaCl; solution = 1050 g; 49.7 / 1050 × 100 = 4.73%.
bank.hint: Assume 1 kg of water, then find the solution's mass.

bank.q: The key difference between molarity and molality is that...
bank.a: Molarity is per liter of solution; molality is per kilogram of solvent
d: Molarity is per kilogram of solvent; molality is per liter of solution
Molarity uses grams; molality uses moles
Molality is used only for gases
bank.why: Molarity: mol / L of solution. Molality: mol / kg of solvent.

bank.q: Normality (N) is expressed as...
bank.a: Gram equivalent weights of solute per liter of solution
d: Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
Grams of solute per 100 mL of solution
Moles of solute per liter of solvent
bank.why: N = equivalents of solute / liters of solution; units N, eq/L or meq/mL.

bank.q: In an acid-base reaction, one equivalent of an acid is the amount that...
bank.why: An equivalent of acid gives 1 mol H⁺; an equivalent of base reacts with 1 mol H⁺.

bank.q: The equivalent weight (EW) of a compound is...
bank.a: Its molar mass divided by its valence
d: Its molar mass times its valence
The number of H atoms it contains
bank.why: EW = MW / valence, where the valence is the replaceable H⁺ (acids), the H⁺ reacted with (bases) or the total positive charge (salts).

bank.q: One equivalent of an acid reacts completely with...
d: One liter of a 1 M base
bank.why: That is the point of equivalents: 1 eq acid neutralizes exactly 1 eq base (N₁V₁ = N₂V₂ in titrations).

bank.q: Which statement about normality is TRUE?
bank.a: For H₂SO₄ in a full neutralization, the normality is twice the molarity.
d: Normality is always equal to molarity.
Equivalent weight equals molar mass multiplied by the valence.
Normality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent.
bank.why: H₂SO₄ gives 2 H⁺, so N = 2 × M. EW = MW ÷ valence, and normality is per liter of solution.

bank.q: What is the equivalent weight of BaCl₂ (molar mass 208.23 g/mol)?
bank.why: BaCl₂ has a total positive charge of 2 (valence 2): EW = 208.23 / 2 = 104.12 g/eq.

bank.q: What is the equivalent weight of K₂CO₃ (molar mass 138.21 g/mol)?
bank.why: K₂CO₃ has a total positive charge of 2 (valence 2): EW = 138.21 / 2 = 69.11 g/eq.

bank.q: What valence (equivalents per mole) is used for Fe₂(SO₄)₃ to find its equivalent weight?
bank.why: Two Fe³⁺ ions give a total positive charge of 2 × 3 = 6 (the slides' table).

bank.q: What valence is used for AlCl₃ when finding its equivalent weight?
bank.why: One Al³⁺: total positive charge 3. EW = 133.34 / 3 ≈ 44.4 g/eq.

bank.q: What is the normality of a solution with 0.587 g of NaOH (40.00 g/mol) in 25.7 mL?
What is the normality of a 0.0521 M H₃PO₄ solution (all three H⁺ react)?
What is the normality of 0.321 g of sodium carbonate (105.99 g/mol) in 250.0 mL of solution?
How many grams of Al₂(SO₄)₃ (342.15 g/mol) are needed to prepare 100.0 mL of a 2.00 N solution with respect to Al³⁺?
What is the normality of 1.5 M H₂SO₄ in a reaction where both protons react?
bank.why: N = M × number of H⁺ = 1.5 × 2 = 3.0 N.

bank.q: Solubility is...
bank.a: The maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent
d: Any amount of solute that has dissolved
The rate at which a solute dissolves
The amount of solvent needed to dissolve 1 g of solute
bank.why: Solubility is a maximum, usually grams of solute per 100 g of solvent. It depends on temperature and is based on a saturated solution.

bank.q: A solution in which no more solute dissolves at a given temperature is...
bank.why: Saturated: it already holds the maximum amount of solute.

bank.q: A supersaturated solution...
bank.a: Holds more solute than its solubility, is unstable, and crystals can form
d: Holds exactly the maximum amount of solute
Is the same as a concentrated solution
bank.why: Supersaturated solutions are unstable; disturbing them makes the excess solute crystallize.

bank.q: Extra solute is added to a saturated solution at the same temperature. What happens?
bank.a: It does not dissolve; the solution stays saturated
d: It dissolves and the solution becomes supersaturated
The solubility of the solute increases
bank.why: A saturated solution cannot dissolve more; the excess stays undissolved. It does not become supersaturated (false item on the past quiz).

bank.q: Henry's law states that the solubility of a gas is...
bank.a: Directly proportional to the pressure of that gas
d: Inversely proportional to the pressure of that gas
bank.why: More gas pressure above the liquid → more gas dissolves.

bank.q: For about 95% of solid solutes, solubility in water...
bank.why: Most solids dissolve better in hotter water.

bank.q: As water is warmed, dissolved gases generally become...
bank.why: Gases are less soluble in warm water (but more soluble in organic solvents as temperature rises).

bank.q: An opened, warm soda loses its fizz faster than a cold, sealed one. Which explanation fits?
bank.a: Higher temperature and lower CO₂ pressure both lower the gas's solubility
d: Higher temperature raises the gas's solubility
Pressure only affects the solubility of solids
Like dissolves like makes CO₂ leave
bank.why: Warmth lowers gas solubility, and opening the bottle lowers CO₂ pressure (Henry's law).

bank.q: 'Like dissolves like' means a solute dissolves best in a solvent that...
bank.why: Polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents; nonpolar solutes in nonpolar solvents.

bank.q: Which solute dissolves best in hexane, a nonpolar solvent?
bank.why: Nonpolar dissolves nonpolar. Ionic and polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents like water.

bank.q: Which statement about solubility is FALSE?
bank.a: Most solid solutes become less soluble in water as the pressure decreases.
d: Gas solubility in water usually decreases as the temperature rises.
A solute dissolves best in a solvent of similar polarity.
bank.why: Pressure matters for gases (Henry's law), not for solid solutes. (False item on the past quiz.)

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: Not every ionic compound is soluble in water.
d: All ionic substances are soluble in water because water is polar.
Cooling the solvent always increases solubility.
The stronger the solute-solvent attraction, the harder the solute dissolves.
bank.why: Many ionic compounds (AgCl, CaCO₃) are insoluble. Cooling usually lowers solid solubility, and strong solute-solvent attraction helps dissolving. (All three were false on the past quiz.)
bank.hint: Three of these were on the past quiz.

bank.q: Which statement about factors affecting solubility is TRUE?
bank.a: Solubility is defined for a saturated solution and varies with temperature.
d: According to Henry's law, gas solubility is indirectly proportional to pressure.
Polar solutes dissolve best in nonpolar solvents.
Adding more solute to a saturated solution makes it supersaturated.
bank.why: Solubility describes the saturated state and changes with temperature. Henry's law is DIRECT proportion, polar dissolves polar, and a saturated solution just leaves the extra solute undissolved.

bank.q: What is the field of chemistry that deals with numbers and measurements?
bank.why: "transportation is the correct answer because there are numbers in license plate and the measurement in engine" - Yuri Yousseff Manago

bank.q: A reversible reaction is a reaction in which...
bank.a: The products can regenerate the original reactants
d: The reactants are completely used up
bank.why: Products re-form reactants. In theory every reaction is reversible; some only under restricted conditions.

bank.q: Chemical equilibrium is reached when...
bank.a: The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction
d: The concentrations of reactants and products are equal
All the reactants have been converted into products
Both the forward and reverse reactions stop
bank.why: Equal RATES, not equal concentrations. The concentrations stay constant because each species forms as fast as it is used up.

bank.q: Equilibrium is described as dynamic because...
bank.a: The forward and reverse reactions keep going at equal rates
bank.why: At equilibrium both reactions continue (it never stops), so nothing changes overall. The double arrow (⇌) shows this.

bank.q: Colorless N₂O₄ is sealed in a flask and turns brown as N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) proceeds. When does it reach equilibrium?
bank.a: When the color stops changing, with both N₂O₄ and NO₂ present
d: When the gas becomes completely brown
When the gas becomes colorless again
When the amounts of N₂O₄ and NO₂ are equal
bank.why: The color stops changing because NO₂ re-forms N₂O₄ as fast as it is made; both gases remain, in constant (not equal) amounts.

bank.q: According to the slides, the rate of a reaction depends on...
d: Only the color of the reactants
Only the size of the container
bank.why: In general, the rate is proportional to concentration; temperature and gas pressure also matter.

bank.q: Which is true about how equilibrium can be reached?
bank.a: From either the reactant side or the product side
d: Only by starting with pure reactants
Only by starting with pure products
Only when a catalyst is present
bank.why: Equilibrium can be reached from either direction (slide summary).

bank.q: Which statement about chemical equilibrium is FALSE?
bank.a: Chemical equilibrium is a static state where all reactions completely stop.
d: In a reversible reaction, the products can react to regenerate the reactants.
At equilibrium, the forward rate equals the reverse rate.
At equilibrium, the concentrations remain constant with time.
bank.why: Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions continue at equal rates (transes mock quiz).

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: At equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products do not have to be equal.
d: A reversible reaction reaches equilibrium because the reactants keep decomposing.
At equilibrium, the reactant and product concentrations are always equal.
Once a reaction reaches equilibrium, it can no longer be disturbed.
bank.why: Equal rates do not mean equal concentrations. Equilibrium comes from equal rates (not constant decomposition of reactants, which was false on the past quiz), and it can be disturbed (Le Châtelier).
bank.hint: Rates are equal, amounts need not be.

bank.q: The equilibrium constant expression comes from the law of mass action proposed by...
bank.why: Guldberg and Waage, 1864. Le Châtelier is the 'disturb an equilibrium' principle.

bank.q: In the equilibrium constant expression...
bank.a: Products go in the numerator and reactants in the denominator
d: Reactants go in the numerator and products in the denominator
Products and reactants are added together
bank.why: K = [products]^coefficients / [reactants]^coefficients.

bank.q: In an equilibrium expression, the coefficients of the balanced equation become...
bank.why: That is why the equation must be balanced first: aA + bB ⇌ pP + qQ gives K = [P]ᵖ[Q]^q / [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ.

bank.q: Which species are left out of the equilibrium constant expression?
bank.a: Pure solids, pure liquids and the solvent
bank.why: Pure solids, pure liquids and the solvent of a dilute solution have no term in K.

bank.q: Kc is based on molar concentrations at equilibrium, while Kp is based on...
bank.a: Partial pressures of the gases in atmospheres
d: Masses of the reactants in grams
Volumes of the solutions in liters
bank.why: For gas-phase species, [Z]ᶻ is replaced by the partial pressure p_Z (atm).

bank.q: The value of the equilibrium constant changes only when...
d: The volume of the container changes
bank.why: K is a temperature-dependent constant. Concentration, pressure and catalysts shift the position, not K.

bank.q: K depends on the reaction's...
bank.why: K is the same regardless of the starting concentrations or the steps taken; it depends on the balanced equation.

bank.q: What does the equilibrium constant tell you about the speed of a reaction?
bank.a: Nothing; K gives no information about rate
d: A large K means a fast reaction
A small K means a fast reaction
K equals the rate of the forward reaction
bank.why: K predicts direction and completeness, not rate. Some reactions with huge K are too slow to use without a catalyst.

bank.q: What is the Kc expression for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
bank.why: Products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient (seatwork 5.1a).

bank.q: What is the Kc expression for N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g)?
bank.why: Seatwork 5.1b: the 2 becomes a square.

bank.q: What is the equilibrium expression for Na₂O₂(s) ⇌ 2Na(s) + O₂(g)?
bank.why: Na₂O₂ and Na are solids, so they are left out; only the gas O₂ remains (seatwork 5.1c).

bank.q: What is the Kc expression for CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)?
bank.why: Water is the solvent (a pure liquid), so it has no term.

bank.q: A 2.0 L vessel contains an equilibrium mixture of 2.0 mol N₂, 0.60 mol H₂ and 0.40 mol NH₃ for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). What is Kc?
bank.why: Molarities first: [N₂] = 1.0 M, [H₂] = 0.30 M, [NH₃] = 0.20 M. Kc = (0.20)² / (1.0 × 0.30³) = 0.040 / 0.027 = 1.48 ≈ 1.5. Using moles instead of molarity gives 0.37. (The transes key's 14.81 is a typo.)

bank.q: In the same 2.0 L vessel (2.0 mol N₂, 0.60 mol H₂, 0.40 mol NH₃), what are the equilibrium molarities?
bank.why: M = mol / L: divide each by 2.0 L.

bank.q: At equilibrium, [H₂] = 0.10 M, [I₂] = 0.20 M and [HI] = 0.80 M for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). What is Kc?
bank.why: Kc = [HI]² / ([H₂][I₂]) = 0.64 / 0.020 = 32. Forgetting the square gives 40.

bank.q: A reaction has Kc = 4.5 × 10⁵. What does this mean?
bank.a: Products are favored; the equilibrium lies to the right
d: Reactants are favored; the equilibrium lies to the left
bank.why: K >> 1: essentially all products, equilibrium lies to the right (transes problem). K says nothing about speed.

bank.q: A reaction has K = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ at 25 °C. At equilibrium the mixture is...
bank.a: Mostly reactants; the equilibrium lies to the left
d: Mostly products; it lies to the right
Equal amounts of reactants and products
Impossible to describe without the rate
bank.why: K << 1: essentially all reactants (the transes table mistakenly says 'right' for this row).

bank.q: The reaction quotient Q is found to be smaller than K. In which direction will the reaction proceed?
bank.a: Forward, toward the products, until Q = K
bank.why: Q < K means too few products, so the reaction goes forward. At equilibrium Q = K.

bank.q: Which statement about the equilibrium constant is FALSE?
bank.a: Pure solids and liquids are included in the K expression regardless of their amounts.
d: The K expression places products in the numerator and reactants in the denominator.
A very large K means the mixture is mostly products at equilibrium.
The coefficients become the exponents in the K expression.
bank.why: Pure solids and liquids are left out (transes mock quiz).

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: K changes when the temperature changes, for any type of reaction.
d: Temperature changes K only if the reactants are gases.
K increases when the concentration of a reactant is increased.
A catalyst increases the value of K.
bank.why: K depends on temperature for every reaction. Adding a substance shifts the position but K stays the same, and catalysts never change K (past-quiz items).

bank.q: Le Châtelier's principle states that when an equilibrium is disturbed, the system...
bank.why: The system shifts in the direction that minimizes the stress.

bank.q: According to the slides, which does NOT affect the equilibrium condition?
bank.a: A catalyst, an inert gas, or a pure solid or solvent
d: Changing the pressure of a gas reaction with unequal moles of gas
bank.why: Catalysts only speed up both directions equally; inert gases and pure solids/solvents have no term in K.

bank.q: Adding a catalyst to a system at equilibrium will...
bank.a: Not shift the equilibrium; it only helps reach equilibrium faster
d: Shift the equilibrium toward the products
Shift the equilibrium toward the reactants
bank.why: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally (false item: 'catalyst alters the position of equilibrium').

bank.q: Adding a product to a system at equilibrium shifts the equilibrium...
bank.a: Toward the reactants (away from the added product)
d: Nowhere; products do not affect equilibrium
In a direction that depends only on the catalyst
bank.why: Adding shifts away from the increase; removing shifts toward the decrease.

bank.q: H₂ is added to N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) at equilibrium. After the new equilibrium is established...
d: Nothing changes because K is constant
bank.why: The system uses up the added H₂, so it also uses N₂ and makes more NH₃ (the slides' Haber example).

bank.q: How does an ammonia plant get the most NH₃ from N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
bank.a: Keep adding N₂ and H₂ and continuously remove NH₃
bank.why: Flood with reactants and remove product, so the equilibrium keeps shifting right (recycling unreacted N₂ and H₂).

bank.q: Increasing the pressure on a gaseous equilibrium (by decreasing the volume) favors the side with...
bank.why: The system shifts to reduce pressure, i.e. toward fewer gas molecules (false item: 'shifts toward the greater number of moles').

bank.q: The pressure on N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is increased. What happens to the amount of NH₃?
bank.why: 4 mol of gas on the left vs 2 on the right: higher pressure favors the right, so more NH₃.

bank.q: The volume of H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) is halved. Which way does the equilibrium shift?
bank.why: 2 mol of gas on each side: pressure has no effect when the moles of gas are equal.

bank.q: A flask of N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) (NO₂ is brown) is compressed. After it re-equilibrates, the mixture becomes...
bank.a: Lighter, because the equilibrium shifts toward N₂O₄
d: Darker, because the equilibrium shifts toward NO₂
Unchanged, because pressure does not affect gases
Colorless, because all the NO₂ disappears
bank.why: Higher pressure favors fewer moles: 1 N₂O₄ vs 2 NO₂, so it shifts left and the brown fades (not to zero).

bank.q: For an endothermic reaction (ΔH > 0), heat can be treated as...
bank.why: Endothermic: heat + reactants ⇌ products. Exothermic: reactants ⇌ products + heat.

bank.q: Heating an exothermic reaction (ΔH < 0) at equilibrium...
bank.a: Favors the reverse reaction and decreases K
d: Favors the forward reaction and increases K
Has no effect on the equilibrium
Favors the forward reaction but K is unchanged
bank.why: Heat is a product, so adding heat shifts left; since temperature changes K, K gets smaller.

bank.q: Cooling an endothermic reaction (ΔH > 0) at equilibrium favors...
bank.why: Heat is a reactant; removing it shifts toward the reactants.

bank.q: Co(H₂O)₆²⁺(aq, pink) + 4Cl⁻(aq) ⇌ CoCl₄²⁻(aq, blue) + 6H₂O(l), ΔH > 0. What color does the solution turn when heated?
bank.a: Blue, because heating favors the forward (endothermic) reaction
d: Pink, because heating favors the reverse reaction
Colorless, because the complex breaks apart
No change, because temperature does not affect K
bank.why: Endothermic: heat is a reactant, so heating forms more blue CoCl₄²⁻; cooling gives the pale pink Co(H₂O)₆²⁺.
bank.hint: Heat goes in on the left.

bank.q: For the same cobalt equilibrium, concentrated HCl (more Cl⁻) is added. The solution becomes...
bank.why: Adding a reactant (Cl⁻) shifts right, toward blue CoCl₄²⁻.

bank.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH < 0, what happens when O₂(g) is added?
d: K increases, but the position does not change
bank.why: Adding a reactant shifts toward the products, so more SO₃ forms. (Seatwork 5.5.)

bank.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH < 0, what happens when the reaction is heated?
d: K increases, but the position does not change
bank.why: ΔH < 0, so heat is a product; adding it shifts left (and K decreases). (Seatwork 5.5.)

bank.term: SO3: the volume of the container is doubled
bank.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH < 0, what happens when the volume of the container is doubled?
d: K increases, but the position does not change
bank.why: Lower pressure favors more moles of gas: 3 on the left vs 2 on the right. (Seatwork 5.5.)

bank.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH < 0, what happens when SO₃(g) is removed?
d: K increases, but the position does not change
bank.why: Removing a product shifts toward the decrease. (Seatwork 5.5.)

bank.term: SO3: an inert gas is added at constant volume
bank.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH < 0, what happens when an inert gas is added at constant volume?
d: K increases, but the position does not change
bank.why: An inert gas does not change any partial pressure in the K expression. (Seatwork 5.5.)

bank.q: For 2PbS(s) + 3O₂(g) ⇌ 2PbO(s) + 2SO₂(g), ΔH > 0, what happens when the system is heated?
bank.why: Endothermic: heat is a reactant, so heating shifts right and K increases (Test IV of the past quiz).

bank.q: For the same PbS equilibrium, SO₂ is removed. The equilibrium...
bank.why: Removing a product shifts toward the decrease.

bank.q: For the same PbS equilibrium, the amount of PbO(s) is doubled. The equilibrium...
bank.why: PbO is a pure solid, so it has no term in K; adding more does nothing (a trap on the past quiz).

bank.q: A catalyst is added to the PbS equilibrium. The equilibrium...
bank.why: Catalysts never shift an equilibrium.

bank.q: For 2PbS(s) + 3O₂(g) ⇌ 2PbO(s) + 2SO₂(g), the pressure is halved. The equilibrium shifts...
bank.a: Left, toward the side with more moles of gas
d: Right, toward the side with fewer moles of gas
Right, because the reaction is endothermic
bank.why: Count only gases: 3 O₂ on the left vs 2 SO₂ on the right. Lower pressure favors more gas moles, so left. Balance the equation first.

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: For an exothermic reaction, raising the temperature favors the reverse reaction.
d: A catalyst changes the final equilibrium concentrations.
Increasing pressure favors the side with more moles of gas.
Adding an inert gas at constant volume shifts the equilibrium.
bank.why: Exothermic: heat is a product, so heating shifts left. The other three are false (transes mock quiz).

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: Adding a reactant to an equilibrium mixture increases the value of K.
d: Adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium toward the products.
Removing a product shifts the equilibrium toward the products.
A pure solid added to the mixture does not shift the equilibrium.
bank.why: Concentration changes shift the position, but K stays the same (only temperature changes K).
bank.hint: K is constant at a given temperature.

bank.q: The self-ionization of water produces...
bank.why: 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻, described by Kw.

bank.q: At 25 °C, the ion-product constant of water Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] equals...
bank.why: In pure water at 25 °C, [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M, so Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴.

bank.q: In pure water at 25 °C, [H₃O⁺] is...
bank.why: Neutral water: [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M.

bank.q: The [OH⁻] in a household ammonia cleaner is 0.0025 M. What is [H⁺] at 25 °C?
bank.why: [H⁺] = Kw / [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 0.0025 = 4.0 × 10⁻¹² M (the transes example). The solution is basic.

bank.q: What is the pH of that ammonia cleaner ([OH⁻] = 0.0025 M)?
At 25 °C, pH + pOH equals...
bank.why: Because [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴.

bank.q: A higher pH means...
bank.a: Fewer H⁺ ions, so the solution is less acidic (more basic)
d: More H⁺ ions, so it is more acidic
More H⁺ ions, so it is more basic
bank.why: More H⁺ → lower pH → more acidic; less H⁺ → higher pH → more basic.
bank.hint: pH goes up as H⁺ goes down.

bank.q: A solution at pH 3 has how many times more H⁺ than a solution at pH 5?
bank.why: Each pH unit is a 10-fold change: 10² = 100.

bank.q: What is the pH of a solution with [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M?
What is the pH of a solution with [H₃O⁺] = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ M?
What is [H₃O⁺] in a solution with pH 4.30?
Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: In a basic solution, [OH⁻] is greater than 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M at 25 °C.
d: A solution with pH 9 is acidic.
More H⁺ ions means a higher pH.
bank.why: Basic means [OH⁻] > [H₃O⁺], so [OH⁻] > 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M. pH 9 is basic, more H⁺ lowers pH, and pH + pOH = 14.

bank.q: According to Arrhenius, an acid is a substance that...
bank.why: Arrhenius: acids give H⁺ in water (ionization); bases give OH⁻ in water (dissociation).

bank.q: A Brønsted-Lowry base is a...
bank.why: BL acid = proton donor; BL base = proton acceptor.

bank.q: A Lewis acid is a(n)...
bank.why: Lewis acid: accepts an electron pair (electrophile). Lewis base: donates an electron pair (nucleophile).

bank.q: A substance that can either donate or accept a proton, such as water, is called...
bank.why: It needs both an H atom and a lone pair. Water can act as a BL acid or a BL base.

bank.q: What is the conjugate acid of ammonia, NH₃?
bank.why: A base that accepts a proton becomes its conjugate acid: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺.

bank.q: When an acid gives a proton to a base, the acid becomes...
bank.why: Acid − H⁺ = conjugate base; base + H⁺ = conjugate acid.

bank.q: For a conjugate acid-base pair, Ka and Kb are related by...
bank.why: Ka × Kb = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, so pKa + pKb = 14.

bank.q: The common ion effect is the shift in equilibrium when you add a compound that...
bank.a: Shares an ion with the dissolved substance
d: Has no ions in common with the solute
bank.why: Adding a common ion decreases the ionization of a weak acid or weak base.

bank.q: A buffer solution contains...
bank.a: A weak acid or weak base plus its salt (conjugate)
d: A strong acid and a strong base
Pure water and a salt of a strong acid
bank.why: e.g. carbonic acid with hydrogen carbonate, or NH₃ with NH₄Cl. The pair must not neutralize each other.

bank.q: A buffer resists pH changes because it contains...
bank.a: An acid to neutralize added OH⁻ and a base to neutralize added H⁺
d: Only an acid to neutralize OH⁻
So much water that ions are diluted
bank.why: Small to moderate amounts of strong acid or base are absorbed by the buffer's two partners.

bank.q: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is...
bank.why: Used to calculate the pH of buffer solutions.

bank.q: A 1.00 L buffer contains 0.0025 mol carbonic acid and 0.025 mol hydrogen carbonate. Ka = 4.3 × 10⁻⁷. What is the pH?
What is the pH of a buffer that is 0.200 M NH₃ and 0.300 M NH₄Cl? (Kb of NH₃ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵)
What ratio [A⁻]/[HA] gives a buffer of pH 4.50 if the pKa is 4.19?
bank.why: 4.50 = 4.19 + log(ratio), so log(ratio) = 0.31 and ratio = 10^0.31 = 2.04 (transes sample problem).

bank.q: A buffer has pKa = 7.46, [A⁻] = 0.159 M and [HA] = 0.072 M. What is its pH?
bank.hint: More base than acid → above pKa.

bank.q: The bicarbonate buffer keeps the pH of extracellular fluid (blood) within...
bank.why: Outside this range is acidosis (below) or alkalosis (above).

bank.q: A patient with a severe asthma attack cannot exhale CO₂ properly. What happens to blood pH?
bank.a: It falls (respiratory acidosis), because CO₂ builds up as carbonic acid
d: It rises (alkalosis), because CO₂ is a base
It stays the same because blood has no buffer
It rises because more O₂ is absorbed
bank.why: Less CO₂ exhaled → more H₂CO₃ → more H⁺ → pH ↓. Asthma, obesity and trauma can cause it.

bank.q: Prolonged vomiting of acidic stomach contents tends to cause...
bank.why: Losing stomach acid lowers H⁺, so blood pH rises.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: A buffer is made from a strong acid and a strong base.
d: A Lewis base donates an electron pair.
Adding a common ion decreases the ionization of a weak acid.
bank.why: A strong acid and strong base just neutralize each other. A buffer needs a WEAK acid/base and its salt.

bank.q: The science of the relationship between heat and other forms of energy is...
bank.why: Thermodynamics (Greek therme, 'heat' + dynamis, 'power') studies energy and its transformations.

bank.q: The area of thermodynamics that studies the heat absorbed or evolved by chemical reactions is...
bank.why: Thermochemistry is one area of thermodynamics.

bank.q: In the word thermodynamics, the Greek root 'dynamis' means...
bank.why: therme = heat; dynamis = power.

bank.q: Energy is defined as...
bank.a: The capacity to do work and transfer heat
d: The energy used to move an object against a force
The heat given off by a reaction
bank.why: Energy = capacity to do work and transfer heat. Work moves an object against a force; heat raises temperature.

bank.q: The energy used to cause an object to move against a force is...
bank.why: Work = energy used to move an object against a force.

bank.q: The energy used to cause the temperature of an object to increase is...
bank.why: Heat raises the temperature of an object.

bank.q: Which is an example of kinetic energy?
d: A book resting on a shelf
bank.why: Kinetic energy is energy in motion; the other three store energy by position or arrangement (slide exercise).

bank.q: Potential energy is best described as...
bank.a: Energy stored due to position or arrangement
d: Energy released during a chemical reaction
bank.why: PE is 'stored' energy from an object's position relative to other objects (attractions and repulsions).

bank.q: The energy associated with the random motion of atoms and molecules is...
bank.why: Thermal energy = random molecular motion.

bank.q: Energy stored within the structural units of chemical substances is...
bank.why: Chemical energy is stored in the structure (bonds) of substances.

bank.q: The energy that comes from the sun is...
bank.why: Radiant or solar energy.

bank.q: Transfer of energy between objects that are in physical contact is...
bank.why: Conduction (diffusion) needs contact.

bank.q: Transfer of energy between an object and its environment due to fluid motion is...
bank.why: Convection = fluid motion carries the heat.

bank.q: Transfer of energy by the emission of electromagnetic radiation is...
bank.why: Radiation needs no contact or medium.

bank.q: Warm air rising from a heater spreads heat through a room. This is an example of...
bank.why: Fluid (air) motion carries the energy: convection.

bank.q: The SI unit of energy is the...
bank.why: The joule is the SI unit; 1000 J = 1 kJ.

bank.q: One calorie is the energy needed to...
bank.a: Raise the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C
d: Raise the temperature of 1 kg of water by 1 °C
bank.why: 1 cal = 4.184 J. The food Calorie (capital C) is 1 kcal = 1000 cal.

bank.q: One food Calorie (Cal) equals...
bank.why: 1000 cal = 1 kcal = 1 Cal.

bank.q: Convert 500 cal to joules.
bank.why: 500 cal × 4.184 J/cal = 2092 J (slide sample).

bank.q: Convert 350 J to calories.
A 0.143 kg baseball travels at 33.5 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
bank.hint: Square the speed; ½ in front.

bank.q: A 0.50 kg object moves at 10.0 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: Heat is the energy used to move an object against a force.
d: Energy is the capacity to do work and transfer heat.
Thermal energy is associated with the random motion of particles.
bank.why: That describes work. Heat is the energy that raises an object's temperature.

bank.q: In thermochemistry, the part of the universe chosen for study is the...
bank.why: System = part studied; surroundings = everything else; boundary separates them; universe = system + surroundings.

bank.q: The universe, in thermodynamics, is...
d: The boundary between system and surroundings
bank.why: Universe = system + surroundings.

bank.q: A system that can exchange both mass and energy with its surroundings is...
bank.why: Open: mass + energy. Closed: energy only. Isolated: neither.

bank.q: A closed system can exchange...
bank.why: Closed = energy only.

bank.term: Classify: Milk kept in a closed thermos flask
bank.q: Classify this system: milk kept in a closed thermos flask.
bank.why: The sealed, insulated flask lets neither mass nor heat through. (slide exercise)

bank.term: Classify: A student reading in a dorm room
bank.q: Classify this system: a student reading in a dorm room.
bank.why: People, air and heat move in and out. (slide exercise)

bank.term: Classify: Air inside a tennis ball
bank.q: Classify this system: air inside a tennis ball.
bank.why: Air (mass) stays in, but heat passes through the rubber. (slide exercise)

bank.q: An exothermic process...
bank.why: Exo = out: heat leaves the system, products have lower enthalpy, ΔH negative.

bank.q: In an endothermic reaction...
bank.a: Heat is absorbed and ΔH is positive
d: Heat is released and ΔH is negative
Heat is absorbed and ΔH is negative
Heat is released and ΔH is positive
bank.why: Endo = in: products have more enthalpy than reactants, so ΔH > 0 (e.g. ice melting).

bank.q: 1 mol of methane burns in oxygen and evolves 890 kJ of heat. What is q?
bank.why: Evolves heat = released = exothermic, so q is negative (slide sample 1).

bank.q: Ba(OH)₂·8H₂O reacts with NH₄NO₃ and the mixture absorbs 170.8 kJ of heat. What is q?
bank.why: Absorbs heat = endothermic, q positive (slide sample 2).

bank.q: 4 mol of NH₃ burns over a platinum catalyst and evolves 1170 kJ of heat. What is q?
bank.why: Heat is evolved, so the reaction is exothermic and q = −1170 kJ for the 4 mol burned (slide exercise).

bank.q: A reaction absorbs 45 kJ of heat from its surroundings. Which is correct?
bank.why: Absorbing heat is endothermic, so ΔH is positive.

bank.q: A property determined only by the current state of a system, regardless of how it got there, is a...
bank.why: Energy, pressure, volume and temperature are state functions: ΔX = X(final) − X(initial).

bank.q: Two hikers reach the same summit by different trails. Their change in potential energy is the same because...
bank.a: Potential energy is a state function
bank.why: Only the start and end states matter (the slides' hiker picture).

bank.q: Which of these is NOT among the four state functions in the lesson?
bank.why: The four: energy, pressure, volume, temperature. Work and heat depend on the path.

bank.q: The first law of thermodynamics states that energy...
bank.a: Can be converted from one form to another but cannot be created or destroyed
d: Can be created but not destroyed
Is lost as heat in every reaction
bank.why: Whatever the system loses, the surroundings gain: ΔE(system) + ΔE(surroundings) = 0.

bank.q: When propane burns (C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O), the chemical energy lost by the system...
bank.a: Equals the energy gained by the surroundings
d: Is greater than the energy gained by the surroundings
bank.why: First law: ΔE(system) = −ΔE(surroundings).

bank.q: The change in internal energy of a system is given by...
bank.why: ΔE = q + w; at constant pressure q = ΔH and w = −PΔV.

bank.q: Enthalpy (H) is used to quantify the heat flow into or out of a system at constant...
bank.why: At constant pressure, q = ΔH. H = E + PV.

bank.q: The enthalpy change of a reaction is calculated as...
bank.why: Final minus initial.

bank.q: If H(products) < H(reactants), the reaction is...
bank.why: Energy goes down, like methane burning: heat released.

bank.q: A balanced equation that includes its ΔH, such as 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g), ΔH = −483.6 kJ, is called a...
bank.why: The negative sign tells us it is exothermic.

bank.q: The heat of reaction is...
bank.a: The q needed to return the system to its starting temperature after the reaction
d: The heat capacity of the calorimeter
bank.why: Ebbing's definition on the slides. At constant pressure it is ΔH(rxn).

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: In an isolated system, neither energy nor mass is exchanged with the surroundings.
d: In a closed system, mass can be exchanged but energy cannot.
An endothermic reaction has a negative ΔH.
bank.why: Closed is the reverse (energy only), work depends on the path, and endothermic ΔH is positive.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: Heat energy must always be available for a reaction to occur; this is called the heat of reaction.
d: The first law says energy is neither created nor destroyed.
Enthalpy describes heat flow at constant pressure.
bank.why: The minimum energy needed to start a reaction is the activation energy, not 'heat energy' or the heat of reaction (a false item on the past quiz).

bank.q: The measurement of heat flow is called...
bank.a: Calorimetry; the device is a calorimeter
d: Thermometry; the device is a thermometer
Spectroscopy; the device is a spectrometer
Titration; the device is a burette
bank.why: Calorimetry uses a calorimeter.

bank.q: The amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of ONE GRAM of a substance by 1 °C is its...
bank.why: Specific heat is per gram; heat capacity C is for a given mass (C = m × s); molar heat capacity is per mole.

bank.q: Heat capacity (C) is related to specific heat (s) by...
bank.why: C = m × s, so q = C × ΔT = m × s × ΔT.

bank.q: The heat absorbed or released when a substance changes temperature is...
bank.why: ΔT = T(final) − T(initial), in °C (or K).

bank.q: When an iron bar cools, the sign of q for the bar is...
bank.a: Negative, because heat is given off
d: Positive, because heat is given off
bank.why: ΔT = final − initial is negative, so q is negative: heat leaves the bar.

bank.q: How much heat is given off when an 869 g iron bar cools from 94 °C to 5 °C? (s of Fe = 0.444 J/g·°C)
A 466 g sample of water is heated from 8.50 °C to 74.60 °C. How much heat does the water absorb? (s = 4.184 J/g·°C)
bank.hint: Convert J to kJ at the end.

bank.q: 50.0 kg of rocks (s = 0.82 J/g·K) warm up by 12.0 °C. How much heat do they absorb?
bank.why: 50.0 kg = 5.00 × 10⁴ g; q = 5.00 × 10⁴ × 0.82 × 12.0 = 4.9 × 10⁵ J. A change of 12.0 °C equals a change of 12.0 K. (The slide's '10⁻⁵' is a typo.)

bank.q: Why can a temperature change in °C be used with a specific heat given in J/g·K?
bank.a: A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K
d: Because K and °C are never interchangeable
Because specific heat does not depend on temperature units
bank.why: The degree sizes are the same; only the zero points differ (273.15).

bank.q: A 25.0 g metal sample absorbs 250.0 J and its temperature rises from 20.0 °C to 42.3 °C. What is its specific heat?
100.0 g of water absorbs 1.50 kJ of heat. By how much does its temperature rise?
The same amount of heat is added to equal masses of water (s = 4.184 J/g·°C) and iron (s = 0.444 J/g·°C). Which is true?
d: Both rise by the same amount
bank.why: ΔT = q / (m s): the smaller the specific heat, the bigger the temperature change. Water resists temperature change.

bank.q: 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g), ΔH = −196 kJ. What is q when 5.00 g of H₂O₂ (34.02 g/mol) decomposes at constant pressure?
bank.why: 0.147 mol H₂O₂ × (−196 kJ / 2 mol H₂O₂) = −14.4 kJ. Forgetting the 2 mol gives −28.8 kJ.

bank.q: How much heat is released when 4.50 g of methane (16.0 g/mol) burns at constant pressure? (ΔH = −890 kJ/mol)
2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g), ΔH = −483.6 kJ. How much heat is released when 1.00 g of H₂ (2.016 g/mol) burns?
Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: Specific heat is the heat needed to raise the temperature of any given mass of a substance by 1 °C.
d: Heat capacity C equals mass times specific heat.
ΔT is the final temperature minus the initial temperature.
A negative q means heat is released by the substance.
bank.why: Specific heat is per GRAM. 'Any given mass' describes heat capacity.

bank.q: Organic chemistry is the study of...
d: Only compounds made by living things
bank.why: Today, organic compounds are those based on carbon structures, whether natural or synthetic.

bank.q: Besides carbon, the chief elements in organic compounds are...
bank.why: C with H, O and N ('CHON'); some also contain S, P or a halogen.

bank.q: The 'vital force' theory held that...
bank.a: Organic compounds could only be produced by living organisms
d: Organic compounds could be made from inorganic ones
Energy cannot be created or destroyed
bank.why: Vitalism said a vital force in living things was needed to make organic compounds. Berzelius was its proponent.

bank.q: The chemist associated with (a proponent of) the vital force theory was...
bank.why: Berzelius supported vitalism; Wöhler's experiment disproved it.
bank.hint: Not the one who disproved it.

bank.q: Who disproved the vital force theory, and when?
bank.why: Wöhler, 1828 (Q&A from the last quiz). Guldberg and Waage (1864) is the law of mass action.

bank.q: Wöhler's experiment produced which organic compound from inorganic starting materials?
bank.why: Heating inorganic ammonium cyanate gave urea, the first synthetic organic compound from inorganic substances.

bank.q: What were the two important results of Wöhler's experiment?
bank.a: It disproved the vital force theory and showed organic compounds can be made from inorganic substances
d: It proved the vital force theory and discovered carbon
It discovered urea in plants and invented the calorimeter
It showed all organic compounds are ionic and that carbon has 4 bonds
bank.why: Both were asked on the last quiz.

bank.q: The two sources of organic compounds are...
bank.a: Plant and animal matter, and synthetic compounds
bank.why: Natural (plant/animal) and synthetic (lab-made).

bank.q: About what percentage of all known compounds are organic?
bank.why: Over 10 million organic compounds vs about 1.7 million inorganic ones, so about 85%.

bank.q: About how many new organic compounds are discovered or made each year?
bank.why: Over 10 million known, about 100,000 new each year; about 1.7 million inorganic compounds.

bank.q: Which of these is classified as INORGANIC even though it contains carbon?
bank.why: Metal carbonate salts and other simple ionic compounds are not included in organic chemistry.

bank.q: Why is organic chemistry the basis of biochemistry?
bank.a: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids and most chemicals of life are organic compounds
d: Living things are made mostly of metals
Organic compounds cannot exist in living things
bank.why: Almost all chemicals in living systems are organic.

bank.q: Compared with sodium chloride, butane (an organic compound) has...
bank.a: Covalent bonds, flammability and a low melting point
d: Ionic bonding and high water solubility
bank.why: Organic: covalent, low mp/bp, insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents, flammable, nonconductor (mock test item).

bank.q: Which pair correctly compares organic and inorganic compounds by bonding?
bank.why: The slides' table: organic (butane) vs inorganic (NaCl). Bonding: organic covalent, inorganic ionic.

bank.q: Which pair correctly compares organic and inorganic compounds by solubility in water?
bank.why: The slides' table: organic (butane) vs inorganic (NaCl). Solubility in water: organic low (insoluble), inorganic high.

bank.q: Which pair correctly compares organic and inorganic compounds by electrical conductivity?
bank.a: Organic: Nonconductor; inorganic: Conducts when dissolved or molten
d: Organic: Conducts when dissolved or molten; inorganic: Nonconductor
Both: Conducts when dissolved or molten
bank.why: The slides' table: organic (butane) vs inorganic (NaCl). Electrical conductivity: organic nonconductor, inorganic conducts when dissolved or molten.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: Organic compounds generally have high melting points because of strong ionic bonds.
d: Organic compounds are generally more soluble in organic solvents than in water.
Wöhler's synthesis of urea led to the demise of the vital force theory.
bank.why: Organic compounds are covalent with weak intermolecular forces, so their melting points are low.

bank.q: The ability of carbon to form stable bonds with other carbon atoms (self-linking) is called...
bank.why: Catenation lets carbon build chains, branches and rings.

bank.q: Which property of carbon best explains the huge number of organic compounds?
bank.a: It forms up to 4 stable covalent bonds, including with other carbons, in chains, branches and rings
d: It loses 4 electrons to form ionic lattices
It is a metal that dissolves in water
It cannot form double or triple bonds
bank.why: Catenation + 4 bonds + multiple bonds + bonds to O, N, S and halogens = nearly limitless arrangements (mock test item).

bank.q: Which describes the bonding of carbon in organic compounds?
d: Two single bonds and a double bond only
Two double bonds, or a single and a triple bond, only
bank.why: Carbon always totals 4 bonds: four single; two single + one double; two double; or one single + one triple (slide exercise).

bank.q: In a neutral organic compound, carbon normally forms...
bank.why: C 4 bonds/0 pairs, H 1/0, N 3/1, O 2/2, halogen 1/3. Bonds + pairs = 4 for every atom except H.

bank.q: In a neutral organic compound, nitrogen normally forms...
bank.why: C 4 bonds/0 pairs, H 1/0, N 3/1, O 2/2, halogen 1/3. Bonds + pairs = 4 for every atom except H.

bank.q: In a neutral organic compound, oxygen normally forms...
bank.why: C 4 bonds/0 pairs, H 1/0, N 3/1, O 2/2, halogen 1/3. Bonds + pairs = 4 for every atom except H.

bank.q: In a neutral organic compound, a halogen normally forms...
bank.why: C 4 bonds/0 pairs, H 1/0, N 3/1, O 2/2, halogen 1/3. Bonds + pairs = 4 for every atom except H.

bank.q: According to VSEPR, the most common bond angles in organic molecules are...
bank.why: Tetrahedral 109.5°, trigonal planar 120°, linear 180°.

bank.q: What is the bond angle around each carbon in methane (CH₄), shown below?
bank.why: Carbon with four single bonds is sp³: tetrahedral, 109.5°.
bank.hint: Count the groups around the carbon.

bank.q: What is the bond angle around each carbon in ethene (C₂H₄), shown below?
bank.why: Carbon with a double bond is sp²: trigonal planar, 120°.
bank.hint: Count the groups around the carbon.

bank.q: What is the bond angle around each carbon in ethyne (C₂H₂), shown below?
bank.why: Carbon with a triple bond is sp: linear, 180°.
bank.hint: Count the groups around the carbon.

bank.q: Hybridization happens when...
bank.a: Atomic orbitals combine to form new, equivalent hybrid orbitals
d: Two molecules combine to form a polymer
bank.why: Q&A from the last quiz: orbitals combine to form new orbitals.

bank.q: Which orbitals combine in the hybridization of carbon?
bank.why: One s with three p = sp³; one s with two p = sp²; one s with one p = sp.

bank.q: What hybridization is found in the double-bonded carbons of alkenes?
bank.why: C=C carbons are sp² (trigonal planar, 120°). Asked on the last quiz.

bank.q: What is the hybridization of the highlighted carbon in propyne?
bank.why: The CH₃ carbon has four single bonds: sp³, tetrahedral.

bank.q: What is the hybridization of the highlighted carbon in propyne?
bank.why: A triple-bonded carbon is sp (linear, 180°).

bank.q: What is the hybridization and bond angle of the highlighted (carbonyl) carbon in acetaldehyde?
bank.why: A C=O carbon has three groups around it: sp², trigonal planar.

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: In a neutral organic compound, oxygen forms two bonds and has two unshared pairs.
d: Nitrogen normally forms four bonds and no unshared pairs.
A tetrahedral carbon has bond angles of 120°.
bank.why: N is 3 bonds + 1 pair, tetrahedral is 109.5°, and alkene carbons are sp².

bank.q: A formula that shows the atoms in a molecule and the bonds connecting them is a...
bank.why: Structural formulas: expanded, condensed or skeletal.

bank.q: An expanded structural formula...
bank.a: Shows all atoms and all bonds, like a Lewis structure without the electron dots
d: Hides all C and H atoms
Implies the bonds without showing them
bank.why: Every bond and atom is drawn.

bank.q: A condensed structural formula...
bank.a: Writes the molecule compactly, with bonds implied rather than shown
d: Shows every bond as a line
bank.why: e.g. CH₃CH₂CH₃ for propane.

bank.q: In a skeletal (line-angle) formula...
bank.a: Each vertex and line end is a carbon, and H atoms on carbon are not shown
d: Each line is a hydrogen atom
bank.why: Lines are C–C bonds; double and triple bonds are still drawn; H on C is deduced so each carbon has 4 bonds.

bank.q: Which condensed formula matches the expanded structure shown?
bank.why: Three carbons in a row, 8 H: propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃.

bank.q: Which condensed formula matches the expanded structure shown?
bank.why: Three-carbon chain with a CH₃ branch on the middle carbon: 2-methylpropane (isobutane).

bank.q: What is the molecular formula of the compound shown?
bank.why: Count carbons at every corner and line end (6), then give each carbon enough H to make 4 bonds: C₆H₁₄.

bank.q: What is the molecular formula of the compound shown (a ring)?
bank.why: Count carbons at every corner and line end (6), then give each carbon enough H to make 4 bonds: C₆H₁₀.

bank.q: What is the molecular formula of the compound shown?
bank.why: Count carbons at every corner and line end (5), then give each carbon enough H to make 4 bonds: C₅H₁₀O.
