bank.q: What is the molecular formula of the compound shown?
bank.why: Count carbons at every corner and line end (7), then give each carbon enough H to make 4 bonds: C₇H₁₂.

bank.q: Which skeletal formula represents CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
bank.why: A five-carbon chain with a CH₃ on the middle (third) carbon: 3-methylpentane.

bank.q: Which is NOT a correct structure for C₃H₈ (propane)?
bank.why: Propane is a 3-carbon chain however it is drawn. The ring is cyclopropane, C₃H₆.

bank.q: In a skeletal formula, how many hydrogens are on a carbon at a line end (bonded to one carbon)?
bank.why: The end carbon has one C–C bond, so it needs 3 H to make 4 bonds: CH₃.

bank.q: A functional group is...
bank.a: An atom or group of atoms with a characteristic set of predictable physical and chemical properties
d: Any carbon chain longer than 3 atoms
A metal ion attached to carbon
The longest chain in a molecule
bank.why: Functional groups determine properties, react the same way in any molecule, define families, and are the basis of naming.

bank.q: Which is NOT a reason functional groups are important?
bank.a: They determine the molar mass of every compound
d: They undergo the same reactions in whatever molecule they are found
They divide organic compounds into families
They provide the basis for naming organic compounds
bank.why: The slides list reactions, properties, families and naming.

bank.q: Which functional group is highlighted in the structure below?
bank.why: Alcohol: an –OH (hydroxyl) group on an sp³ carbon.

bank.q: Which functional group is highlighted in the structure below?
bank.why: Ether: an O single-bonded between two carbons (R–O–R).

bank.q: Which functional group is highlighted in the structure below?
bank.why: Aldehyde: a carbonyl carbon bonded to at least one H.

bank.q: Which functional group is highlighted in the structure below?
bank.why: Ketone: a carbonyl carbon bonded to two carbons.

bank.q: Which functional group is highlighted in the structure below?
bank.why: Carboxylic acid: a –COOH group.

bank.q: Which functional group is highlighted in the structure below?
bank.why: Ester: a carbonyl carbon single-bonded to an –OR (alkoxy) group.

bank.q: Which functional group is highlighted in the structure below?
bank.why: Amide: a carbonyl carbon bonded to N.

bank.q: Which functional group is highlighted in the structure below?
bank.why: Amine: a nitrogen bonded to carbon (–NH₂), not next to C=O.

bank.q: Which functional group is highlighted in the structure below?
bank.why: Thiol: an –SH (sulfhydryl) group.

bank.q: Which functional group is highlighted in the structure below?
bank.why: Alkyl halide: a carbon single-bonded to a halogen.

bank.q: Which functional group is highlighted in the structure below?
bank.why: Alkyne: a carbon-carbon triple bond.

bank.q: Oleic acid (in olive oil) is shown below. Which functional groups does it contain?
bank.why: The –COOH makes it a fatty acid; the cis C=C makes it monounsaturated (slide exercise).

bank.q: Which functional group in oleic acid classifies it as a fatty acid?
bank.why: A fatty acid is a long-chain carboxylic acid; the alkene only makes it unsaturated.

bank.q: To which family does CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO belong?
bank.why: –CHO at the end of the chain is an aldehyde.

bank.q: To which family does HC≡CCH₃ belong?
bank.why: ≡ is a triple bond.

bank.q: To which family does CH₃CH₂SH belong?
bank.why: –SH is the sulfhydryl (mercapto) group.

bank.q: To which family does CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ belong?
bank.why: –COO– between two carbon groups is an ester.

bank.q: To which family does CH₃COCH₃ belong?
bank.why: A C=O in the middle of the chain (between two carbons) is a ketone.

bank.q: To which family does CH₃CONH₂ belong?
bank.why: A carbonyl carbon bonded to N: acetamide (mock test item).

bank.q: To which family does CH₃OCH₂CH₃ belong?
bank.why: O between two carbon groups, no C=O.

bank.q: How does an aldehyde differ from a ketone?
bank.a: An aldehyde's carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one H; a ketone's is bonded to two carbons
d: Aldehydes contain nitrogen; ketones contain sulfur
Aldehydes have a single-bonded O; ketones a double-bonded O
Aldehydes are always cyclic; ketones are always open-chain
bank.why: Both have C=O; the difference is what the carbonyl carbon is attached to.

bank.q: Which functional group has a carbonyl carbon attached directly to an alkoxy (–OR) group?
bank.why: Ester: R–COO–R′. A carboxylic acid has –OH instead of –OR.

bank.q: Which family has an oxygen single-bonded between two carbon atoms?
bank.why: Ether: R–O–R (R groups on either side of O).

bank.q: Which family has a carbon single-bonded to F, Cl, Br or I?
bank.why: The halo group.

bank.q: Which families all contain a C=O (carbonyl) group?
bank.a: Aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters and amides
bank.why: The C–Z single-bond families (halides, alcohols, ethers, amines, thiols) have no C=O.

bank.q: Which structure is an ester?
bank.why: Methyl acetate: C=O with an –OCH₃. The others are a carboxylic acid, an ether and a ketone.

bank.q: Which structure is a ketone?
bank.why: Butanone: the C=O carbon is between two carbons. The others are an aldehyde, an alcohol and an ether.

bank.q: Which structure is an amine?
bank.why: Ethylamine: N bonded to carbon with no C=O. CH₃CONH₂ is an amide.

bank.q: Which structure is an alcohol?
bank.why: 2-Propanol has –OH on an sp³ carbon.

bank.q: A compound that contains a benzene ring is classified as...
bank.why: Aromatic compounds contain the benzene (phenyl) ring.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: An amide contains nitrogen bonded to a carbon that is not part of a C=O.
d: An ester contains a carbonyl carbon bonded to an –OR group.
A carboxylic acid contains a –COOH group.
bank.why: In an amide, N is bonded to the carbonyl carbon. N bonded to a non-carbonyl carbon is an amine.

bank.q: Isomers are compounds with...
bank.a: The same molecular formula but different structures
d: The same structure but different formulas
bank.why: Different structures give them different physical and chemical properties.

bank.q: Constitutional (structural) isomers have the same molecular formula but different...
bank.why: Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but a different 3-D arrangement.

bank.q: Stereoisomers have...
bank.a: The same molecular formula and connectivity but a different arrangement in space
bank.why: Geometric (cis-trans), conformational and optical isomers are stereoisomers.

bank.q: The three kinds of constitutional isomers in the lesson are...
bank.a: Skeletal, positional and functional group isomers
bank.why: Skeleton, position, or functional group changes.

bank.q: The two structures below are both C₅H₁₂. What kind of isomers are they?
bank.why: Pentane is straight; 2-methylbutane is branched. The carbon skeleton changes.
bank.hint: What changed: skeleton, position or group?

bank.q: The two structures below are both C₄H₁₀. What kind of isomers are they?
bank.why: Butane vs 2-methylpropane: straight vs branched chain.
bank.hint: What changed: skeleton, position or group?

bank.q: The two structures below are both C₄H₈. What kind of isomers are they?
bank.why: 1-Butene vs 2-butene: same skeleton, the double bond moves.
bank.hint: What changed: skeleton, position or group?

bank.q: The two structures below are both C₃H₈O. What kind of isomers are they?
bank.why: 1-Propanol vs 2-propanol: the –OH moves.
bank.hint: What changed: skeleton, position or group?

bank.q: The two structures below are both C₄H₈O. What kind of isomers are they?
bank.why: Butanal (aldehyde) vs 2-butanone (ketone).
bank.hint: What changed: skeleton, position or group?

bank.q: The two structures below are both C₂H₆O. What kind of isomers are they?
bank.why: Ethanol (alcohol) vs dimethyl ether (ether), both C₂H₆O.
bank.hint: What changed: skeleton, position or group?

bank.q: Are the two structures below isomers of each other?
bank.a: No; they have different molecular formulas (C₅H₁₂ and C₅H₁₀)
d: Yes; they are functional group isomers
bank.why: Pentane is C₅H₁₂, cyclopentane is C₅H₁₀. Isomers must have the same formula. (1-Pentene and cyclopentane ARE isomers, both C₅H₁₀.)

bank.q: 1-Pentene and cyclopentane are shown below. Which is true?
bank.why: Same formula, but one is a chain with a C=C and the other a ring: different connectivity.

bank.q: Which is NOT an isomer of hexane (C₆H₁₄)?
bank.why: 2,2-Dimethylpentane has 5 + 2 = 7 carbons (C₇H₁₆). The others all have 6 carbons (slide knowledge check).

bank.q: How does the number of possible constitutional isomers change as the number of carbons increases?
bank.why: Butane has 2 isomers, pentane 3, hexane 5, and decane 75.

bank.q: Geometric (cis-trans) isomers arise because of...
bank.a: Restricted rotation around a double bond or in a ring
d: A carbon bonded to four different groups
bank.why: No rotation around C=C (or in a ring) fixes groups on the same side (cis, Z) or opposite sides (trans, E).

bank.q: Which structure is cis-2-butene?
bank.why: Cis: both CH₃ groups on the same side of the C=C. The second is trans-2-butene; the others are 1-butene and 2-methylpropene.

bank.q: Is the compound shown below cis or trans?
bank.a: Trans; the two Cl atoms are on opposite sides of the double bond
d: Cis; the two Cl atoms are on the same side
Neither; it cannot have cis-trans isomers
Cis; Cl atoms are always cis
bank.why: trans-1,2-Dichloroethene, also called (E).

bank.q: Why does the compound shown (1,1-dichloroethene) have no cis-trans isomers?
bank.a: One carbon of the double bond has two identical substituents
d: It has free rotation around the C=C
bank.why: If either C=C carbon carries two identical groups, there are no cis-trans isomers.

bank.q: How many isomers have the formula C₂H₂Cl₂?
bank.why: 1,1-dichloroethene, cis-1,2-dichloroethene and trans-1,2-dichloroethene.

bank.q: Isomers that interconvert by rotation around single bonds (e.g. chair and boat cyclohexane) are...
bank.why: Staggered/eclipsed ethane and chair/boat cyclohexane are conformations.

bank.q: Optical isomers usually arise from a chiral center, which is a carbon bonded to...
bank.why: Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: Isomers always have the same physical properties because they have the same formula.
d: Butanal and 2-butanone are functional group isomers.
Cis-trans isomerism is caused by restricted rotation.
bank.why: Different structures give isomers different physical and chemical properties.

bank.q: A hydrocarbon is a compound composed of...
bank.why: Hydro (H) + carbon (C), nothing else.

bank.q: Hydrocarbons are divided into which two classes?
bank.why: Saturated: only single bonds. Unsaturated: at least one double or triple bond (slide exercise).

bank.q: Alkanes are hydrocarbons that contain...
d: At least one C=C double bond
At least one C≡C triple bond
bank.why: The first two alkanes are methane and ethane.

bank.q: To which class of hydrocarbon does the compound shown belong?
bank.why: It has only single bonds.
bank.hint: Look at the bonds and rings.

bank.q: To which class of hydrocarbon does the compound shown belong?
bank.why: It has a C=C double bond.
bank.hint: Look at the bonds and rings.

bank.q: To which class of hydrocarbon does the compound shown belong?
bank.why: It has a C≡C triple bond.
bank.hint: Look at the bonds and rings.

bank.q: To which class of hydrocarbon does the compound shown belong?
bank.why: It has a ring with only single bonds.
bank.hint: Look at the bonds and rings.

bank.q: To which class of hydrocarbon does the compound shown belong?
bank.why: It has a benzene ring.
bank.hint: Look at the bonds and rings.

bank.q: The IUPAC prefix 'hept-' means a chain of how many carbons?
bank.why: meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4, pent 5, hex 6, hept 7, oct 8, non 9, dec 10.

bank.q: Which prefix is used for a chain of 9 carbons?
bank.why: non = 9, dec = 10, undec = 11.

bank.q: Which prefix shows 4 carbons?
bank.why: meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4.

bank.q: The prefix 'eicos-' means...
bank.why: undec 11, dodec 12, ... hexadec 16, ... nonadec 19, eicos 20.
bank.hint: The last one in the table.

bank.q: In an unbranched alkane's IUPAC name, the suffix -ane shows that...
bank.a: The compound is a saturated hydrocarbon
d: The compound has a double bond
bank.why: Prefix = number of carbons; -ane = saturated.

bank.q: An alkyl group is...
bank.a: A substituent formed by removing one H atom from an alkane, named with -yl
d: An alkane with a double bond
The longest chain in a molecule
bank.why: Drop -ane, add -yl: methane → methyl. It is often written R–.

bank.q: A ___ is a group attached to a carbon chain, and an ___ is formed by removing an H from an alkane.
bank.why: Slide exercise.

bank.q: What is the name of the alkyl group (CH₃)₂CH–?
bank.why: Methyl CH₃–, ethyl CH₃CH₂–, propyl CH₃CH₂CH₂–, isopropyl (CH₃)₂CH–, tert-butyl (CH₃)₃C–.
bank.hint: Count the carbons and the branching.

bank.q: What is the name of the alkyl group (CH₃)₃C–?
bank.why: Methyl CH₃–, ethyl CH₃CH₂–, propyl CH₃CH₂CH₂–, isopropyl (CH₃)₂CH–, tert-butyl (CH₃)₃C–.
bank.hint: Count the carbons and the branching.

bank.q: What is the name of the alkyl group CH₃CH₂CH₂–?
bank.why: Methyl CH₃–, ethyl CH₃CH₂–, propyl CH₃CH₂CH₂–, isopropyl (CH₃)₂CH–, tert-butyl (CH₃)₃C–.
bank.hint: Count the carbons and the branching.

bank.q: In common names, 'iso' shows that one end of an otherwise unbranched chain ends in...
bank.why: e.g. isobutane is (CH₃)₂CHCH₃ = 2-methylpropane.
bank.hint: Two methyls on the end carbon.

bank.q: In the common naming system, all alkanes with the formula C₄H₁₀ are called...
bank.why: The number of carbons decides the common name; iso- and n- tell the branching.

bank.q: Natural gas is mostly...
bank.why: Natural gas: 90-95% methane, 5-10% ethane, plus propane, butane and isobutane.

bank.q: Petroleum is...
bank.a: A thick liquid mixture of thousands of compounds, mostly hydrocarbons, from decomposed marine plants and animals
d: A pure compound made in the laboratory
bank.why: It is separated by fractional distillation.

bank.q: According to the slides' exercise, gasoline is expensive because...
bank.a: It is obtained from crude oil
d: It is made by complex laboratory synthesis
Drilling for natural gasoline is dangerous
bank.why: Gasoline is refined from petroleum (crude oil), a limited natural resource.

bank.q: What is the general formula of an open-chain alkane?
bank.why: e.g. C₅H₁₂. Alkenes and cycloalkanes are CₙH₂ₙ; alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.

bank.q: A hydrocarbon has the formula C₄H₈. It could be...
bank.why: CₙH₂ₙ fits both one C=C and one ring (e.g. 1-butene or cyclobutane).

bank.q: When naming a branched alkane, the parent chain is...
bank.a: The longest continuous chain of carbon atoms
d: The chain with the most hydrogens
The chain with the fewest branches
bank.why: Its name is the root name.

bank.q: With one substituent, number the parent chain from the end that...
bank.a: Gives the substituent the lower number
d: Gives the substituent the higher number
bank.why: Lowest locants.

bank.q: If the same substituent occurs more than once, you...
bank.a: Use di-, tri-, tetra- and separate the numbers with commas
d: Repeat the substituent name each time
bank.why: e.g. 2,2-dimethylbutane. Hyphens join numbers to words; commas separate numbers.

bank.q: Two or more different substituents are listed...
bank.a: In alphabetical order, ignoring di-, tri- and sec-/tert-
d: In the order of their numbers
Alphabetically, counting the di- or tri- prefix
bank.why: e.g. 4-ethyl-2,2-dimethylhexane: compare 'ethyl' and 'methyl', not 'dimethyl'.

bank.q: Different substituents sit at equivalent positions from both ends. Which gets the lower number?
bank.a: The one that comes first alphabetically
bank.why: e.g. 3-ethyl-5-methylheptane, not 5-ethyl-3-methylheptane.

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: Five-carbon parent, methyl on C2 (numbering from the end closer to the branch).
bank.hint: Longest chain, lowest numbers, alphabetical order.

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: Six-carbon parent; methyls on C2 and C4. Use 'di' with commas, not the name twice.
bank.hint: Longest chain, lowest numbers, alphabetical order.

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: Seven-carbon parent with groups at 3 and 5 from either end, so the alphabetically first group (ethyl) gets 3.
bank.hint: Longest chain, lowest numbers, alphabetical order.

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: Number from the end nearer the first branch (2,2,4 beats 3,5,5). Alphabetize ethyl before methyl, ignoring 'di'.
bank.hint: Longest chain, lowest numbers, alphabetical order.

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: The longest chain runs through both ethyl-looking ends: 8 carbons, methyls on 3 and 6 (slide exercise a).
bank.hint: Longest chain, lowest numbers, alphabetical order.

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: Eight-carbon parent; numbering from the left gives 3,4,4,5 (lower than 4,5,5,6). Four methyls = tetramethyl (slide exercise b).
bank.hint: Longest chain, lowest numbers, alphabetical order.

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: Isooctane, the gasoline standard: number from the end nearer the C(CH₃)₂ so the locants are 2,2,4.
bank.hint: Longest chain, lowest numbers, alphabetical order.

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: Ring of six = cyclohexane; one substituent needs no number.

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: Two ring substituents: start numbering at the one that comes first alphabetically (ethyl = C1). Slide exercise b.
bank.hint: Longest chain, lowest numbers, alphabetical order.

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: Locants 1,2,4 beat 1,3,4, so the methyls get 1 and 2; then list ethyl first alphabetically (slide exercise c).
bank.hint: Longest chain, lowest numbers, alphabetical order.

bank.q: Which structure is 2,3-dimethylbutane?
bank.why: A four-carbon chain with a CH₃ on C2 and on C3. The others are 2,2-dimethylbutane, 2-methylpentane and 3-methylpentane.

bank.q: Which structure is 3-ethylpentane?
bank.why: A five-carbon chain with an ethyl on the middle carbon. (A 'chain' drawn with an ethyl on C2 really has a longer parent.)

bank.q: A student names a compound '2-ethylbutane'. What is the correct IUPAC name?
bank.why: An ethyl on C2 extends the chain: the longest chain is 5 carbons with a methyl on C3.

bank.q: To name a cycloalkane with ONE substituent, you...
bank.a: Add cyclo- to the alkane name and give the substituent no number
d: Name the ring as a substituent of the chain
bank.why: e.g. methylcyclohexane.

bank.q: Which rings are especially abundant in nature?
bank.why: Slides: 5- and 6-membered rings are especially common.

bank.q: The most important physical property of alkanes and cycloalkanes is...
bank.a: Their almost complete lack of polarity
bank.why: C–H electronegativity difference 2.5 − 2.1 = 0.4, so C–H is nonpolar covalent.

bank.q: The electronegativity difference between C and H on the Pauling scale is...
The only attractions between alkane molecules are...
bank.why: Nonpolar molecules have only weak dispersion forces.

bank.q: As the molecular weight of unbranched alkanes increases, their boiling points...
bank.why: Bigger molecules have stronger dispersion forces (methane −164 °C ... decane 174 °C).

bank.q: Compared with other compounds of the same molecular weight, alkanes have boiling points that are...
bank.a: Lower than almost any other type
d: Higher than almost any other type
bank.why: Only weak dispersion forces hold them together.

bank.q: Arrange in order of INCREASING boiling point: butane, decane, hexane.
bank.why: More carbons, higher boiling point (slide exercise a).

bank.q: Arrange in order of INCREASING boiling point: 2-methylheptane, octane, 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (all C₈H₁₈).
d: They all boil at the same temperature
bank.why: Same formula: more branching = more compact = less surface contact = lower bp (slide exercise b).

bank.q: Which C₅H₁₂ isomer has the highest boiling point?
bank.why: Unbranched pentane has the most surface contact. (Cyclopentane is C₅H₁₀, not an isomer.)

bank.q: Which unbranched alkane is still a gas at room temperature?
bank.why: Methane through butane are gases; pentane is the first liquid.

bank.q: Alkanes and cycloalkanes are...
bank.why: They cannot form hydrogen bonds with water (slide exercise). Like dissolves like.

bank.q: Liquid alkanes dissolve well in...
bank.a: Other alkanes and nonpolar solvents like toluene and diethyl ether
bank.why: Like dissolves like.

bank.q: Liquid alkanes (about 0.7 g/mL) poured onto water will...
bank.a: Float, because they are less dense and insoluble
bank.why: All liquid and solid alkanes are less dense than water (1.0 g/mL).

bank.q: Compared with an alkane of the same number of carbons, an alkene usually has a ___ melting point.
bank.why: Slide exercise: the double bond's kink lowers packing, so alkenes melt lower.

bank.q: Arrange the butenes in order of INCREASING boiling point: cis-2-butene, trans-2-butene, 1-butene.
d: All three boil at the same temperature
bank.why: 1-Butene −6 °C, trans-2-butene about 1 °C, cis-2-butene about 4 °C. Cis is slightly polar (from the lab long quiz).

bank.q: Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are constitutional isomers. Which is true?
bank.a: They are different compounds with different physical properties
bank.why: Constitutional isomers are different compounds (pentane bp 36 °C; 2,2-dimethylpropane bp 10 °C).

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: Alkenes and alkynes float on water and do not dissolve in it.
d: Alkanes form hydrogen bonds with water.
Branching raises the boiling point of an alkane.
The C–H bond is polar covalent.
bank.why: Nonpolar, density below 1.0 g/mL. Alkanes cannot hydrogen-bond, branching lowers bp, and C–H (0.4) is nonpolar.

bank.q: The simplest alkene is...
bank.why: Ethylene, CH₂=CH₂. The simplest alkyne is acetylene, HC≡CH.

bank.q: The simplest alkyne is...
bank.why: Acetylene, HC≡CH, used in welding torches.

bank.q: VSEPR predicts what bond angle about each carbon of a C=C double bond?
bank.why: In substituted alkenes the angles can be a bit larger than 120° because of repulsion between groups.

bank.q: An alkene shows cis-trans isomerism when...
bank.a: Each carbon of the C=C has two different groups
d: One C=C carbon has two identical groups
It has free rotation about the double bond
bank.why: Restricted rotation plus two different groups on each C=C carbon.
bank.hint: Two different groups on each end.

bank.q: 1-Butene and 2-butene are examples of...
bank.why: Same skeleton, the double bond is in a different position (slide exercise).

bank.q: When naming an alkene, the chain is numbered from the end that...
bank.a: Gives the lower number to the carbons of the C=C
d: Gives the lower number to the branches
Is farthest from the double bond
bank.why: The parent is the longest chain CONTAINING the C=C; the C=C gets the lowest number.

bank.q: The ending that shows a carbon-carbon triple bond is...
bank.why: Alkynes are named like alkenes with -yne.

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: Number from the end nearer the C=C: the double bond starts at C2, and the methyl is on C5 (slide exercise a).

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: The C=C carbons are 1 and 2, numbered toward the first substituent: ethyl on 3, methyl on 4 (slide exercise b).

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: Four carbons, two double bonds starting at C1 and C3: a diene (slide exercise c).

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: The triple bond gets the lowest number (C2); choose the chain with more substituents: ethyl on 4, methyl on 5 (mock test).

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: Six-carbon chain containing the C=C, numbered so the C=C starts at C2: methyls on 2, 4 and 4 (mock test).

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: Five carbons, triple bond starting at C2 (not 3: number from the nearer end).

bank.q: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
bank.why: The two chain parts are on the same side of the C=C: cis (Z).

bank.q: Which structure is 2-methyl-2-butene?
bank.why: Four-carbon chain, C=C from C2 to C3, methyl on C2. The others are 2-methyl-1-butene, 3-methyl-1-butene and 2-pentene.

bank.q: Which structure is trans-2-butene?
bank.why: Trans: the CH₃ groups are on opposite sides of the C=C.

bank.q: When naming a cycloalkene, the double-bond carbons are numbered...
bank.a: 1 and 2, so the double bond's position need not be written
d: Only if there is no substituent
bank.why: e.g. 3-ethyl-4-methylcyclohexene.

bank.q: Alkenes with several double bonds are generally called...
bank.why: Greek poly = many. Two C=C = alkadiene, three = alkatriene.

bank.q: The common names ethylene, propylene and acetylene correspond to...
bank.why: Common names are still used for small alkenes and alkynes.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: The parent chain of an alkene is always the longest chain, even if it does not contain the C=C.
d: Cis-trans isomerism is due to restricted rotation about the C=C.
Alkynes are named with the ending -yne.
bank.why: For alkenes, the parent is the longest chain that CONTAINS the double bond.

bank.q: When alkanes burn with enough oxygen, the products are...
bank.why: Complete combustion: CO₂ + H₂O (+ heat). It is the basis of natural gas, LPG and gasoline as fuels.

bank.q: Balance: CH₄ + __O₂ → CO₂ + __H₂O.
bank.why: 4 H → 2 H₂O; O on the right = 2 + 2 = 4 → 2 O₂.
bank.hint: Balance C, then H, then O.

bank.q: What is the coefficient of O₂ in the balanced combustion of propane, C₃H₈ + __O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O?
bank.why: O on the right: 3 × 2 + 4 × 1 = 10 atoms = 5 O₂.

bank.q: In the balanced equation 2C₄H₁₀ + __O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O, the coefficient of O₂ is...
bank.why: O on the right: 8 × 2 + 10 = 26 atoms = 13 O₂.

bank.q: The halogenation of an alkane (CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl) is a(n)...
bank.why: A halogen atom replaces (substitutes for) a hydrogen atom.

bank.q: Methane reacts with chlorine in light. Which organic product forms first?
bank.why: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl: one H is replaced by Cl.

bank.q: Most alkene addition reactions are exothermic. This means...
bank.a: The products are more stable, but the reaction may still be slow and need a catalyst
d: The products have more energy than the reactants
bank.why: The rate depends on the activation energy, not on ΔH.

bank.q: Adding HX (HCl, HBr or HI) to an alkene gives a(n)...
bank.why: H adds to one C of the C=C and X to the other.

bank.q: Markovnikov's rule: when HX adds to an alkene, H adds to the...
bank.a: Less substituted carbon (the one with more H), and X to the more substituted carbon
d: More substituted carbon, and X to the less substituted one
bank.why: 'The rich get richer': H goes to the C=C carbon that already has more hydrogens.

bank.q: A reaction in which one direction of bond forming is preferred over all others is called...
bank.why: HX addition to an unsymmetrical alkene is regioselective (Markovnikov).

bank.q: What is the major product when HCl adds to propene?
bank.why: Markovnikov: H goes to the CH₂ end, Cl to the middle carbon: 2-chloropropane.
bank.hint: Cl on the more substituted carbon.

bank.q: What is the major product when HBr adds to 2-methylpropene?
bank.why: Br goes to the more substituted carbon (the one with two CH₃ groups): 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
bank.hint: Br on the carbon with no H.

bank.q: HCl adds to 2-butene. What is the product?
bank.why: Both C=C carbons are equivalent, so H adds to one and Cl to the other: 2-chlorobutane. Step 1 forms a 2° carbocation.

bank.q: In the first step of HCl addition, adding H⁺ to the C=C gives a carbocation, which is...
bank.a: A carbon with only three bonds and a positive charge
d: A free radical with no charge
bank.why: In 2-butene the intermediate is a secondary (2°) carbocation.

bank.q: An electrophile is...
bank.a: An electron-poor species that accepts a pair of electrons to form a new bond
d: An electron-rich species that donates an electron pair
A neutral molecule that cannot react
bank.why: Nucleophile = electron-rich, donates a pair. A carbocation is an electrophile; Cl⁻ is a nucleophile.

bank.q: In a reaction mechanism, a curved arrow shows...
bank.a: The movement of an electron pair from its tail (origin) to its head (new position)
d: The movement of a proton only
bank.why: Arrows show which bonds break and form.

bank.q: The acid-catalyzed addition of water to an alkene is called...
bank.why: It follows Markovnikov's rule: OH goes to the more substituted carbon.

bank.q: Propene is hydrated with H₂O and H₂SO₄. What is the major product?
bank.why: Markovnikov: OH on the middle carbon gives 2-propanol (isopropyl alcohol).
bank.hint: OH on the more substituted carbon.

bank.q: 1-Methylcyclohexene is hydrated (H₂O, H₂SO₄). What is the major product?
bank.why: OH adds to the ring carbon that carries the CH₃ (the more substituted carbon of the C=C).

bank.q: Markovnikov's rule says the hydrogen of HCl or H₂O attaches to the unsaturated carbon that...
bank.why: Slide exercise answer (a).

bank.q: Ethene reacts with Br₂. What is the product?
bank.why: Br₂ adds across the C=C: one Br on each carbon (1,2-dibromoethane).

bank.q: Bromine solution is added dropwise to an unknown hydrocarbon and its deep red color disappears. This shows...
bank.a: The compound has a C=C double bond
bank.why: Br₂ adds to the C=C, forming a colorless dibromoalkane: the Br₂ test for unsaturation.

bank.q: Adding H₂ to an alkene (with a Pd, Pt or Ni catalyst) is called...
bank.why: Virtually all alkenes add H₂ over a transition metal catalyst, giving an alkane.

bank.q: Propene reacts with H₂ over a Pt catalyst. The product is...
bank.why: Hydrogenation turns the C=C into a C–C: propene → propane.

bank.q: Which is a common catalyst for adding H₂ to an alkene?
bank.why: Pd, Pt or Ni. H₂SO₄ catalyzes hydration instead.

bank.q: Which reagent turns an alkene into an alcohol?
bank.why: Hydration gives an alcohol; H₂ gives an alkane; Br₂ a dibromoalkane; HCl a chloroalkane.

bank.q: From the industry's point of view, the single most important reaction of alkenes is...
bank.why: Alkene monomers join into long chains (polyethylene, polypropylene, PVC...).

bank.q: The small repeating unit that bonds together to form a polymer is a(n)...
bank.why: Greek mono = single, meros = part; poly = many (slide exercise).

bank.q: In a polymer's structure, the repeating unit is written...
bank.a: In parentheses with a subscript n
d: In square brackets with a superscript +
bank.why: n shows that the unit repeats n times.

bank.q: Which monomer is used to make polypropylene?
bank.why: Propene (propylene). Ethylene → polyethylene, vinyl chloride → PVC, styrene → polystyrene.

bank.q: Poly(vinyl chloride), PVC, is made from which monomer?
bank.why: Vinyl chloride, CH₂=CHCl. Tetrafluoroethylene makes Teflon.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: Halogenation of an alkane is an addition reaction.
d: Br₂ loses its red color when it reacts with an alkene.
Hydration of an alkene follows Markovnikov's rule.
Addition of H₂ to an alkene needs a metal catalyst such as Pt.
bank.why: Alkane halogenation is SUBSTITUTION (H is replaced). Alkenes undergo addition.

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: Because alkene additions are exothermic, they still may need a catalyst to go at a useful rate.
d: Markovnikov's rule puts H on the more substituted carbon.
Polymerization breaks long chains into monomers.
bank.why: Rate depends on activation energy. Markovnikov puts H on the LESS substituted carbon, and polymerization joins monomers.

bank.q: The ion product of water (Kw) is...
bank.a: The product of the molar concentrations of H⁺ and OH⁻ at a given temperature
d: The molar concentration of pure water
bank.why: Kc[H₂O] = Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]; water's own concentration is folded into the constant.

bank.q: Why does [H₂O] not appear in Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]?
bank.a: Water is the solvent; its concentration is essentially constant, so it is folded into the constant
d: Water does not ionize at all
bank.why: Kc × [H₂O] = Kw. The same reason [H₂O] is left out of Ka and Kb.

bank.q: At 25 °C, Kw equals...
bank.why: So in neutral water [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ M.

bank.q: A solution has [H⁺] = 4 × 10⁻⁹ M. Is it acidic, basic or neutral at 25 °C?
bank.why: [H⁺] = 4 × 10⁻⁹ M and [OH⁻] = 2 × 10⁻⁶ M. Acidic if [H⁺] > [OH⁻], basic if [OH⁻] > [H⁺], neutral if equal (slide sample problem).

bank.q: A solution has [OH⁻] = 1 × 10⁻⁷ M. Is it acidic, basic or neutral at 25 °C?
bank.why: [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻⁷ M and [OH⁻] = 1 × 10⁻⁷ M. Acidic if [H⁺] > [OH⁻], basic if [OH⁻] > [H⁺], neutral if equal (slide sample problem).

bank.q: A solution has [OH⁻] = 7 × 10⁻¹³ M. Is it acidic, basic or neutral at 25 °C?
bank.why: [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻² M and [OH⁻] = 7 × 10⁻¹³ M. Acidic if [H⁺] > [OH⁻], basic if [OH⁻] > [H⁺], neutral if equal (slide sample problem).

bank.q: A solution has [H₃O⁺] = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ M. Is it acidic, basic or neutral at 25 °C?
bank.why: [H⁺] = 3 × 10⁻⁴ M and [OH⁻] = 3 × 10⁻¹¹ M. Acidic if [H⁺] > [OH⁻], basic if [OH⁻] > [H⁺], neutral if equal (slide sample problem).

bank.q: The [OH⁻] in a household ammonia cleaner is 0.0025 M. What is [H⁺] at 25 °C?
What is the pH of 2.5 × 10⁻³ M HCl?
bank.why: Strong acid: it dissociates completely, so [H⁺] = 0.0025 M; pH = −log(0.0025) = 2.60.

bank.q: What is the pH of 0.0010 M HNO₃?
bank.why: Strong acid: it dissociates completely, so [H⁺] = 0.0010 M; pH = −log(0.0010) = 3.00.

bank.q: What is the pH of 0.020 M HCl?
bank.why: Strong acid: it dissociates completely, so [H⁺] = 0.020 M; pH = −log(0.020) = 1.70.

bank.q: What is the pH of 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ M NaOH?
bank.why: Strong base: it dissociates completely, so [OH⁻] = 0.00040 M; pOH = 3.40, pH = 14 − pOH = 10.60.

bank.q: What is the pH of 0.010 M Ba(OH)₂?
bank.why: Strong base: it dissociates completely, so [OH⁻] = 0.020 M (two OH⁻ per Ba(OH)₂); pOH = 1.70, pH = 14 − pOH = 12.30.

bank.q: What is the pH of 0.0050 M KOH?
bank.why: Strong base: it dissociates completely, so [OH⁻] = 0.0050 M; pOH = 2.30, pH = 14 − pOH = 11.70.

bank.q: If pOH = 3.25 at 25 °C, what is the pH?
What is [OH⁻] when pH = 11.30?
If the pH of a solution changes from 4 to 2, [H⁺] increases by a factor of...
bank.why: Each pH unit is a 10× change; two units = 10² = 100.

bank.q: According to the slides, the higher the pH...
d: The closer it is to neutral
bank.why: pH measures hydronium; higher pH = less H₃O⁺.

bank.q: At 25 °C, which solution is acidic?
bank.why: Acidic means pH < 7. pOH 3.0 means pH 11, basic.

bank.q: What is the pH of 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ M HCl at 25 °C, roughly?
bank.a: Slightly below 7, because water's own H⁺ cannot be ignored
d: Above 7, because the acid is so dilute
bank.why: −log(10⁻⁸) = 8 would make an acid solution basic, which is impossible. Water's 10⁻⁷ M H⁺ dominates, giving about 6.98.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
d: In a neutral solution at 25 °C, pH = pOH = 7.00.
bank.why: [H₃O⁺] > [OH⁻] is acidic (pH < 7).

bank.q: When a weak acid or weak base dissolves in water...
d: It does not dissociate at all
bank.why: That is why we need Ka and Kb.

bank.q: Which is the Ka expression for HNO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + NO₂⁻?
bank.why: Products over reactants; [H₂O] is left out because it is hardly changed by the dissociation.

bank.q: Which is the Kb expression for NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻?
bank.why: Same pattern as Ka.

bank.q: For a conjugate pair such as NH₄⁺/NH₃, which relation holds?
bank.why: Multiplying the Kb of NH₃ by the Ka of NH₄⁺ cancels everything except [H₃O⁺][OH⁻].

bank.q: The Ka of an acid is 1.0 × 10⁻⁶. What is the Kb of its conjugate base at 25 °C?
The Ka of an acid is 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. What is the Kb of its conjugate base at 25 °C?
The Ka of an acid is 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰. What is the Kb of its conjugate base at 25 °C?
Which acid is the strongest?
bank.why: Larger Ka = more ionization = stronger acid (chlorous acid, 1.1 × 10⁻², vs acetic, HCN, HClO).

bank.q: Which pKa belongs to the strongest acid?
bank.why: Lower pKa = larger Ka = stronger acid.

bank.q: What is the pKa of an acid with Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴?
bank.why: pKa = −log Ka = 4.00.

bank.q: Ka of acetic acid is 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. What is [H₃O⁺] in 0.15 M CH₃COOH?
bank.why: x²/(0.15 − x) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵; with x << 0.15, x = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.15) = 1.6 × 10⁻³ M (slide sample problem). 0.15 M would assume complete ionization.

bank.q: What is the pH of 0.15 M acetic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵)?
bank.why: [H₃O⁺] = 1.6 × 10⁻³ M, so pH = 2.78. Treating it as a strong acid gives −log 0.15 = 0.82.

bank.q: Kb of NH₃ is 1.75 × 10⁻⁵. What is [OH⁻] in 0.0750 M NH₃?
What is the pH of 0.0750 M NH₃ (Kb = 1.75 × 10⁻⁵)?
What is the degree (percent) of ionization of 0.0750 M NH₃ (Kb = 1.75 × 10⁻⁵)?
What is the degree of ionization of nitrous acid in a 0.20 M solution? (Ka = 7.1 × 10⁻⁴)
bank.why: Ka > 10⁻⁵, so solve the quadratic x² + Ka·x − Ka·C = 0: x = 1.2 × 10⁻² M; 1.2 × 10⁻²/0.20 × 100 = 5.8% (the shortcut √(KaC) gives 6.0%).

bank.q: What is the percent ionization of 0.075 M HCN (Ka = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁰)?
When can '−x' be dropped from (C − x) in a weak-acid calculation, according to the slides?
bank.a: When the ionization constant is about 10⁻⁵ or smaller
bank.why: A small K means x is tiny compared with C. With a larger Ka (or a very dilute acid), use the quadratic.

bank.q: What is wrong with calculating the pH of 0.10 M acetic acid as −log(0.10) = 1.00?
bank.a: It assumes the weak acid ionizes completely
bank.why: Weak acids ionize partially; use Ka.

bank.q: A 0.10 M weak acid has Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. What is its approximate pH?
bank.why: [H⁺] ≈ √(10⁻⁵ × 0.10) = 10⁻³ M, pH 3.00. 1.00 would be a strong acid.

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: Ka changes with temperature but not with the acid's concentration.
d: Ka increases when more acid is added.
A smaller Ka means a stronger acid.
Ka is the same as the acid's initial concentration.
bank.why: Ka is an equilibrium constant: temperature-dependent only. Smaller Ka = weaker acid.

bank.q: An Arrhenius acid is a hydrogen-containing compound that...
bank.a: Produces H⁺ ions in water through ionization
d: Produces OH⁻ ions in water through dissociation
bank.why: e.g. HCl, HNO₃. Ionization: ions are produced from a molecular compound.

bank.q: An Arrhenius base is a hydroxide-containing compound that...
bank.a: Produces OH⁻ ions in water through dissociation
bank.why: e.g. NaOH, KOH. Dissociation: ions already in an ionic compound are released.

bank.q: What is the difference between ionization and dissociation in Arrhenius theory?
bank.a: Ionization makes ions from a molecular compound (acids); dissociation releases ions from an ionic compound (bases)
d: Ionization releases ions from an ionic compound; dissociation makes ions from a molecule
bank.why: Figure 10-1 in the slides.

bank.q: A Brønsted-Lowry acid is a...
bank.why: BL base = proton acceptor.

bank.q: Why must a Brønsted-Lowry acid and base appear together?
bank.a: A proton donated by one substance must be accepted by another
d: Acids and bases cannot exist separately in water
Because water is always the acid
bank.why: You cannot have one without the other.

bank.q: The white haze on lab glassware forms from HCl(g) + NH₃(g) → NH₄Cl(s). Which is the Brønsted-Lowry acid?
bank.why: HCl donates H⁺ to NH₃, forming NH₄⁺Cl⁻.

bank.q: In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, which species is the Brønsted-Lowry acid?
bank.why: Water donates a proton to ammonia. NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid; OH⁻ the conjugate base.

bank.q: The structural requirement for an amphiprotic substance is...
bank.a: Both a hydrogen atom and a lone pair of electrons
bank.why: It can donate H⁺ (needs H) and accept H⁺ (needs a lone pair). Water is the most common.

bank.q: In H₃PO₄ + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + H₂PO₄⁻, water acts as a...
bank.why: Water accepts the proton from H₃PO₄, becoming H₃O⁺ (its conjugate acid).

bank.q: What is the conjugate base of H₂PO₄⁻?
bank.why: Remove one H⁺: H₂PO₄⁻ → HPO₄²⁻. H₃PO₄ is its conjugate acid.

bank.q: Which is a conjugate acid-base pair?
bank.why: A conjugate pair differs by exactly one H⁺.

bank.q: A Lewis acid is a species that...
bank.a: Accepts an electron pair and has vacant orbitals (electrophile)
bank.why: Lewis base: donates a lone pair (nucleophile).

bank.q: Ammonia's lone pair bonds to boron in BF₃. Which is the Lewis acid?
bank.a: BF₃, because boron accepts the electron pair
d: NH₃, because it donates the electron pair
bank.why: The slides' example: B accepts the pair (Lewis acid); NH₃ donates it (Lewis base).

bank.q: Which is a Lewis base?
bank.a: NH₃ (has a lone pair to donate)
bank.why: Lewis bases have lone pairs; BF₃, H⁺ and Al³⁺ accept pairs.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: A Brønsted-Lowry base is a proton donor.
d: A Lewis base is a nucleophile.
An Arrhenius base produces OH⁻ in water.
bank.why: A BL base is a proton ACCEPTOR.

bank.q: The presence of a common ion ___ the ionization of a weak acid or weak base.
bank.why: e.g. adding CH₃COONa to CH₃COOH shifts CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ to the left.

bank.q: Sodium acetate is added to acetic acid. What happens?
bank.a: Acetic acid ionizes less and the pH rises
d: Acetic acid ionizes more and the pH falls
bank.why: Extra CH₃COO⁻ (common ion) pushes the equilibrium back to CH₃COOH; fewer H⁺, so pH rises. Ka is unchanged.

bank.q: Which pair is listed in the slides as a buffer?
bank.why: Slide examples: CH₃COOH/CH₃COONa, H₂CO₃/NaHCO₃, NaH₂PO₄/Na₂HPO₄. Strong acid + its salt is not a buffer.

bank.q: A small amount of HCl is added to an acetic acid/acetate buffer. Which reaction absorbs it?
bank.why: The conjugate base consumes added H⁺.

bank.q: A small amount of NaOH is added to the same buffer. Which reaction absorbs it?
bank.why: The weak acid neutralizes added OH⁻.

bank.q: A buffer has equal concentrations of HA and A⁻. Its pH equals...
bank.why: log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa.

bank.q: Which buffer has the greatest capacity (same acid/base ratio)?
bank.why: More of each component can neutralize more added acid or base; the pH is the same, the capacity is not.

bank.q: A buffer has pKa = 4.76, [A⁻] = 0.10 M and [HA] = 0.20 M. What is its pH?
A buffer has pKa = 6.35, [A⁻] = 0.50 M and [HA] = 0.050 M. What is its pH?
A 1.00 L buffer has 0.0025 mol H₂CO₃ and 0.025 mol HCO₃⁻ (Ka = 4.3 × 10⁻⁷). What is its pH?
What is the pH of a buffer that is 0.200 M NH₃ and 0.300 M NH₄Cl (Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵)?
What ratio [Na₂C₂O₄]/[NaHC₂O₄] gives a buffer of pH 4.5? (Ka = 6.4 × 10⁻⁵)
A buffer is made from 0.600 L of 0.12 M HClO and 0.300 L of 0.53 M NaClO (Ka of HClO = 3.5 × 10⁻⁸). What is its pH?
bank.why: Use moles (same total volume): HClO = 0.0720 mol, ClO⁻ = 0.159 mol. pKa = 7.46; pH = 7.46 + log(0.159/0.0720) = 7.80. Using the two molarities directly ignores the different volumes.

bank.q: 0.030 mol NaOH is added to that HClO/NaClO buffer (no volume change). What is the new pH?
bank.hint: Base converts acid to conjugate base.

bank.q: A buffer has 0.20 mol HA and 0.20 mol A⁻. 0.05 mol OH⁻ is added. What are the new amounts?
bank.why: OH⁻ + HA → A⁻ + H₂O.

bank.q: A buffer's [A⁻]/[HA] changes from 1 to 100. Its pH...
bank.why: log 100 − log 1 = 2.

bank.q: Buffers, especially bicarbonate, keep extracellular fluid at pH...
bank.why: Acid-base disturbances are checked with arterial blood pH and venous CO₂.

bank.q: Which condition can cause respiratory acidosis?
bank.why: Retained CO₂ → more carbonic acid → lower pH. Vomiting causes alkalosis.

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: Both parts of a buffer must be present, and they must not neutralize each other.
d: A buffer keeps the pH exactly constant no matter how much acid is added.
HCl and NaCl make a good buffer.
Adding a common ion increases the ionization of a weak acid.
bank.why: Buffers resist small to moderate additions only; strong acid + its salt is not a buffer; common ions decrease ionization.

bank.q: Titration is a method to...
bank.a: Determine the concentration of an unknown solution by adding a known reagent that gives a known reaction
d: Separate a mixture by boiling point
Weigh a precipitate to find its mass
Measure the melting point of a solid
bank.why: A known reagent is added until a known reaction (color change or electrical signal) shows completion.

bank.q: Which is an advantage of titration over gravimetric analysis?
bank.a: Superior speed and lower cost, with a little sacrifice in accuracy
d: Higher accuracy than any other method
bank.why: Faster, convenient, less expensive and fewer materials; slightly less accurate and precise.

bank.q: Which requirement for a successful titration is described: 'A definite, reproducible relationship exists between the reacting substances'?
bank.why: The three requirements: stoichiometric, quantitative, fast.

bank.q: Which requirement for a successful titration is described: 'The reaction goes to completion when an equivalent amount of titrant is added'?
bank.why: The three requirements: stoichiometric, quantitative, fast.

bank.q: Which requirement for a successful titration is described: 'Slow reactions make the equivalence point hard to estimate'?
bank.why: The three requirements: stoichiometric, quantitative, fast.

bank.q: Which use of titration is this? Measuring the exact amount of hCG in a blood sample.
bank.why: From the slides' list of uses of acid-base titrations.

bank.q: Which use of titration is this? Monitoring pH, ammonia, nitrites, nitrates and phosphates for pets.
bank.why: From the slides' list of uses of acid-base titrations.

bank.q: Which use of titration is this? Finding the right proportion of medicines in an IV drip.
bank.why: From the slides' list of uses of acid-base titrations.

bank.q: Which use of titration is this? Testing free fatty acids, vitamin C and the readiness of cheese.
bank.why: From the slides' list of uses of acid-base titrations.

bank.q: Which use of titration is this? Finding the proper concentration of anesthetic for test animals.
bank.why: From the slides' list of uses of acid-base titrations.

bank.q: The general reaction in an acid-base titration is...
bank.why: OH⁻ neutralizes H⁺ to form water; the rest forms a salt.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: Slow reactions are best for titration because the endpoint is easier to see.
d: Titration is faster and cheaper than gravimetric analysis.
The reaction must go to completion.
The reaction must have a definite stoichiometry.
bank.why: Slow reactions make the equivalence point hard to estimate; the reaction must be fast.

bank.q: Which term matches: 'The solution of known concentration added from the burette'?
bank.why: Titrant: the solution of known concentration added from the burette.

bank.q: Which term matches: 'The sample of unknown concentration being titrated'?
bank.why: Analyte: the sample of unknown concentration being titrated.

bank.q: Which term matches: 'The point where moles of H⁺ and OH⁻ are exactly equal (stoichiometric completion)'?
bank.why: Equivalence point: the point where moles of h⁺ and oh⁻ are exactly equal (stoichiometric completion).

bank.q: Which term matches: 'The point where the indicator changes color'?
bank.why: End point: the point where the indicator changes color.

bank.q: Which term matches: 'A substance that changes color when the reaction is over'?
bank.why: Indicator: a substance that changes color when the reaction is over.

bank.q: Which term matches: 'A solution of accurately known concentration'?
bank.why: Standard solution: a solution of accurately known concentration.

bank.q: How do the equivalence point and the end point differ?
bank.a: Equivalence is the stoichiometric completion; the end point is the observed indicator color change
d: They are always exactly the same moment
The end point comes before any titrant is added
Equivalence depends on the indicator's color
bank.why: A good indicator makes the end point fall very close to the equivalence point.

bank.q: Phenolphthalein is...
bank.a: Colorless in acidic and neutral solutions, reddish pink in basic solutions
d: Pink in acid, colorless in base
Blue in acid, yellow in base
bank.why: One extra drop of NaOH past equivalence turns the KHP solution pink.

bank.q: During the KHP titration the flask is colorless at equivalence, then turns pink with one more drop of NaOH. Why?
bank.a: The solution has just become basic
bank.why: Excess OH⁻ makes it basic and phenolphthalein turns pink.

bank.q: The acid commonly used to standardize NaOH is potassium hydrogen phthalate (KHP), which is...
bank.why: One acidic H, so KHP : NaOH = 1 : 1.

bank.q: To standardize an NaOH solution means to...
bank.a: Find its exact concentration by titrating it against an acid of accurately known amount
bank.why: NaOH is standardized against KHP.

bank.q: In the KHP standardization, where is each solution placed?
bank.a: NaOH in the burette; KHP solution in the Erlenmeyer flask
d: KHP in the burette; NaOH in the flask
NaOH in a beaker; KHP in a test tube
bank.why: Figure 4.21: NaOH is added from the buret to KHP in the flask.

bank.term: pH at equivalence Strong acid-strong base
bank.q: In a strong acid-strong base titration (HCl vs NaOH), the pH at the equivalence point is...
bank.why: The salt formed decides: no hydrolysis (7), a basic conjugate base (>7) or an acidic conjugate acid (<7).

bank.term: pH at equivalence Weak acid-strong base
bank.q: In a weak acid-strong base titration (acetic acid vs NaOH), the pH at the equivalence point is...
bank.why: The salt formed decides: no hydrolysis (7), a basic conjugate base (>7) or an acidic conjugate acid (<7).

bank.term: pH at equivalence Strong acid-weak base
bank.q: In a strong acid-weak base titration (HCl vs ammonia), the pH at the equivalence point is...
bank.why: The salt formed decides: no hydrolysis (7), a basic conjugate base (>7) or an acidic conjugate acid (<7).

bank.q: Which type of titration is HCl versus NaOH?
bank.why: The three types in the slides, with their examples.
bank.hint: Strong or weak on each side.

bank.q: Which type of titration is HCl versus ammonia?
bank.why: The three types in the slides, with their examples.
bank.hint: Strong or weak on each side.

bank.q: Which type of titration is NaOH versus acetic acid?
bank.why: The three types in the slides, with their examples.
bank.hint: Strong or weak on each side.

bank.q: When the sample being analyzed is an acid, the titration is called...
bank.why: Acidimetry: sample is an acid. Alkalimetry: sample is a base.

bank.q: At the half-equivalence point of a weak acid titrated with a strong base...
bank.why: Half the HA is now A⁻, so [HA] = [A⁻].

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: The titrant has a known concentration and is added from the burette.
d: The analyte is the solution of known concentration.
The end point is where moles of acid equal moles of base, by definition.
bank.why: Analyte is unknown; equivalence is the stoichiometric point; phenolphthalein is pink in base.

bank.q: For a 1:1 acid-base reaction at the equivalence point...
bank.why: Moles acid = moles base. For other ratios, use the balanced equation.

bank.q: 23.48 mL of NaOH neutralizes 0.5468 g of KHP (204.2 g/mol). What is the molarity of the NaOH?
28.50 mL of NaOH neutralizes 0.6134 g of KHP (204.2 g/mol). What is the molarity of the NaOH?
25.00 mL of H₂SO₄ needs 43.79 mL of 0.1172 M NaOH. What is the molarity of the H₂SO₄?
bank.why: mol NaOH = 0.005132; H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, so mol H₂SO₄ = 0.002566; ÷ 0.02500 L = 0.1026 M. Forgetting the 1:2 ratio doubles it.

bank.q: 60.2 mL of 0.427 M KOH neutralizes 10.1 mL of H₂SO₄. What is the molarity of the H₂SO₄?
bank.why: mol KOH = 0.0257; ÷ 2 = 0.0129 mol H₂SO₄; ÷ 0.0101 L = 1.27 M (slide exercise answer 1.27 M).

bank.q: 35.00 mL of HCl is titrated with 0.1250 M NaOH; 29.15 mL are needed. What is the HCl concentration?
45.8 mL of 0.215 M Ba(OH)₂ neutralizes 25.0 mL of H₃PO₄ (3Ba(OH)₂ + 2H₃PO₄ → Ba₃(PO₄)₂ + 6H₂O). What is [H₃PO₄]?
How much 0.100 M NaOH neutralizes 25.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl?
bank.why: 1:1 and equal molarities → equal volumes.

bank.q: A 20.0 mL sample of 0.150 M monoprotic acid is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. What volume of NaOH is needed?
What volume of 0.200 M NaOH is needed to neutralize 50.0 mL of 0.250 M H₂SO₄?
bank.why: mol H₂SO₄ = 0.0125; NaOH needed = 0.0250 mol; ÷ 0.200 = 125 mL.

bank.q: What mass of KHP (204.2 g/mol) reacts with 20.00 mL of 0.1054 M NaOH?
A student adds NaOH past the end point (deep pink). How does this affect the calculated NaOH molarity in a KHP standardization?
bank.a: It comes out too low, because the recorded NaOH volume is too large
bank.why: M = mol KHP / V; a larger V gives a smaller M.

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: For H₂SO₄ titrated with NaOH, the moles of NaOH at equivalence are twice the moles of H₂SO₄.
d: CₐVₐ = C_bV_b applies to every reaction regardless of ratio.
bank.why: CₐVₐ = C_bV_b is only for 1:1; KHP is monoprotic; the burette holds the titrant.

bank.q: Which property distinguishes gases from most liquids and solids?
bank.a: Large spaces between particles, so gases are highly compressible
bank.why: Gases: large spaces, very low density, highly compressible, expand to fill their container.

bank.q: Pressure is defined as...
bank.a: The force applied per unit area
bank.why: P = force / area.

bank.q: What causes the pressure of a gas in a sealed container?
bank.a: Gas particles colliding with the container walls
d: Attractions between the particles and the walls
bank.why: The force comes from constant collisions with the walls.

bank.q: A device used to measure atmospheric pressure is a...
bank.why: A manometer measures the pressure of a gas sample (like the CO₂ flask).

bank.q: Standard atmospheric pressure equals...
bank.why: Also 1.01325 bar and 14.7 psi.

bank.q: Convert 291.4 mmHg to atm.
bank.why: 291.4 mmHg = 0.3834 atm, using 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101.325 kPa = 14.7 psi.

bank.q: Convert 0.3834 atm to kPa.
bank.why: 0.3834 atm = 38.85 kPa, using 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101.325 kPa = 14.7 psi.

bank.q: Convert 1.50 atm to mmHg.
bank.why: 1.50 atm = 1140 mmHg, using 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101.325 kPa = 14.7 psi.

bank.q: Convert 730 mmHg to atm.
bank.why: 730 mmHg = 0.961 atm, using 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101.325 kPa = 14.7 psi.

bank.q: Convert 2.00 atm to psi.
bank.why: 2.00 atm = 29.4 psi, using 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101.325 kPa = 14.7 psi.

bank.q: CO₂ from heated limestone is collected in a flask on a closed-end manometer; Δh = 291.4 mmHg. What is the CO₂ pressure?
bank.why: 1 mmHg = 1 torr; 291.4/760 = 0.3834 atm; × 101.325 = 38.85 kPa (slide sample problem).
bank.hint: Closed-end: Δh is the gas pressure.

bank.q: Which statement describes Boyle's law?
bank.a: Pressure is inversely proportional to volume at constant temperature (and amount)
d: Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant pressure
Pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant volume
Volume is directly proportional to moles at constant temperature and pressure
bank.why: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.
bank.hint: Which two variables, and what is held constant?

bank.q: Which equation is Boyle's law?
bank.why: Boyle's law: pressure is inversely proportional to volume at constant temperature (and amount).

bank.q: Which statement describes Charles's law?
bank.a: Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant pressure
d: Pressure is inversely proportional to volume at constant temperature (and amount)
Pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant volume
Volume is directly proportional to moles at constant temperature and pressure
bank.why: Charles's law: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.
bank.hint: Which two variables, and what is held constant?

bank.q: Which equation is Charles's law?
bank.why: Charles's law: volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant pressure.

bank.q: Which statement describes Gay-Lussac's law?
bank.a: Pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant volume
d: Pressure is inversely proportional to volume at constant temperature (and amount)
Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant pressure
Volume is directly proportional to moles at constant temperature and pressure
bank.why: Gay-Lussac's law: P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂.
bank.hint: Which two variables, and what is held constant?

bank.q: Which equation is Gay-Lussac's law?
bank.why: Gay-Lussac's law: pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant volume.

bank.q: Which statement describes Avogadro's law?
bank.a: Volume is directly proportional to moles at constant temperature and pressure
d: Pressure is inversely proportional to volume at constant temperature (and amount)
Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant pressure
Pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature at constant volume
bank.why: Avogadro's law: V₁/n₁ = V₂/n₂.
bank.hint: Which two variables, and what is held constant?

bank.q: Which equation is Avogadro's law?
bank.why: Avogadro's law: volume is directly proportional to moles at constant temperature and pressure.

bank.q: Which must stay constant for Boyle's law to apply?
bank.why: Boyle relates P and V only.

bank.q: A gas is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature and amount. Its pressure...
bank.why: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂: half the volume, twice the pressure.

bank.q: Why must temperatures be in kelvin in Charles's and Gay-Lussac's laws?
bank.a: The proportionality only holds on an absolute temperature scale
d: Kelvin removes the need to know the pressure
Celsius can never be used, even after converting
Kelvin makes volume independent of temperature
bank.why: At 0 °C a Celsius ratio would divide by zero; volume and pressure are proportional to absolute T. K = °C + 273.15.

bank.q: A sealed, rigid container of gas is heated. What happens?
bank.a: Pressure increases while volume stays constant
bank.why: Gay-Lussac: rigid → constant V; P ∝ T.

bank.q: The absolute temperature of a gas in a rigid container doubles. The pressure...
bank.a: Doubles, because P ∝ T at constant volume
bank.why: Gay-Lussac's law.

bank.q: Air occupying 12.0 dm³ at 98.9 kPa is compressed to 119.0 kPa at constant temperature. What is the new volume?
bank.why: V₂ = P₁V₁/P₂ = 98.9 × 12.0 / 119.0 = 9.97 dm³ (slide sample).

bank.q: 785 L of oxygen at 1.00 atm and 21.0 °C. What would the volume be at 28.0 °C (same pressure)?
bank.why: V₂ = V₁ × T₂/T₁ = 785 × 301.15/294.15 = 804 L. Using °C gives 1050 L (wrong).

bank.q: A gas's pressure is 765 torr at 23 °C. At what temperature will the pressure be 560 torr (constant volume)?
bank.why: T₂ = T₁ × P₂/P₁ = 296 K × 560/765 = 217 K = −56 °C (slide sample).

bank.q: A balloon expands from 5.0 L to 35.2 L at constant T and P. It started with 0.30 mol. How many moles were added?
bank.why: n₂ = n₁ × V₂/V₁ = 0.30 × 35.2/5.0 = 2.11 mol; added = 2.11 − 0.30 = 1.8 mol (slide answer 1.812 mol). 2.1 mol is the total, not the amount added.

bank.q: A gas has a volume of 2.00 L at 3.00 atm. If the volume increases to 6.00 L at constant temperature, what is the final pressure?
0.500 mol of gas occupies 11.2 L. What volume will 1.50 mol occupy at the same T and P?
Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: According to Charles's law, volume is inversely proportional to temperature.
d: Avogadro's law holds temperature and pressure constant.
bank.why: Charles: V is DIRECTLY proportional to absolute T.

bank.q: The combined gas law for a fixed amount of gas is...
bank.why: It merges Boyle's (V ∝ 1/P) and Charles's (V ∝ T): V ∝ T/P.

bank.q: The combined gas law comes from combining...
bank.a: Boyle's law and Charles's law (with Gay-Lussac's)
bank.why: V ∝ 1/P and V ∝ T → V ∝ T/P.

bank.q: 39.8 mg of caffeine gives 10.1 cm³ of N₂ at 23 °C and 746 mmHg. What is the N₂ volume at 0 °C and 760 mmHg?
bank.why: V₂ = V₁ × (P₁/P₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 10.1 × (746/760) × (273.15/296.15) = 9.14 cm³ (slide sample). The 39.8 mg is not needed.

bank.q: A gas at 1.50 atm, 2.00 L and 27 °C changes to 3.00 L and 127 °C. What is its final pressure?
STP in the lesson is...
bank.why: At STP one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 L.

bank.q: At STP, one mole of any ideal gas occupies...
bank.why: The molar volume of a gas.

bank.q: Why does one mole of ANY gas occupy the same volume at the same T and P?
bank.a: At the same temperature all gas particles have the same average kinetic energy and hit the walls with the same force
d: All gases have the same molar mass
All gas molecules are the same size
bank.why: Slides: equal kinetic energy → equal force on the walls.

bank.q: What volume does 2.00 mol of a gas occupy at STP?
What volume does 0.250 mol of a gas occupy at STP?
How many moles of gas are in 5.60 L at STP?
The ideal gas law, which combines all the gas laws, is...
bank.why: Relates the four variables P, V, n, T.

bank.q: Which value of R is used with pressure in atm and volume in liters?
bank.why: R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) or 8.315 dm³·kPa/(mol·K).

bank.q: What pressure (atm) do 1.82 mol of SF₆ exert in a 5.43 L steel vessel at 45.0 °C?
bank.why: P = nRT/V = 1.82 × 0.0821 × 318.15 / 5.43 = 8.75 atm (slide sample). Using 45.0 instead of 318.15 K gives 1.24.

bank.q: A gas occupies 5.00 L at 1.00 atm and 25 °C. How many moles are present? (R = 0.0821)
Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: At STP, 2.00 mol of any ideal gas occupy about 44.8 L.
d: The combined gas law includes the number of moles.
bank.why: STP is 0 °C; 8.315 goes with dm³·kPa; the combined law is for a fixed amount.

bank.q: Which is NOT a postulate of the kinetic molecular theory?
bank.a: Gas particles stay stationary between collisions
d: Gas molecules are in continuous, random motion
The molecules' own volume is negligible compared with the container
Attractive and repulsive forces between molecules are negligible
bank.why: The five postulates: random motion, negligible volume, negligible forces, energy transferred but average KE constant at constant T, average KE ∝ absolute T.

bank.q: Two different gases are at the same temperature. According to KMT...
bank.a: Their molecules have the same average kinetic energy
d: Their molecules have the same average speed
They must have the same molar mass
Their molecules exert gravitational forces on the container
bank.why: Average KE depends only on absolute temperature. (Lighter molecules move faster to have the same KE.)

bank.q: When the absolute temperature of a gas increases, the average kinetic energy of its molecules...
d: Stays constant if pressure is constant
bank.why: Average KE ∝ absolute temperature.

bank.q: During collisions between gas molecules at constant temperature...
bank.a: Energy can be transferred, but the average kinetic energy stays the same
d: The average kinetic energy keeps rising
bank.why: KMT postulate 4.

bank.q: The gas state is described in the slides as...
bank.a: Kinetic energy (disruptive forces) completely dominating potential energy (cohesive forces)
bank.why: Attractions are so weak they are taken as zero; particles move independently and randomly.

bank.q: Dalton's law of partial pressures states that...
bank.a: The total pressure of a gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures
d: The total pressure is the average of the partial pressures
Each gas's pressure equals the total divided by the number of gases
bank.why: P_total = P_A + P_B + P_C + ...; each partial pressure obeys P_AV = n_ART.

bank.q: A mixture has partial pressures of 0.25 atm, 0.40 atm and 0.85 atm. What is the total pressure?
A mixture of O₂ and N₂ has a total pressure of 760 mmHg. O₂ contributes 160 mmHg. What is the partial pressure of N₂?
A 1.00 L sample of dry air at 25.0 °C and 786 mmHg contains 0.925 g N₂ (28.02 g/mol). What is the partial pressure of N₂?
bank.hint: P_A = n_ART/V; 786 mmHg is the total.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: At the same temperature, all gas molecules move at the same average speed.
d: At the same temperature, all gases have the same average kinetic energy.
The total pressure of a mixture is the sum of its partial pressures.
Attractive forces between gas molecules are considered negligible.
bank.why: Same KE, but lighter molecules are faster.

bank.q: Isomers are compounds that have...
bank.a: The same molecular formula but different structures
d: Different molecular formulas but identical structures
The same physical and chemical properties in all cases
Only the same number of carbon atoms
bank.why: Because the structures differ, their physical and chemical properties often differ.

bank.q: Why can isomers have different physical and chemical properties?
bank.a: Their atoms are connected or arranged differently
d: They have different numbers of electrons
bank.why: Same atoms, different arrangement.

bank.q: Which type of isomer has the same molecular formula but a different connectivity of atoms?
bank.why: Different connections.

bank.q: Which type has the same formula and connectivity but a different 3-D arrangement?
bank.why: Geometric, conformational and optical isomers are stereoisomers.

bank.q: Which is NOT a type of stereoisomerism?
bank.why: Positional isomers are constitutional.

bank.q: Skeletal isomers are also commonly called...
bank.why: Transes: skeletal = chain isomers; positional = regioisomers; functional = functional group isomers.

bank.q: Positional isomers are also known as...
bank.why: The functional group's region (position) changes.

bank.q: Two compounds have the same formula and functional group, but the carbon skeleton differs. What kind of constitutional isomers are they?
bank.why: Skeleton, position or group.

bank.q: Two compounds have the same carbon skeleton and functional group, but the group is in a different position. What kind of constitutional isomers are they?
bank.why: Skeleton, position or group.

bank.q: Two compounds have the same molecular formula but different functional groups. What kind of constitutional isomers are they?
bank.why: Skeleton, position or group.

bank.q: Which pair best illustrates positional isomerism?
bank.why: The –OH moves from C1 to C2.

bank.q: Which pair best illustrates functional group isomerism?
bank.why: Alcohol vs ether, both C₂H₆O.

bank.q: Which compound is NOT an isomer of hexane, C₆H₁₄?
bank.why: 2,2-Dimethylpentane has 7 carbons.

bank.q: What kind of isomers are the two structures shown?
bank.why: Same formula; check whether the skeleton, the group's position or the group itself changed.

bank.q: What kind of isomers are the two structures shown?
bank.why: Same formula; check whether the skeleton, the group's position or the group itself changed.

bank.q: What kind of isomers are the two structures shown?
bank.why: Same formula; check whether the skeleton, the group's position or the group itself changed.

bank.q: What kind of isomers are the two structures shown?
bank.why: Same formula; check whether the skeleton, the group's position or the group itself changed.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: Constitutional isomers must be mirror images of each other.
d: Constitutional isomers have different atom connectivity.
More carbon atoms allow more isomers.
bank.why: Mirror images are an optical (stereo) idea; constitutional isomers just connect atoms differently.

bank.q: Geometric isomerism results from...
bank.a: Restricted rotation, usually around a double bond or within a ring
d: A carbon with four different groups
bank.why: Rigid C=C or ring.

bank.q: In a compound with a double bond, what does 'cis' mean for two identical substituents?
bank.a: They are on the same side of the double bond
d: They are on the opposite side
They are attached to the same carbon
bank.why: cis = same side (Z); trans = opposite sides (E), for both double bonds and rings.

bank.q: In a compound with a double bond, what does 'trans' mean for two identical substituents?
bank.a: They are on the opposite side of the double bond
d: They are on the same side
They are attached to the same carbon
bank.why: cis = same side (Z); trans = opposite sides (E), for both double bonds and rings.

bank.q: In a compound with a ring, what does 'cis' mean for two identical substituents?
bank.a: They are on the same side of the ring
d: They are on the opposite side
They are attached to the same carbon
bank.why: cis = same side (Z); trans = opposite sides (E), for both double bonds and rings.

bank.q: In a compound with a ring, what does 'trans' mean for two identical substituents?
bank.a: They are on the opposite side of the ring
d: They are on the same side
They are attached to the same carbon
bank.why: cis = same side (Z); trans = opposite sides (E), for both double bonds and rings.

bank.q: Cis and trans correspond to which letters?
bank.why: Z (zusammen, together) and E (entgegen, opposite).

bank.q: Why can 1,1-dichloroethene (shown) NOT exhibit cis-trans isomerism?
bank.a: One double-bond carbon carries two identical substituents
bank.why: Both Cl on one carbon (and both H on the other).

bank.q: Which pair is used in the slides as an example of geometric isomers?
bank.why: Also cis- and trans-1,2-dichlorocyclohexane.

bank.q: Which compound can show cis-trans isomerism?
bank.why: 1,2-Dichloroethene: each C=C carbon has two different groups (H and Cl).
bank.hint: Two different groups on each end.

bank.q: The isomer of 2-butene shown is...
bank.why: Both CH₃ groups are on the same side of the C=C.

bank.q: The fatty acid shown (an octadecenoic acid) is the...
bank.why: The chain continues on opposite sides of the C=C (elaidic acid). Its cis isomer, oleic acid, is bent.
bank.hint: Follow the chain across the C=C.

bank.q: A C=C has two identical substituents on one of its carbons. Which conclusion is correct?
bank.a: It cannot show cis-trans isomerism at that double bond
d: It cannot have any stereoisomers of any kind
bank.why: Swapping the two identical groups gives the same molecule.

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: Cis-trans isomerism can occur in rings as well as at double bonds.
d: Cis-trans isomers interconvert by rotation around single bonds.
bank.why: Rings restrict rotation too (cis/trans-1,2-dichlorocyclohexane).

bank.q: Conformational isomers interconvert by...
bank.why: No bonds break; they are different shapes of the same molecule.

bank.q: Which two conformations of cyclohexane are shown in the slides?
bank.why: Ethane's are staggered and eclipsed.

bank.q: Which two conformations of ethane are shown in the slides?
bank.why: Staggered: H's spread out. Eclipsed: H's line up.

bank.q: Which cyclohexane conformation is more stable, and why?
d: Boat, because the H's line up
bank.why: The chair is the one found in nature, especially in carbohydrates.

bank.q: Which ethane conformation is more stable?
bank.a: Staggered, because the H atoms are spread out and repulsion is minimized
d: Eclipsed, because the H atoms line up
bank.why: In eclipsed, H's align and repel more.

bank.q: The chair conformation is common in nature, especially in...
bank.why: Glucose rings adopt chairs.

bank.q: Which statement best distinguishes conformational isomers from geometric isomers?
bank.a: Conformational isomers interconvert by rotation around single bonds; geometric isomers cannot
d: Conformational isomers have different molecular formulas
Geometric isomers are always mirror images
bank.why: Geometric isomers need a bond to break (C=C) to interconvert.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: The eclipsed conformation of ethane is more stable than the staggered one.
d: The chair is more stable than the boat.
Chair and boat are conformations of cyclohexane.
bank.why: Staggered is more stable.

bank.q: A chiral object is one whose mirror image is...
bank.a: Non-superimposable (it has left- and right-handed forms)
bank.why: Like your hands. Achiral objects have superimposable mirror images.

bank.q: An achiral object has a mirror image that is...
bank.why: e.g. a plain ball or cup.

bank.q: A chiral center is typically...
bank.a: A carbon atom bonded to four different groups
d: A carbon bonded to four identical groups
Any carbon in a double bond
bank.why: Optical isomers usually arise from a chiral center.

bank.q: Optical isomers are...
bank.a: Stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images
d: Shapes that differ by single-bond rotation
bank.why: Same formula and connectivity, different 3-D arrangement.

bank.q: Dextrorotatory (+) means the isomer rotates plane-polarized light...
bank.why: Levorotatory (−) is counterclockwise.

bank.q: Levorotatory (−) means rotation of plane-polarized light...
bank.why: Laevus = left.

bank.q: Using 2ⁿ, how many stereoisomers can a molecule with three chiral centers have at most?
bank.why: 2³ = 8 (the slides' n = 3 example).

bank.q: How many enantiomers does a molecule with one chiral center have?
bank.why: 2¹ = 2: a pair of mirror images.

bank.q: How many chiral centers does 2-butanol (shown) have?
bank.why: Look for carbons with four different groups: 2-butanol has 1.

bank.q: How many chiral centers does 2-methylbutane (shown) have?
bank.why: Look for carbons with four different groups: 2-methylbutane has 0.

bank.q: How many chiral centers does alanine (shown) have?
bank.why: Look for carbons with four different groups: alanine has 1.

bank.q: How many chiral centers does ephedrine (shown) have?
bank.why: Look for carbons with four different groups: ephedrine has 2. Maximum stereoisomers = 2^2 = 4.

bank.q: How many chiral centers does open-chain glucose (shown) have?
bank.why: Look for carbons with four different groups: open-chain glucose has 4. Maximum stereoisomers = 2^4 = 16.

bank.q: How many chiral centers does ibuprofen (shown) have?
bank.why: Look for carbons with four different groups: ibuprofen has 1.

bank.q: Open-chain glucose has 4 chiral centers. How many stereoisomers are possible at most?
Which compound is chiral?
bank.why: 2-Chlorobutane: C2 bears H, Cl, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃, four different groups. The others have two identical groups on every carbon.

bank.q: Which carbon is a chiral center?
bank.a: A carbon bonded to H, OH, CH₃ and COOH
d: A carbon bonded to two CH₃ groups, H and OH
A CH₂ carbon in a chain
A carbon in a C=C double bond
bank.why: Lactic acid's central carbon has four different groups.

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: A molecule with n chiral centers can have up to 2ⁿ stereoisomers.
d: Achiral objects have non-superimposable mirror images.
A chiral center has two identical groups.
bank.why: Achiral = superimposable; dextro = clockwise; a chiral center has four different groups.

bank.q: Enantiomers are...
bank.a: Non-superimposable mirror images of each other
d: Isomers differing in a functional group's position
bank.why: Stereoisomers are either enantiomers or diastereomers.

bank.q: Which is true of a pair of enantiomers?
bank.a: Same formula, connectivity and physical properties, but they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions
bank.why: One is (+), the other (−).

bank.q: Diastereomers are...
bank.a: Stereoisomers that are not mirror images and not superimposable
d: Isomers differing only in the carbon skeleton
bank.why: Common when there are two or more chiral centers.

bank.q: Compared with enantiomers, diastereomers generally have...
bank.a: Noticeably different physical and chemical properties
bank.why: Different boiling points, solubility and reactivity.

bank.q: Two stereoisomers are non-superimposable mirror images. Their relationship is...
bank.why: Definition.

bank.q: Two stereoisomers are not mirror images of each other. They are...
bank.why: Definition.

bank.q: According to the slides, (S)-(+)-lactic acid and (R)-(−)-lactic acid come from...
bank.why: Specific rotations +13.5° and −13.5°: equal and opposite, as for any enantiomers.

bank.q: One enantiomer has a specific rotation of +13.5°. The other enantiomer's specific rotation is...
bank.why: Enantiomers rotate light by equal amounts in opposite directions.

bank.q: The slides' methamphetamine example shows that enantiomers can...
bank.a: Have very different effects in the body: l-(R) is in Vicks inhaler, d-(S) is the illegal drug
bank.why: Same physical properties, different biological activity.

bank.q: What is the relationship between the two lactic acid structures shown?
bank.why: One chiral center, opposite configuration: non-superimposable mirror images.

bank.q: What is the relationship between the two structures shown?
bank.why: Two chiral centers: one is the same, the other is flipped. Stereoisomers that are not mirror images = diastereomers.

bank.q: What is the relationship between the two structures shown?
bank.why: Both chiral centers are flipped: mirror images, so enantiomers.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: Enantiomers have different boiling points and densities.
d: Enantiomers rotate light in opposite directions.
Diastereomers are common when there are two or more chiral centers.
bank.why: Enantiomers share the same physical properties except the direction of optical rotation.

bank.q: The melting point of a substance is the temperature at which...
bank.a: Its solid and liquid phases exist in equilibrium
bank.why: Boiling point is liquid → gas.

bank.q: A pure crystalline organic substance usually...
bank.a: Has a sharp melting point and melts completely over a short range
bank.why: A narrow range is a sign of purity.

bank.q: How do impurities usually affect a melting point?
bank.a: They lower the melting point and broaden the range
d: They raise it and narrow the range
bank.why: A broad, low range suggests an impure sample.

bank.q: According to the experiment, the melting point of a pure substance is influenced by...
bank.a: The electrostatic and intermolecular forces holding its particles, and its size
bank.why: Stronger forces and bigger molecules → higher MP.

bank.q: In the capillary method, the sample is...
bank.a: Finely powdered and packed into a capillary sealed at one end
d: Poured as a liquid into an open tube
bank.why: The powder sits at the sealed end.

bank.q: The capillary is fastened to a ___ and heated in a ___.
bank.why: Stirring keeps the temperature even.

bank.q: T₁ in the melting-point experiment is the temperature at which the sample...
bank.why: T₂ is when it is completely liquefied.

bank.q: T₂ is the temperature at which the sample...
bank.why: Range = T₁ to T₂.

bank.q: The width of the melting range is...
bank.why: Final minus onset.

bank.q: Benzoic acid: T₁ = 122 °C and T₂ = 124 °C. What is the width of its melting range?
Salicylic acid: T₁ = 157 °C and T₂ = 159 °C. What is the width of its melting range?
A sample: T₁ = 80 °C and T₂ = 86 °C. What is the width of its melting range?
Oxalic acid: T₁ = 100 °C and T₂ = 102 °C. What is the width of its melting range?
T₁ = 135 °C and ΔT = 3 °C. What is T₂?
bank.why: T₂ = T₁ + ΔT.

bank.q: Oxalic acid melted from 100 °C (T₁) to 102 °C (T₂). How is its melting range written?
bank.why: From T₁ to T₂.

bank.q: Sample X melts at 121-122 °C and sample Y at 115-121 °C. Both should be benzoic acid. Which is purer?
bank.a: X, because its range is narrow and close to the true value
d: Y, because its range is wider
bank.why: Impurities lower and broaden the range (Y).

bank.q: Which statement from the experiment's pretest is TRUE?
bank.a: Both the size of the molecule and the strength of the forces affect its melting point.
d: A pure crystalline organic substance melts over a wide range.
Stronger forces generally give a lower melting point.
