Melting point is where liquid and gas are in equilibrium.
bank.why: Pretest 5 items: 1 T, 2 F, 3 T, 4 F, 5 T.

bank.q: The three factors affecting melting point in the experiment are...
bank.a: The bond holding the particles, intermolecular forces, and molecular size
bank.why: Bond type, IMFs, size.

bank.q: Why do ionic compounds generally have higher melting points than covalent (molecular) compounds?
bank.a: Ionic bonds are stronger than the intermolecular forces holding molecules together
d: Covalent compounds have stronger bonds between molecules
bank.why: Melting a molecular solid only overcomes IMFs, not covalent bonds.

bank.q: Which has the highest melting point: NaCl (801 °C), CaF₂ or CaO?
bank.a: CaO (2580 °C), with doubly charged Ca²⁺ and O²⁻
bank.why: Ions with multiple charges attract more strongly: NaCl 801, CaF₂ 1180, CaO 2580 °C.

bank.q: The order of common intermolecular forces from strongest to weakest is...
bank.why: So polar molecules melt higher than nonpolar ones.

bank.q: Intramolecular forces are ___, while intermolecular forces are ___.
bank.a: Within a compound (bonds, about 920 kJ/mol for H–O–H); between particles (about 40.7 kJ/mol to boil water)
d: Only in gases; only in solids
bank.why: Intramolecular forces decide stability; intermolecular forces decide the phase at room temperature.

bank.q: Which forces determine whether a compound is a solid, liquid or gas at room temperature?
bank.why: Breaking H₂O molecules apart takes 920 kJ/mol; just separating them (boiling) takes 40.7 kJ/mol.

bank.q: An ion-dipole force is an attraction between...
bank.a: An ion and a polar molecule
d: Two ions of the same charge
bank.why: e.g. Na⁺ with water.

bank.q: Dipole-dipole interactions occur between...
bank.a: Polar molecules, lining up positive and negative ends
bank.why: The more polar the molecules, the stronger the attraction.

bank.q: As the polarity of molecules increases, dipole-dipole interactions...
bank.why: Greater polarity, greater strength.

bank.q: Hydrogen bonds form when H is covalently bonded to...
bank.a: A small, highly electronegative atom: F, O or N
bank.why: Only F, O and N.

bank.q: Why are hydrogen bonds unusually strong dipole-dipole interactions?
bank.a: H is left with a large partial positive charge and is small enough to approach a lone pair closely
d: H has the largest atomic radius
bank.why: The two factors in the slides.

bank.q: Which statement about London dispersion forces is correct?
bank.a: All molecules have them; they are the only force in small nonpolar molecules
d: They are stronger than every hydrogen bond
bank.why: Small nonpolar molecules are usually gases at room temperature.

bank.q: The more electrons a molecule or atom has, the dispersion forces become...
bank.why: Bigger electron clouds polarize more easily.

bank.q: Why do alcohols hydrogen-bond more strongly than amines?
bank.a: O–H is more polar than N–H
d: N is more electronegative than O
bank.why: Oxygen is more electronegative.

bank.q: Ethanol and dimethyl ether (shown) are both C₂H₆O. Which has the higher boiling point, and why?
bank.a: Ethanol, because its –OH forms hydrogen bonds
d: Dimethyl ether, because it is more branched
They boil at the same temperature
Dimethyl ether, because it has more oxygen
bank.why: Hydrogen bonding increases the attractions between ethanol molecules.

bank.q: Why are the melting and boiling points of carboxylic acids very high?
bank.a: Strong hydrogen bonds between their molecules
bank.why: –COOH has both a C=O and an O–H.

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: Nonpolar molecules generally have higher melting points than polar molecules of similar size.
d: Ionic bonds are stronger than typical intermolecular forces.
Hydrogen bonds involve H bonded to F, O or N.
bank.why: Polar molecules have extra dipole forces, so they usually melt higher.

bank.q: How does the experiment estimate the size of a molecule?
bank.why: Larger size → higher MP, when the forces are the same.

bank.q: With the same kind of intermolecular forces, a larger molecule generally has a ___ melting point because of ___.
bank.a: Higher; more surface area in contact
bank.why: More contact = more attraction.

bank.q: A homologous series is a group of compounds in which each successive member differs by...
bank.why: e.g. methane, ethane, propane...

bank.q: As the carbon chain gets longer in a homologous series, the melting and boiling points...
bank.why: Methane bp −164 °C ... decane bp 174 °C.

bank.q: Which unbranched alkane in the table has the highest boiling point (174 °C) and melting point (−30 °C)?
bank.why: The longest chain listed.

bank.q: Increasing branching in an alkane makes the molecule more ___ and ___ its boiling point.
bank.why: Less surface area, weaker dispersion forces.

bank.q: Which C₆H₁₄ isomer has the lowest boiling point?
bank.why: 2,2-Dimethylbutane, the most branched (bp 49.7 °C). Hexane is highest (68.7 °C).

bank.q: Which C₆H₁₄ isomer has the highest boiling point?
bank.why: The unbranched isomer has the most surface area.

bank.q: Which is the safest statement about the melting points of the C₆H₁₄ isomers?
bank.a: They differ, but they do not follow a simple 'more branching = lower melting point' rule
d: More branching always lowers the melting point
They all have the same melting point
bank.why: 2-Methylpentane melts lowest (−154 °C), not the most-branched 2,2-dimethylbutane (−98 °C). The branching rule in the slides is for boiling point.

bank.q: Which C₆H₁₄ isomer has the lowest listed melting point?
bank.why: From the experiment's table.

bank.q: Hexane's boiling and melting points in the C₆H₁₄ table are...
bank.why: The others belong to 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane and 2,2-dimethylbutane.

bank.q: Which statement is TRUE?
bank.a: Within a homologous series, a longer chain usually means higher melting and boiling points.
d: Molecular size has no effect on melting point.
Each member of a homologous series differs by an –OH group.
bank.why: Branching lowers bp; size matters; members differ by –CH₂–.

bank.q: What is the listed melting point of sodium chloride?
bank.why: Sodium chloride (NaCl): 801 °C; ionic bond (ion-dipole forces in water).

bank.q: What is the formula of sodium chloride?
bank.why: Sodium chloride = NaCl.

bank.q: What is the listed melting point of salicylic acid?
bank.why: Salicylic acid (C₇H₆O₃): 158 °C (157-159 °C); two h-bonds (–oh and –cooh).

bank.q: What is the formula of salicylic acid?
bank.why: Salicylic acid = C₇H₆O₃.

bank.q: What is the listed melting point of benzoic acid?
bank.why: Benzoic acid (C₇H₆O₂): 123 °C (122-124 °C); h-bond; bigger molecule than oxalic acid.

bank.q: What is the formula of benzoic acid?
bank.why: Benzoic acid = C₇H₆O₂.

bank.q: What is the listed melting point of oxalic acid?
bank.why: Oxalic acid (C₂H₂O₄): 101 °C (100-102 °C); h-bond; small molecule.

bank.q: What is the formula of oxalic acid?
bank.why: Oxalic acid = C₂H₂O₄.

bank.q: Order the experiment's compounds from highest to lowest melting point.
bank.a: NaCl > salicylic acid > benzoic acid > oxalic acid
bank.why: Ionic NaCl first; among the acids, salicylic has two H-bonding groups; benzoic is bigger than oxalic.
bank.hint: Ionic first, then H-bonds and size.

bank.q: NaCl and salicylic acid are heated side by side. What is observed?
bank.a: Salicylic acid melts first; NaCl melts last
d: Both melt at the same time
bank.why: Ionic bonds (NaCl) vs intermolecular forces (salicylic acid).

bank.q: Salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) is known as...
bank.a: A component of aspirin, a fever and pain reliever used in anti-inflammatory medicines
d: A toxic acid also called ethanedioic acid
An ingredient very soluble in alcohol, called benzene-carbonic acid
bank.why: Molar mass 138.121 g/mol.

bank.q: Oxalic acid is also called...
bank.why: C₂H₂O₄, 90.03 g/mol.

bank.q: Benzoic acid is...
bank.a: A white crystalline carboxylic acid, very soluble in alcohol (C₆H₅COOH)
bank.why: Molecular weight 122.12 g/mol, mp about 123 °C.

bank.q: Which structure is salicylic acid?
bank.why: 2-Hydroxybenzoic acid: –COOH and –OH on neighboring ring carbons. The others are benzoic acid, oxalic acid and phenol.

bank.q: Benzoic acid melts higher than oxalic acid (shown), though both hydrogen-bond. Why?
bank.a: Benzoic acid is the bigger molecule
bank.why: Same kind of force, so size decides (the experiment's explanation).

bank.q: Which statement is FALSE?
bank.a: Salicylic acid melts higher than NaCl because it has two hydrogen-bonding groups.
d: Oxalic acid is the smallest of the three acids.
bank.why: NaCl's ionic bonds are far stronger: 801 °C vs 158 °C.

bank.q: In the reaction 2Fe³⁺ + Sn²⁺ → 2Fe²⁺ + Sn⁴⁺, which species acts as the oxidizing agent?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Fe³⁺ gains an electron (is reduced) to Fe²⁺, so it is the oxidizing agent. Sn²⁺ is the reducing agent.

bank.q: Which reaction represents a disproportionation reaction?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Oxygen in H₂O₂ (−1) is both reduced (to −2 in H₂O) and oxidized (to 0 in O₂).

bank.q: Which salt produces an acidic aqueous solution at 25 °C?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. NH₄⁺ (from the weak base NH₃) donates H⁺ to water; Cl⁻ from the strong acid HCl does not hydrolyze.

bank.q: A student dissolves sodium acetate in water. Which explanation best describes why the resulting solution is basic?
bank.a: CH₃COO⁻ accepts a proton from water, producing OH⁻.
d: Na⁺ reacts with water to produce OH⁻.
CH₃COO⁻ donates a proton to water.
Sodium acetate is a strong base that dissociates to release OH⁻ directly.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Acetate is the conjugate base of a weak acid: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻. Na⁺ does not hydrolyze.

bank.q: Which statement about normality is correct?
bank.a: Normality depends on the reaction and the number of equivalents per mole.
d: Normality is always equal to molarity.
Normality is independent of the chemical reaction involved.
Normality is expressed in moles of solute per kilogram of solvent.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. N = M × equivalents per mole, and the equivalents depend on the reaction (e.g. how many H⁺ react).

bank.q: Which solution has the greatest molality?
bank.a: 0.5 mol of solute dissolved in 0.25 kg of water.
d: 1 mol of solute dissolved in 1 kg of water.
1 mol of solute dissolved in 2 kg of water.
2 mol of solute dissolved in 4 kg of water.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Molalities: A 1 m, B 0.5 m, C 0.5 m, D 0.5/0.25 = 2 m.

bank.q: Which change generally increases the solubility of a gas in a liquid?
bank.a: Increasing the gas pressure above the liquid at constant temperature.
d: Increasing temperature while holding pressure constant.
Decreasing the gas pressure above the liquid.
Adding more solvent without changing the gas pressure.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Henry's law: gas solubility is directly proportional to the gas pressure. Warming lowers it.

bank.q: Which pair of aqueous solutions will form a precipitate when mixed?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s), an insoluble white solid. Nitrates and Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺ salts are soluble.

bank.q: Consider N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g). What happens when the pressure is increased by decreasing the volume at constant temperature?
bank.a: Equilibrium shifts right because the product side has fewer moles of gas.
d: Equilibrium shifts left because the pressure increases.
Equilibrium remains unchanged because pressure does not affect equilibrium.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. 4 mol of gas on the left vs 2 on the right; higher pressure favors fewer moles. K does not change.

bank.q: For CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), what happens when more solid CaCO₃ is added to a system already at equilibrium?
bank.a: The equilibrium position does not change, assuming both solids remain present.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Pure solids have no term in K (K = [CO₂]), so adding one does nothing.

bank.q: For an endothermic forward reaction, increasing temperature will:
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Heat is a reactant in an endothermic reaction, so heating shifts right (and K increases).

bank.q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), which expression represents Kc?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Products over reactants, coefficients as exponents.

bank.q: A reaction absorbs 85 kJ of heat from its surroundings at constant pressure. Which statement is correct?
bank.a: The reaction is endothermic and ΔH = +85 kJ.
d: The reaction is exothermic and ΔH = −85 kJ.
The reaction is exothermic and ΔH = +85 kJ.
The reaction is endothermic and ΔH = −85 kJ.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Absorbing heat = endothermic = positive ΔH.

bank.q: Which statement best explains why carbon forms a large variety of organic compounds?
bank.a: Carbon can form four covalent bonds and stable chains and rings.
d: Carbon readily forms five stable covalent bonds in ordinary organic molecules.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Four bonds plus catenation (chains, branches, rings).

bank.q: Which pair represents functional isomers?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Both C₂H₆O: an alcohol and an ether. Butane/2-methylpropane are skeletal isomers; the others are not isomers.

bank.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a homologous series?
bank.a: Consecutive members differ by a CH₂ unit and share a general functional pattern.
d: Every member has the same molecular formula.
All members have identical physical properties.
All members must have the same number of carbon atoms.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. e.g. methane, ethane, propane... each adds one CH₂. Same formula would make them isomers.

bank.q: Which type of bond is generally the most difficult to rotate around without breaking the bond?
d: A carbon–carbon sigma bond in an alkane.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Restricted rotation about C=C is what causes cis-trans isomerism.

bank.q: Which formula represents an acyclic alkene containing one carbon–carbon double bond?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, one C=C removes 2 H: CₙH₂ₙ. Alkynes are CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.

bank.q: Which compound can exhibit cis-trans (geometric) isomerism?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Each C=C carbon of 2-butene has two different groups (H and CH₃). The others have a C=C carbon with two identical groups.

bank.q: Which reaction is characteristic of alkanes under appropriate conditions?
bank.a: Free-radical substitution with chlorine under ultraviolet light.
d: Electrophilic addition of bromine across a double bond.
Addition of hydrogen across a triple bond.
Hydration of a carbon–carbon double bond.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Alkanes undergo halogenation, a substitution reaction. The rest need a C=C or C≡C.

bank.q: In a redox reaction, oxidation involves an increase in oxidation number.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Oxidation = loss of electrons = oxidation number goes up.

bank.q: The conjugate base of a weak acid can hydrolyze in water and produce a basic solution.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. e.g. CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻.

bank.q: A 1.0 M solution of sulfuric acid is always exactly 1.0 N, regardless of the reaction in which it participates.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. If both H⁺ react, 1.0 M H₂SO₄ is 2.0 N. Normality depends on the reaction.

bank.q: Molality is based on the mass of the solvent, while molarity is based on the volume of the solution.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. m = mol / kg solvent; M = mol / L solution.

bank.q: A catalyst changes the equilibrium constant by lowering the activation energy of the forward reaction.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. A catalyst lowers the activation energy of BOTH directions equally, so K and the position do not change.

bank.q: At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal, but the concentrations of reactants and products do not necessarily have to be equal.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Equal rates, constant (not equal) concentrations.

bank.q: For an exothermic reaction, heat can be treated as a product when predicting the direction of an equilibrium shift.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Exothermic: reactants ⇌ products + heat.

bank.q: If a reaction releases heat to its surroundings at constant pressure, its enthalpy change is positive.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Releasing heat is exothermic: ΔH is negative.

bank.q: The enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the physical states of the reactants and products.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. States matter: forming H₂O(l) releases more heat than forming H₂O(g). That is why thermochemical equations show (s), (l), (g).

bank.q: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different atom connectivity.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Structural = constitutional isomers.

bank.q: Alkanes are generally more reactive toward electrophilic addition than alkenes.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Alkanes have no C=C to add to; alkenes undergo addition.

bank.q: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon in excess oxygen produces carbon dioxide and water.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. CO₂ + H₂O.

bank.q: In acidic solution, consider MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺. What is the coefficient of Fe²⁺ in the balanced equation using the smallest whole-number coefficients?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Mn goes from +7 to +2 (gains 5 e⁻); each Fe²⁺ loses 1 e⁻, so 5 Fe²⁺: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O.

bank.q: What is the molarity of a solution prepared by dissolving 14.6 g of NaCl in enough water to make 500.0 mL of solution? Molar mass NaCl = 58.44 g/mol.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. 14.6 / 58.44 = 0.250 mol; ÷ 0.5000 L = 0.500 M.

bank.q: A 0.250 M H₂SO₄ solution is used in a complete acid-base neutralization where both acidic protons react. What is its normality?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. N = 0.250 × 2 = 0.500 N.

bank.q: What volume of 6.00 M HCl is required to prepare 250.0 mL of 0.750 M HCl?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. V₁ = 0.750 × 250.0 / 6.00 = 31.3 mL.

bank.q: A solution is made by dissolving 18.0 g of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) in 200.0 g of water. What is the molality? Molar mass glucose = 180.0 g/mol.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. 0.100 mol / 0.2000 kg = 0.500 m.

bank.q: A 25.00 mL sample of H₂SO₄ is completely neutralized by 30.00 mL of 0.200 N NaOH. What is the normality of the acid?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. N₁V₁ = N₂V₂: N = 0.200 × 30.00 / 25.00 = 0.240 N.

bank.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), the equilibrium concentrations are [SO₂] = 0.20 M, [O₂] = 0.10 M, and [SO₃] = 0.60 M. Calculate Kc.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Kc = 0.60² / (0.20² × 0.10) = 0.36 / 0.0040 = 90.

bank.q: For a reaction, Kc = 25 and the current reaction quotient is Qc = 5. What will happen as the system moves toward equilibrium?
bank.a: The net reaction proceeds toward the products.
d: The net reaction proceeds toward the reactants.
The system is already at equilibrium.
The equilibrium constant must decrease to 5.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Q < K: too few products, so the reaction goes forward until Q = K.

bank.q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), initially [H₂] = 1.00 M, [I₂] = 1.00 M, and [HI] = 0. At equilibrium, [HI] = 1.20 M. Calculate Kc.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Making 1.20 M HI uses 0.60 M each of H₂ and I₂, leaving 0.40 M. Kc = 1.20² / (0.40 × 0.40) = 9.00.

bank.q: A 100.0 g metal sample at 95.0 °C is placed in 200.0 g of water at 25.0 °C. The final temperature is 29.0 °C. Assume no heat is lost to the surroundings. Specific heat of water = 4.184 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. What is the specific heat of the metal?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Heat gained by water = 200.0 × 4.184 × 4.0 = 3347 J = heat lost by metal = 100.0 × s × 66.0, so s = 0.507 J/g·°C. (The original choices did not include this answer; 0.507 replaces the 1.20 choice.)

bank.q: How much heat is required to raise 50.0 g of water from 20.0 °C to 80.0 °C? Use c = 4.184 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. q = 50.0 × 4.184 × 60.0 = 12,552 J = 12.55 kJ.

bank.q: A hydrocarbon has a molar mass of approximately 56.1 g/mol and follows the general formula CₙH₂ₙ. Which compound is consistent with these data?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. 14.03n = 56.1 gives n = 4: C₄H₈, butene. Butane is C₄H₁₀ and pentene is C₅H₁₀ (70.1).

bank.q: What volume of O₂ at STP is theoretically required for the complete combustion of 2.00 mol of propane? C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Use 22.4 L/mol at STP.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. 2.00 mol × 5 = 10.0 mol O₂ × 22.4 L/mol = 224 L.

bank.q: A weak acid, HA, has a concentration of 0.20 M and a Ka of 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. What is its approximate pH?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. [H⁺] ≈ √(1.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.20) = 1.4 × 10⁻³ M, pH 2.85. (The original choices did not include 2.85; it replaces 5.00.)

bank.q: A gas occupies 2.50 L at 300 K and 1.20 atm. What volume will it occupy at 450 K and 0.800 atm?
Which pair represents constitutional isomers?
d: Two identical molecules drawn in different orientations
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Different connectivity (alcohol vs ether). cis/trans are stereoisomers; conformations are the same compound.

bank.q: A 25.00 mL sample of 0.120 M HCl is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. What volume of NaOH is required to reach the equivalence point?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. 25.00 × 0.120 / 0.100 = 30.0 mL.

bank.q: A buffer contains equal concentrations of CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻. If the pKa of CH₃COOH is 4.76, what is the buffer pH?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa.

bank.q: A gas mixture contains 2.0 mol N₂ and 1.0 mol O₂ at a total pressure of 900 mmHg. Assuming ideal behavior, what is the partial pressure of O₂?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. O₂ is 1/3 of the moles: 900 × 1/3 = 300 mmHg.

bank.q: Which compound exhibits geometric (cis–trans or E/Z) isomerism?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Each C=C carbon of 2-butene has two different groups.

bank.q: At the equivalence point of a titration between a weak acid and a strong base, the solution is generally:
bank.a: Basic because the conjugate base hydrolyzes water.
d: Acidic because the original acid was weak.
Always at pH 7.00 regardless of temperature.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. A⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HA + OH⁻.

bank.q: A gas occupies 4.00 L at 27°C. At constant pressure, what will its volume be at 127°C?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. 4.00 × 400/300 = 5.33 L (kelvin!). 16.9 L comes from using °C.

bank.q: Which change would most likely produce a broader observed melting range for a pure organic compound during an experimental measurement?
d: Using a slower heating rate near the melting point
Packing the sample uniformly and using a small quantity
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Fast heating makes the thermometer lag behind the sample, widening the observed range.

bank.q: A weak base B has Kb = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶. What is the approximate pH of a 0.10 M solution of B at 25°C?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. [OH⁻] ≈ √(4.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.10) = 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ M; pOH 3.20; pH 10.80. (The original choices did not include 10.80; it replaces 5.70.)

bank.q: Which statement about enantiomers is correct?
bank.a: They are nonsuperimposable mirror images and generally have identical melting points in an achiral environment.
d: They always have different melting points in an achiral environment.
They must have different molecular formulas.
They differ only by rotation around a single bond.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Same physical properties except the direction of optical rotation.

bank.q: A gas occupies 6.0 L at 2.0 atm. If temperature and amount remain constant, what pressure will it exert when compressed to 1.5 L?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. P₂ = 2.0 × 6.0 / 1.5 = 8.0 atm.

bank.q: Which indicator is generally most appropriate for a titration between a weak acid and a strong base?
bank.a: Phenolphthalein, whose transition range is approximately pH 8.2–10.0
d: An indicator that changes color near pH 2
An indicator that changes color near pH 5
An indicator that changes color only at pH 7.00
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. The equivalence point is basic, so the indicator should change above 7.

bank.q: A buffer has pH 5.76 and the acid's pKa is 4.76. What is the ratio [A⁻]/[HA]?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. log(ratio) = 1, ratio = 10.

bank.q: Which pair consists of stereoisomers but not constitutional isomers?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Same connectivity, different arrangement around the C=C.

bank.q: A 0.500 mol gas sample is held in a 10.0 L container at 27°C. What is its approximate pressure? Use R = 0.08206 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. P = 0.500 × 0.08206 × 300 / 10.0 = 1.23 atm.

bank.q: Why does contamination commonly lower the melting point of a crystalline organic compound?
bank.a: It disrupts the regular crystal lattice, often lowering the temperature at which the solid begins to melt.
d: It converts the compound into a constitutional isomer.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Impurities lower and broaden the melting range.

bank.q: A 50.0 mL sample of 0.100 M weak acid HA is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. At the half-equivalence point, which relationship applies?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Half the HA has become A⁻, so pH = pKa.

bank.q: A solution contains 0.20 M NH₃ and 0.10 M NH₄Cl. Given pKb(NH₃) = 4.75, what is the approximate pH at 25°C?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. pKa(NH₄⁺) = 9.25; pH = 9.25 + log(0.20/0.10) = 9.55.

bank.q: A 20.0 mL aliquot of an unknown monoprotic acid requires 24.0 mL of 0.150 M NaOH to reach equivalence. Assuming a 1:1 reaction, what is the acid concentration?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. 0.150 × 24.0 / 20.0 = 0.180 M.

bank.q: A student prepares two 0.10 M solutions, one of HCl and one of a weak acid HA. The student claims both solutions must have the same pH because their concentrations are equal. Which response is best?
bank.a: Incorrect, because HCl ionizes essentially completely while HA ionizes only partially.
d: Correct, because pH depends only on concentration.
Correct, because all acids have the same Ka.
Incorrect, because weak acids cannot donate protons.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. The weak acid makes less H⁺, so its pH is higher.

bank.q: During titration of an unknown acid, a student overshoots the endpoint by adding excess NaOH. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
bank.a: The calculated acid concentration will be overestimated if the excess volume is used as the endpoint volume.
d: The calculated acid concentration will generally be underestimated if the excess volume is used as the endpoint volume.
The endpoint and equivalence point are always identical, so the error is irrelevant.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. C(acid) = C(NaOH) × V(NaOH) / V(acid): too much V(NaOH) makes the acid look more concentrated. (Bea's choice A had the direction backwards; B is reworded.)

bank.q: A sealed, rigid container of gas is heated from 300 K to 600 K. What happens to its pressure if the gas behaves ideally and its amount remains constant?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Gay-Lussac: P ∝ T at constant volume.

bank.q: A student argues that all compounds with the same molecular formula must have the same melting point. Which example most directly disproves this claim?
bank.a: Two constitutional isomers with different molecular structures and crystal packing.
d: Two identical samples measured with different thermometers.
A gas measured at two different pressures.
Two samples of the same pure polymorph.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. e.g. the C₆H₁₄ isomers all melt at different temperatures.

bank.q: An unknown organic compound melts over a broad range and begins melting below the expected temperature. Which interpretation is most reasonable?
bank.a: The sample may contain impurities, although measurement technique and heating rate should also be checked.
d: The sample is definitely a new compound.
The sample must be enantiomerically pure.
The compound's molecular formula has necessarily changed.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Broad and low = likely impure.

bank.q: A buffer initially contains equal amounts of HA and A⁻. A small amount of strong base is added. Which process best explains the buffer's resistance to a large pH change?
bank.a: HA reacts with added OH⁻ to form A⁻ and water.
d: A⁻ reacts with added OH⁻ to form HA.
All added OH⁻ remains free in solution.
The acid's Ka increases to compensate.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. The weak acid neutralizes added base.

bank.q: Equal numbers of moles of two ideal gases are placed in separate identical containers at the same temperature and pressure. Which statement is true?
bank.a: The gases have equal volumes under these conditions.
d: The gases must have equal masses.
The gases must have different volumes.
The heavier gas has a higher ideal-gas pressure.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Avogadro: equal moles at the same T and P occupy equal volumes.

bank.q: A student measures the melting point of a compound using a large, tightly packed sample and heats it rapidly. The observed melting range is wider than expected. What is the best improvement?
bank.a: Use a small, uniformly packed sample and heat slowly near the expected melting point.
d: Use more sample and heat faster.
Grind the sample less and increase the heating rate.
Ignore the melting range and report only the first visible change.
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. Small, even, finely powdered sample; slow heating near the melting point.

bank.q: A weak acid is titrated with a strong base. At the half-equivalence point, the student measures a pH of 4.20. Assuming ideal behavior and negligible activity effects, what is the best inference?
bank.why: From Bea's practice exam. At half-equivalence, pH = pKa.

bank.q: A 0.150 M monoprotic weak acid has Ka = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵. What is its pH?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. Ka > 10⁻⁵, so solve x² + Ka·x − Ka·C = 0: x = [H⁺] = 0.00192 M, pH = 2.72.

bank.q: For that 0.150 M acid (Ka = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵), what is the percent ionization?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. 0.00192 / 0.150 × 100 = 1.28%.

bank.q: A 1.00 L buffer has 0.250 mol CH₃COOH and 0.150 mol CH₃COONa (pKa = 4.76). What is its pH?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. pH = 4.76 + log(0.150/0.250) = 4.54.

bank.q: 0.0200 mol HCl is added to that buffer (0.250 mol CH₃COOH, 0.150 mol CH₃COONa, pKa 4.76). What is the new pH?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. H⁺ converts acetate to acetic acid: 0.130 mol A⁻, 0.270 mol HA; pH = 4.76 + log(0.130/0.270) = 4.44. In pure water, 0.0200 M HCl would give pH 1.70.

bank.q: A 0.0800 M methylamine (CH₃NH₂) solution has Kb = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴. What is its pH?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. Kb is large, so use the quadratic: [OH⁻] = 0.00572 M, pOH 2.24, pH 11.76.

bank.q: What is the percent ionization of 0.0800 M methylamine (Kb = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴)?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. 0.00572 / 0.0800 × 100 = 7.1% (the shortcut √(KbC) would give 7.4%).

bank.q: A 40.00 mL sample of 0.125 M HA is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. What volume of NaOH reaches equivalence?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. 40.00 × 0.125 / 0.100 = 50.00 mL.

bank.q: In that titration (40.00 mL of 0.125 M HA, Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵, with 0.100 M NaOH), what is the pH after 25.00 mL of NaOH?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. 25.00 mL is half of 50.00 mL: half-equivalence, so [HA] = [A⁻] and pH = pKa = 5.00.

bank.q: 35.00 mL of 0.180 M HCl is mixed with 20.00 mL of 0.200 M NaOH. What is the final pH?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. H⁺ 6.30 mmol − OH⁻ 4.00 mmol = 2.30 mmol H⁺ left (NaOH limiting) in 55.00 mL = 0.0418 M; pH 1.38.

bank.q: A 25.00 mL sample of a monoprotic acid needs 31.60 mL of 0.0850 M NaOH to reach equivalence. What is the acid concentration?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. CₐVₐ = C_bV_b: 0.0850 × 31.60 / 25.00.

bank.q: From only the equivalence volume of a weak acid titration, can you calculate the acid's Ka?
bank.a: No; you need pH data, such as the pH at half-equivalence
d: Yes; Ka equals the NaOH volume
Yes, but only for strong acids
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. The equivalence volume gives moles only. pH at half-equivalence = pKa.

bank.q: A gas occupies 3.20 L at 745 mmHg and 22°C. It moves to 810 mmHg and 85°C. What is its new volume?
A 0.842 g sample of a volatile compound occupies 325 mL at 98.0 kPa and 95°C. What is its molar mass? (R = 8.314 L·kPa/(mol·K))
H₂ is collected over water at 25°C. The total pressure is 755 mmHg and water's vapor pressure is 23.8 mmHg. What is the pressure of the dry H₂?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. Dalton: P(H₂) = 755 − 23.8 = 731.2 mmHg.

bank.q: That H₂ (731.2 mmHg, 425 mL, 25°C) has what mass? (R = 0.08206, M = 2.016 g/mol)
A vessel holds 4.00 g He and 28.0 g N₂ at a total pressure of 2.50 atm. What is the partial pressure of each gas?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. 1.00 mol He and 1.00 mol N₂: mole fraction 0.500 each, so 0.500 × 2.50 = 1.25 atm each.

bank.q: What is the relationship between cis-2-butene and trans-2-butene?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. Same connectivity, different arrangement at the C=C, and not mirror images.

bank.q: Two nonsuperimposable mirror-image forms of 2-butanol are...
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. 2-Butanol has one chiral center.

bank.q: Two drawings of the same molecule, rotated in space, are...
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. Rotating a drawing does not make a new compound.

bank.q: Samples of one compound melt at A: 121–122 °C, B: 114–121 °C and C: 123–124 °C; the reference melts at 123–124 °C. Which sample most strongly suggests contamination?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. B is both broad and depressed. C matches the reference.

bank.q: Why is a melting range often more useful than a single melting temperature?
bank.a: Its width shows purity: pure samples melt over a narrow range
d: It is easier to read the thermometer once
It gives the boiling point too
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. Impure samples melt lower and over a wider range.

bank.q: 25.00 mL of 0.100 M HA (Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵) is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. What is the pH at the equivalence point?
bank.why: From Bea's problem set. All HA is now A⁻: 2.50 mmol in 50.00 mL = 0.0500 M; Kb = 1.0 × 10⁻⁹; [OH⁻] = 7.1 × 10⁻⁶ M; pH 8.85. (Before NaOH: 3.00; halfway: 5.00.)

Chemical equilibrium is a static state where all chemical reactions completely stop.

The presence of a catalyst alters the position of equilibrium and changes the final equilibrium concentrations.

A reversible reaction has Kc = 4.5 × 10⁵. Does it favor reactants or products, and where does the equilibrium lie?
items.why: Kc > 1 (far from 1): products favored, equilibrium lies to the right.

What is the pH of 2.5 × 10⁻³ M HCl?
items.why: HCl is a strong acid, so pH = −log(2.5 × 10⁻³) = 2.60. A implies a higher H⁺ concentration; C implies a lower H⁺ concentration; D is basic.

items.q: If pOH = 3.25 at 25°C, what is pH?
items.why: pH = 14.00 − 3.25 = 10.75. A repeats pOH; B is neutral; D is not the calculated pH.

items.q: What is [OH⁻] when pH = 11.30?
items.why: pOH = 2.70, so [OH⁻] = 10⁻²·⁷ ≈ 2.0 × 10⁻³ M. A is approximately [H⁺]; C is too high; D is too low.

items.q: What is the pH of 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ M NaOH?
items.why: pOH = −log(4.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.40; pH = 14 − 3.40 = 10.60. A is pOH; B and D do not match the calculation.

items.q: A solution has pH 5.00. What is [H⁺]?
items.why: [H⁺] = 10⁻⁵ M. B is approximately [OH⁻]; C is physically unreasonable; D is Kw, not [H⁺].

items.q: What is the pH of 0.0010 M HNO₃?
items.why: HNO₃ is a strong monoprotic acid, so [H⁺] = 0.0010 M and pH = 3.00. A and B imply higher concentrations; D is basic.

items.q: What is the pH of 0.010 M Ba(OH)₂, assuming complete dissociation?
items.why: Each Ba(OH)₂ produces two OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 0.020 M. pOH ≈ 1.70 and pH ≈ 12.30. A is pOH; B ignores the second OH⁻; D uses 0.010 M OH⁻.

items.q: If pH changes from 4 to 2, [H⁺] increases by what factor?
items.why: A two-unit decrease means a 100-fold increase in [H⁺]. A treats pH linearly; B is one pH unit; D is three pH units.

items.q: At 25°C, which solution is acidic?
items.why: An acidic solution has pH below 7 at 25°C. A is basic; B is neutral; D gives pH 11 and is basic.

items.q: What is the approximate pH of 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ M HCl when water autoionization is considered?
items.why: Accounting for water gives pH ≈ 5.996, slightly below 6. A neglects water; C ignores added acid; D incorrectly predicts a basic solution.

items.q: A 0.10 M weak acid has Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. Approximate its pH.
items.why: [H⁺] ≈ √(KaC) = √(10⁻⁶) = 10⁻³ M, so pH = 3. A assumes complete ionization; B gives too much H⁺; D gives too little.

items.q: A 0.20 M weak acid has Ka = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶. Approximate percent ionization.
items.why: [H⁺] ≈ √(8.0 × 10⁻⁷) = 8.94 × 10⁻⁴ M. Percent ionization ≈ (0.000894/0.20) × 100 = 0.45%. A underestimates; C and D overestimate.

items.q: Which acid is strongest?
items.why: A larger Ka means greater ionization and stronger acid. A, B, and D have smaller Ka values.

items.q: A 0.10 M weak base has Kb = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴. Approximate pH.
items.why: [OH⁻] ≈ √(KbC) = 3.16 × 10⁻³ M; pOH ≈ 2.50, so pH ≈ 11.50. A and B are acidic; C is too low.

items.q: If Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶, what is the conjugate base's Kb at 25°C?
items.why: Kb = Kw/Ka = 10⁻¹⁴/10⁻⁶ = 10⁻⁸. A is too small; C incorrectly equates Ka and Kb; D is Kw.

items.q: What is the pKa of an acid with Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴?
items.why: pKa = −log Ka = 4. A corresponds to Ka = 10⁻²; C to 10⁻¹⁰; D is pKw at 25°C.

items.q: Which acid is strongest based on pKa?
items.why: Lower pKa means larger Ka and stronger acid. B and C are weaker; D is the weakest listed.

items.q: Which expression correctly represents Ka for HA in water?
items.why: Pure liquid water is omitted from the equilibrium expression. B and D reverse the expression; C incorrectly includes liquid water.

items.q: What is the conjugate base of H₂PO₄⁻?
items.why: Removing one H⁺ gives HPO₄²⁻. A is the conjugate acid; C requires losing more than one proton; D is unrelated.

items.q: In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, which is the Brønsted–Lowry acid?
items.why: Water donates H⁺ to NH₃. NH₃ accepts H⁺; NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid; OH⁻ is the conjugate base of water.

items.q: Which salt produces a basic aqueous solution?
items.why: Acetate is the conjugate base of a weak acid and generates OH⁻ by hydrolysis. NH₄Cl and AlCl₃ are acidic; NaCl is approximately neutral.

items.q: What is the approximate pH of 0.10 M sodium acetate if Ka for acetic acid is 1.0 × 10⁻⁵?
items.why: Kb = 10⁻¹⁴/10⁻⁵ = 10⁻⁹. [OH⁻] ≈ √(10⁻¹⁰) = 10⁻⁵ M; pOH = 5 and pH = 9. A is acidic; B ignores hydrolysis; C is too low.

items.q: Which combination forms an effective buffer?
items.why: A weak acid and its conjugate base form a buffer. The other pairs contain strong acids or bases and do not provide an effective conjugate pair.

items.q: A buffer has equal HA and A⁻ concentrations. What is its pH?
items.why: Henderson–Hasselbalch gives pH = pKa + log(1) = pKa. A is not necessarily true; C and D are not the general buffer relation.

items.q: A buffer has pKa = 4.76, [A⁻] = 0.10 M, and [HA] = 0.20 M. Find pH.
items.why: pH = 4.76 + log(0.10/0.20) ≈ 4.46. B assumes equal concentrations; C reverses the ratio; D is unrelated.

items.q: What happens when a small amount of HCl is added to an HA/A⁻ buffer?
items.why: A⁻ reacts with H⁺ to form HA. HA does not consume added H⁺ in the buffer reaction; HCl supplies H⁺; Ka is constant at fixed temperature.

items.q: What happens to acetic acid ionization when sodium acetate is added?
items.why: Added acetate is a common ion and shifts equilibrium toward HA. A is the opposite; Ka does not change at fixed temperature; D overstates the effect.

items.q: A buffer has pKa = 6.35 and [A⁻]/[HA] = 10. What is its pH?
items.why: pH = 6.35 + log 10 = 7.35. A uses the reciprocal ratio; B assumes equal concentrations; D does not follow from the data.

items.q: Which buffer has the greatest capacity if the acid/base ratio is identical?
items.why: Higher total buffer concentration gives greater capacity. A and B contain fewer buffer components; D confuses similar pH with equal capacity.

items.q: A buffer has pKa = 4.80. Strong acid is added, lowering [A⁻]/[HA]. What happens to pH?
items.why: A smaller ratio lowers the logarithmic term in Henderson–Hasselbalch. A is the opposite; C ignores concentration changes; D is unsupported.

items.q: What is the pH at equivalence in a strong acid–strong base titration at 25°C?
items.why: The resulting salt does not appreciably hydrolyze, so pH is approximately 7. A is acidic; C and D describe other titration types.

items.q: At equivalence in a weak acid–strong base titration, pH is generally…
items.why: The conjugate base hydrolyzes to form OH⁻. A is typical of weak base–strong acid; B ignores hydrolysis; D is incorrect.

items.q: At the half-equivalence point of a weak acid titrated with strong base, what is true?
items.why: Half the acid is converted to conjugate base, so [HA] = [A⁻] and pH = pKa. B is not universal; C uses the wrong constant; D is unrelated.

items.q: How much 0.100 M NaOH is needed to neutralize 25.0 mL of 0.100 M HCl?
items.why: The reaction is 1:1 and both solutions have equal molarity, so equal volumes are required. A is half; C is double; D is four times the required volume.

items.q: Which indicator is often suitable for a weak acid–strong base titration?
items.why: Phenolphthalein changes around pH 8.2–10, suitable for many basic equivalence points. The other indicators change too far into the acidic range.

items.q: What is the difference between endpoint and equivalence point?
items.a: Equivalence is stoichiometric completion; endpoint is observed indicator change
items.why: Equivalence is determined by reaction stoichiometry; endpoint is the observed indicator signal. A ignores indicator error; C is incorrect; D confuses observation with stoichiometry.

items.q: A 20.0 mL sample of 0.150 M monoprotic acid is neutralized by 0.100 M NaOH. What volume is needed?
items.why: Moles acid = 0.0200 × 0.150 = 0.00300 mol. Volume base = 0.00300/0.100 = 0.0300 L = 30.0 mL. A and B are too small; D is too large.

items.q: During titration of a weak acid with strong base, what dominates at equivalence?
items.why: The weak acid has been converted to its conjugate base. A ignores neutralization; C describes before equivalence; D requires excess strong base.

items.q: Which condition makes the weak-acid approximation C − x ≈ C least reliable?
items.a: Relatively large Ka, very low concentration
items.why: A larger Ka and low concentration can produce substantial fractional ionization. The other conditions generally make ionization a smaller fraction of initial concentration.

items.q: A buffer initially contains 0.20 mol HA and 0.20 mol A⁻. Add 0.05 mol OH⁻. What are the final moles?
items.why: OH⁻ converts HA into A⁻. HA decreases to 0.15 mol and A⁻ increases to 0.25 mol. A reverses the changes; C and D omit one change.

items.q: If Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴, what is Kb of the conjugate base at 25°C?
items.why: Kb = Kw/Ka = 10⁻¹⁴/10⁻⁴ = 10⁻¹⁰. B is Kw; C is too large; D is too small.

items.q: Which statement about Ka is correct?
items.why: Ka is temperature-dependent. Concentration and common-ion changes shift equilibrium composition, not Ka at constant temperature. D confuses a constant with concentration.

items.q: Why does a weak acid generally have a higher pH than a strong acid at the same initial concentration?
items.a: It ionizes partially and produces less H⁺
items.why: Weak acids ionize incompletely and typically produce less H⁺. A reverses the strength relationship; C is false; D is opposite to strong-acid behavior.

items.q: What is the main error in calculating the pH of 0.10 M weak acid as −log(0.10)?
d: pOH must always be calculated first
items.why: The calculation assumes [H⁺] = 0.10 M, not generally true for a weak acid. A is unnecessary; C is not a general pH equation; D is incorrect.

items.q: A buffer ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes from 1 to 100. By how much does pH change?
items.why: The log term changes from log 1 = 0 to log 100 = 2. A has the wrong direction; B underestimates; D treats a logarithmic change as linear.

items.q: Which is a conjugate acid–base pair?
items.why: NH₄⁺ and NH₃ differ by one proton. The other pairs do not differ by exactly one H⁺.

items.q: Which statement describes a neutral solution at 25°C?
items.why: At neutrality, [H⁺] = [OH⁻], each 10⁻⁷ M at 25°C. A and B are incorrect; D is strongly acidic.

items.q: A weak base has Kb = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. What is pKb?
items.why: pKb = −log Kb = 5. A corresponds to 10⁻²; C to 10⁻⁹; D is pKw, not this base's pKb.

items.q: Which change generally increases buffer capacity?
items.a: Increasing both component concentrations while maintaining their ratio
items.why: Greater total concentrations increase the amount of acid/base neutralized. A lowers capacity; C and D weaken the buffer.

items.q: What best describes the common-ion effect?
items.a: Shifts equilibrium when an ion already present is added
items.why: A is false at fixed temperature; C is not universal; D misunderstands equilibrium. A common ion changes the equilibrium position.

notes: Redox
Oxidation = loss of e⁻, ox# goes up | Reduction = gain of e⁻, ox# goes down | OIL RIG | Both always happen together | Oxidizing agent is reduced; reducing agent is oxidized
Oxidation-number rules
Free element = 0 | Monatomic ion = its charge | O = −2 (peroxides −1) | H = +1 (metal hydrides −1) | Group 1 = +1, group 2 = +2 | Sum = 0 (compound) or the ion's charge
Types of redox

Combination A + B → AB | Decomposition AB → A + B | Single displacement (metal or halogen activity series) | Combustion with O₂ | Disproportionation: one element is both oxidized and reduced (H₂O₂, Cu₂O + H₂SO₄, I₂ + OH⁻)
Half-reactions
Split into oxidation and reduction | Balance atoms, then charge with e⁻ | Multiply so e⁻ lost = e⁻ gained | MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ gains 5 e⁻
Salt hydrolysis

Strong acid + strong base → neutral (NaCl, KBr, NaNO₃) | Strong acid + weak base → acidic (NH₄Cl, FeCl₃, AlCl₃) | Weak acid + strong base → basic (CH₃COONa, NaCN, KF, NaNO₂) | Small, highly charged metal ions (Al³⁺, Fe³⁺) make solutions acidic
Percent
% w/w = g solute / g solution × 100 | % v/v = mL solute / mL solution × 100 (liquid in liquid) | % w/v = g solute / mL solution × 100 (solid in liquid) | Solution = solute + solvent
Molarity and molality
M = mol solute / L of solution | m = mol solute / kg of solvent | 1 M = 1 mmol/mL | Dilution: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ | Density × % → g of solute per liter
Normality

N = equivalents / L of solution = M × valence | EW = MW / valence | Valence: H⁺ given (acids), H⁺ taken (bases), total + charge (salts) | H₂SO₄: N = 2M; H₃PO₄: N = 3M; Al₂(SO₄)₃: valence 6 | N₁V₁ = N₂V₂
Solubility

Maximum solute in a given solvent at a given temperature | Unsaturated < saturated < supersaturated (unstable) | Henry's law: gas solubility ∝ pressure | Most solids: more soluble when hot | Gases: less soluble when hot | Like dissolves like
Units check
mg/dL = g/L × 100 | 0.95 g/L = 95 mg/dL (past quiz: not normal, limit 10.5 mg/dL)
Equilibrium
Forward rate = reverse rate | Dynamic: never stops | Concentrations constant, not necessarily equal | Reachable from either side
K

Products over reactants, coefficients as exponents | Leave out pure solids, pure liquids and the solvent | Kc uses M; Kp uses partial pressures (atm) | Only temperature changes K | K >> 1 products (right); K << 1 reactants (left) | Q < K → forward; Q = K → at equilibrium | Guldberg and Waage, 1864
Le Châtelier

Add → shift away; remove → shift toward | More pressure → fewer gas moles | Equal gas moles → no pressure effect | Endothermic: heat is a reactant | Exothermic: heat is a product | No effect: catalyst, inert gas, pure solids/liquids
Water and pH
Kw = [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C | pH = −log[H₃O⁺] | pH + pOH = 14 | 1 pH unit = 10× [H⁺] | [H⁺] = Kw / [OH⁻]
Acids, bases, buffers

Arrhenius: H⁺ / OH⁻ in water | Brønsted-Lowry: H⁺ donor / acceptor | Lewis: electron-pair acceptor / donor | Amphiprotic: water | Kw = Ka × Kb | Buffer: weak acid/base + its salt | pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) | Blood 7.35-7.45; acidosis from CO₂ build-up, alkalosis from vomiting
Energy

Energy: capacity to do work and transfer heat | Work: moves an object against a force | Heat: raises temperature | Kinetic, potential, radiant, chemical, thermal | Conduction (contact), convection (fluid), radiation (EM waves)
Units
1 J = 1 kg·m²/s² | 1 cal = 4.184 J | 1 Cal = 1 kcal = 1000 cal | KE = ½mv²
Systems
Open: mass + energy | Closed: energy only | Isolated: neither | Thermos = isolated; person in a room = open; air in a tennis ball = closed
Enthalpy and the first law

Energy is not created or destroyed: ΔE(sys) = −ΔE(surr) | ΔE = q + w | At constant P: q = ΔH | ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) | Exothermic ΔH < 0 (released); endothermic ΔH > 0 (absorbed) | State functions: E, P, V, T
Heat math
q = m × s × ΔT | C = m × s | ΔT = final − initial (cooling gives negative q) | Enthalpy stoichiometry: g → mol → × ΔH per mol in the equation | Rocks: 4.9 × 10⁵ J (slide typo says 10⁻⁵)
History
Vital force theory (Berzelius) | Wöhler, 1828: urea from an inorganic salt, ending vitalism | ~85% of compounds are organic | >10 million organic vs ~1.7 million inorganic
Organic vs inorganic
Covalent vs ionic | Low vs high mp/bp | Insoluble vs soluble in water | Flammable vs not | Nonconductor vs conducts in solution
Bonding
C 4 bonds/0 pairs | N 3/1 | O 2/2 | Halogen 1/3 | H 1/0 | sp³ 109.5° tetrahedral | sp² 120° trigonal planar | sp 180° linear | s and p orbitals hybridize
Formulas
Expanded: every bond | Condensed: CH₃CH₂CH₃ | Skeletal: corners and ends are C; H on C not shown
Functional groups
Alcohol –OH | Ether R–O–R | Aldehyde –CHO | Ketone R–CO–R | Carboxylic acid –COOH | Ester –COO–R | Amide –CONH₂ | Amine –NH₂ | Thiol –SH | Alkyl halide C–X
Isomers

Same formula, different structure | Constitutional: skeletal, positional, functional group | Stereo: geometric (cis/trans), conformational, optical | No cis-trans if one C=C carbon has two identical groups
Classes
Saturated: alkanes, cycloalkanes | Unsaturated: alkenes (C=C), alkynes (C≡C), aromatics | Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ | Alkenes, cycloalkanes CₙH₂ₙ | Alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂
Naming

Longest chain (with the C=C or C≡C) | Lowest numbers | di-, tri-, tetra- with commas | Alphabetical, ignoring di-/tri-/sec-/tert- | Ties: alphabetical first gets the lower number | Rings: cyclo-; one group needs no number | Cycloalkene: C=C is C1-C2
Prefixes and groups
meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4, pent 5, hex 6, hept 7, oct 8, non 9, dec 10 | -ane → -yl | isopropyl (CH₃)₂CH– | tert-butyl (CH₃)₃C–
Properties
Nonpolar (C–H ΔEN 0.4) | London forces only | bp rises with size, falls with branching | Insoluble in water, float (≈0.7 g/mL) | Alkenes melt lower than alkanes | cis-2-butene bp > trans
Reactions

Combustion → CO₂ + H₂O | Alkane + X₂ → substitution | Alkene + HX → haloalkane (Markovnikov) | + H₂O/H₂SO₄ → alcohol (Markovnikov) | + Br₂ → dibromoalkane (red → colorless test) | + H₂/Pt, Pd, Ni → alkane (reduction) | Polymerization: monomers → ( )ₙ
Kw and pH
Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ (25 °C) | pH = −log[H₃O⁺], pOH = −log[OH⁻], pH + pOH = 14 | [H₃O⁺] > [OH⁻] acidic (pH < 7) | Strong acid/base: [H⁺] or [OH⁻] = C × number of H⁺/OH⁻ (Ba(OH)₂ gives 2)
Weak acids and bases

Partial dissociation | Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA], no [H₂O] | Kw = Ka × Kb | Bigger Ka (smaller pKa) = stronger | x = √(Ka·C) when K ≤ 10⁻⁵, else quadratic | Degree of ionization = x/C × 100 | 0.0750 M NH₃: [OH⁻] 0.00115 M, pH 11.06, 1.53%
Theories

Arrhenius: H⁺ by ionization / OH⁻ by dissociation | Brønsted-Lowry: H⁺ donor / acceptor, always together | Amphiprotic needs an H and a lone pair (water) | Conjugate pairs differ by one H⁺ | Lewis: acid accepts a pair (BF₃), base donates (NH₃)
Buffers

Weak acid/base + its salt: CH₃COOH/CH₃COONa, H₂CO₃/NaHCO₃, NaH₂PO₄/Na₂HPO₄ | A⁻ eats added H⁺; HA eats added OH⁻ | pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) | Equal amounts → pH = pKa | Common ion lowers ionization | HClO buffer: 7.80, then 8.11 after 0.030 mol NaOH
Titration

Known reagent added to an unknown until a known reaction | vs gravimetric: faster, cheaper, slightly less accurate | Requirements: stoichiometric, quantitative, fast | Uses: hCG pregnancy test, aquarium water, blood sugar, IV drips, food (fatty acids, vitamin C, wine, cheese), anesthetic for lab animals
Terms

Titrant (known, burette) | Analyte (unknown, flask) | Equivalence point: mol H⁺ = mol OH⁻ | End point: indicator changes color | Standard solution | Phenolphthalein: colorless in acid, pink in base | Acidimetry (acid sample), alkalimetry (base sample)
Math
CₐVₐ = C_bV_b only for 1:1 | KHP KHC₈H₄O₄ 204.2 g/mol, monoprotic: mol KHP = mol NaOH | H₂SO₄ needs 2 NaOH | 3Ba(OH)₂ : 2H₃PO₄ | 0.5468 g KHP / 23.48 mL → 0.1140 M NaOH
Pressure
Force per area | 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 760 torr = 101.325 kPa = 1.01325 bar = 14.7 psi | Barometer (atmosphere), manometer (sample) | Caused by collisions with the walls
Laws
Boyle P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ (constant T, n) | Charles V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ (constant P, n) | Gay-Lussac P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂ (constant V) | Avogadro V₁/n₁ = V₂/n₂ | Combined P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ | Always kelvin (°C + 273.15)
Ideal gas
PV = nRT | R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) = 8.315 dm³·kPa/(mol·K) | STP 0 °C, 1 atm: 22.4 L/mol | SF₆ sample: 8.75 atm
KMT and Dalton

Random motion, negligible volume, no attractions, average KE constant at constant T, KE ∝ absolute T (same for all gases at one T) | P_total = sum of partial pressures | N₂ in air sample: 0.808 atm = 614 mmHg
Types
Constitutional: skeletal (chain), positional (regio), functional group | Stereo: geometric, conformational, optical
Geometric
Restricted rotation (C=C or ring) | cis = same side (Z), trans = opposite (E) | None if a C=C carbon has two identical groups
Conformational
Single-bond rotation | Cyclohexane chair (more stable, in carbohydrates) vs boat | Ethane staggered (more stable) vs eclipsed
Optical

Chiral center: C with 4 different groups | Chiral = non-superimposable mirror image | Dextro (+) clockwise, levo (−) counterclockwise | Up to 2ⁿ stereoisomers | Enantiomers: mirror images, same physical properties, opposite rotation (lactic acid ±13.5°) | Diastereomers: not mirror images, different properties
Method

MP: solid ⇌ liquid equilibrium | Pure = sharp, narrow; impure = lower, broader | Powder in a capillary sealed at one end, tied to a thermometer, well-stirred oil bath | T₁ first liquid, T₂ all liquid, ΔT = T₂ − T₁
Factors

Bond type (ionic > IMFs) | IMFs: H-bond > dipole-dipole > dispersion | Size (molar mass, surface area) | Multiple charges raise MP: NaCl 801, CaF₂ 1180, CaO 2580 °C | H-bonds need H on F, O or N | Dispersion in all molecules, stronger with more electrons
Trends

Longer chain → higher mp and bp | Branching → more spherical, lower bp | C₆H₁₄ bp: hexane 68.7 > 3-methylpentane 63.3 > 2-methylpentane 60.3 > 2,3-dimethylbutane 58.0 > 2,2-dimethylbutane 49.7 | Ethanol bp > dimethyl ether
Compounds
NaCl 801 °C (ionic, melts last) | Salicylic acid C₇H₆O₃ 157-159 °C, two H-bonds | Benzoic acid C₇H₆O₂ 122-124 °C | Oxalic acid C₂H₂O₄ 100-102 °C, smallest
